title: Spaghetti al Pomodoro
summary: Spaghetti in a quick sauce of tomatoes, olive oil, garlic and basil, finished in the pan with its own cooking water. It opens the dinner course because it teaches two habits every later dish leans on: reducing a sauce to the right body, and marrying pasta to sauce rather than spooning one over the other.
equipment: Large pot, at least 6 quarts (6 litres)
12 inch (30 cm) skillet or sauté pan, wide enough to toss the pasta
Heatproof measuring jug for pasta water

ingredients.note: San Marzano style if you can; whole tomatoes are better quality than crushed
1/4 cup (60 ml) for the sauce, the rest to finish
peeled and sliced thin, about 1/16 inch (2 mm)
half for the sauce, half torn to finish
bronze cut dried pasta holds sauce best

ingredients.item: Kosher salt for the pasta water

mise: Fill the large pot with 4 quarts (4 litres) of water, cover and set it over high heat.
Tip the tomatoes and their juice into a bowl and crush them by hand to rough 1/2 inch (1 cm) pieces, pulling out any hard stem cores.
Peel and slice the garlic thin and even so every slice cooks at the same speed.
Pick the basil leaves; keep them dry and whole until the last minute so they do not blacken.
Grate the cheese and set a heatproof jug beside the stove for the pasta water.
Weigh the pasta and the salt for the water.

timeline.do: Water on to boil. Crush the tomatoes, slice the garlic.
Garlic into the cold oil, then the tomatoes; start the simmer.
Salt the boiling water and drop the spaghetti.
Scoop out a cup of pasta water. Move the pasta into the sauce two minutes short of done.
Toss over high heat until the sauce clings. Finish off the heat with basil, oil and butter.
Plate in twisted nests and serve at once.

steps.do: Put 1/4 cup (60 ml) of the olive oil and the sliced garlic into the cold skillet, then set it over medium-low heat. Starting cold lets the garlic warm with the oil so it cooks evenly instead of scorching at the edges.
steps.look: After 2 to 3 minutes the garlic sizzles gently with small, steady bubbles, turns soft and pale gold at the edges and smells sweet, not sharp.
steps.mistake: Starting the garlic in hot oil, or walking away, so it turns brown and bitter in seconds.
steps.fix: If any slice goes darker than light gold, tip the oil out, wipe the pan and start again: burnt garlic flavours the whole sauce and cannot be covered.

steps.do: Add the chilli flakes for 10 seconds, then pour in the crushed tomatoes and their juice all at once. They will spit, so stand back. Add 1/2 tsp (3 g) fine salt and 6 whole basil leaves, and raise the heat to bring it to a lively simmer.
steps.look: A loud hiss as the tomatoes land, then steady bubbling across the whole surface within a minute or two.
steps.mistake: Adding the tomatoes slowly, which lets the garlic keep frying and browning while you pour.
steps.fix: Pour in one go; if the garlic darkened while you hesitated, taste and judge whether to start over.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium and simmer uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring and scraping the base every few minutes. Crush any large pieces against the side with the spoon.
steps.look: The sauce reduces by about a third, darkens from bright red to a deeper brick red, and small beads of orange oil gather on the surface. A spoon dragged across the pan leaves a track that slowly closes.
steps.mistake: Boiling it hard so it catches on the base, or pulling it while it is still thin and watery.
steps.fix: If it catches, move it to a clean pan without scraping up the burnt layer. If it is thin, give it 5 more minutes; it should coat a spoon, not run off it.

steps.do: When the sauce has about 12 minutes left, salt the boiling water with the 2 tbsp (24 g) of kosher salt. It should taste pleasantly salty, like a well seasoned soup. Drop in the spaghetti and stir for the first full minute so the strands do not glue together.
steps.look: The water returns to a rolling boil within a minute. The strands soften and sink within 30 seconds.
steps.mistake: Adding oil to the water, or not stirring, so the pasta clumps in a mat.
steps.fix: Separate any clump with tongs immediately; oil in the water only makes the sauce slide off later.

steps.do: Cook the pasta 2 minutes less than the packet says. Bite a strand to check: it should bend but still have a thin, firm, slightly white core. Just before it is ready, scoop 1 cup (240 ml) of the cloudy water into the jug.
steps.look: The cut strand shows a pinpoint of pale core in the centre. The water is milky with starch.
steps.mistake: Cooking the pasta fully in the water, so it goes soft and swollen once it meets the sauce.
steps.fix: If it is already fully cooked, toss it in the sauce for only 30 seconds and use less water.

steps.do: Remove the basil leaves from the sauce. With tongs, lift the spaghetti straight from the pot into the skillet, letting some water cling. Add 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the reserved water and turn the heat to high.
steps.look: The pasta lands with a hiss and the sauce loosens into a glossy, bubbling liquid.
steps.mistake: Draining the pasta in a colander and letting it sit until it sticks and dries.
steps.fix: If it has stuck, loosen it with a splash of hot pasta water before it meets the sauce.

steps.do: Toss and stir constantly for 1 to 2 minutes, lifting the pasta with tongs and shaking the pan, until the sauce thickens and clings to every strand. Add more pasta water a splash at a time if it tightens.
steps.look: The sauce turns from loose and watery to creamy and glossy, coating each strand with nothing pooling in the pan. You hear a soft sputter, not a dry sizzle.
steps.mistake: Leaving the pasta still, or letting the pan dry out so the sauce becomes sticky and dull.
steps.fix: Loosen with 2 tbsp (30 ml) pasta water and keep tossing; starch plus movement is what binds it.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Add the butter if using, the remaining 2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil and half the torn basil, and toss for 20 seconds more. Taste a strand and adjust the salt.
steps.look: The sauce gains a high shine and the basil smells bright and peppery.
steps.mistake: Adding the finishing oil over high heat, which drives off its fresh flavour.
steps.fix: Always finish off the heat. If it tastes flat, add salt a pinch at a time; if sharp, a little more butter softens it.

steps.do: Plate immediately: lift a portion with tongs, hold it over the plate and twist it into a tall nest. Spoon any sauce left in the pan over the top, add the remaining basil and a little cheese.
steps.look: A neat, high nest with sauce on every strand and a little gloss on the plate around it, not a puddle.
steps.mistake: Letting the pasta sit in the pan while you set the table; it keeps absorbing sauce and goes stodgy.
steps.fix: Have warm plates ready before the pasta goes in the sauce. If it has tightened, a splash of pasta water and a quick toss revives it.

science: Tomatoes are mostly water, so a quick sauce depends on evaporation: simmering uncovered drives off water and concentrates sugars, acids and the savoury glutamates tomatoes are rich in. Frying the garlic in oil first matters because many of its flavour compounds dissolve in fat, not water, so the oil carries garlic through the sauce. The magic at the end is starch. Pasta sheds starch into its cooking water, and when that cloudy water meets the oil and tomato over high heat, the starch acts as a binder, holding fat and water together in a light emulsion that clings to the pasta. Finishing the pasta in the sauce also lets each strand absorb flavoured liquid in its final two minutes instead of plain water.
plating: Use a warm, wide, shallow bowl. Twist the pasta into a tall nest in the centre with a carving fork or tongs inside a ladle, spoon the remaining sauce over the top so it slides down the sides, then finish with torn basil, a thread of raw olive oil and a fine snow of Parmigiano. Wipe the rim with a clean cloth before it goes out.

pairing.drink: A young Chianti Classico. Sangiovese has bright acidity that matches tomato rather than fighting it, and light tannin that will not clash with the olive oil.
pairing.brennans: Fattoria di Fèlsina Chianti Classico 2022: the Sangiovese on the list, bright enough for tomato

variations: Pomodoro with fresh tomatoes in high summer: score, blanch 30 seconds, peel and chop 2 lb (900 g) ripe plum tomatoes, and simmer 10 minutes only.
Arrabbiata: double the chilli flakes and leave out the butter and cheese.
Pomodoro e ricotta: dot each plate with a spoon of fresh ricotta at the table.
safety: Carry a full pot of boiling water with both hands and a clear path, or lift the pasta out with tongs instead of draining it.
Tomato sauce spits when it boils; keep your face back and stir with a long spoon.

title: Ratatouille
summary: The Provençal summer stew of aubergine, courgettes, peppers, onion and tomato, with each vegetable browned on its own before they meet. It is in the course because it trains an even 3/4 inch (2 cm) dice and teaches the most useful lesson in vegetable cookery: different vegetables cook at different speeds, so they get separate turns in the pan.
equipment: Heavy pot or Dutch oven, about 4 quarts (4 litres)
Chef’s knife and a large board
Two sheet pans or large plates to hold the browned vegetables

ingredients.note: or one 14 oz (400 g) can whole tomatoes, crushed
used in rounds, a few tablespoons per vegetable

ingredients.item: Herbes de Provence or dried thyme

mise: Wash and dry all the vegetables; wet vegetables spit and steam.
Cut the aubergine into 3/4 inch (2 cm) cubes. Do this first, toss with 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt in a colander and leave 20 minutes to draw out water.
Halve the courgettes lengthways, cut into 3/4 inch (2 cm) strips, then into cubes the same size as the aubergine.
Core and seed the peppers, remove the white ribs, and cut into 3/4 inch (2 cm) squares.
Cut the onion into 3/4 inch (2 cm) pieces. Slice the garlic.
Score the tomatoes with a shallow X, blanch in boiling water 20 seconds, cool in iced water, peel, seed and chop into 1/2 inch (1 cm) pieces, keeping the juice.
Set out two sheet pans to hold each vegetable after browning.

timeline.do: Cut the aubergine and salt it. Cut everything else.
Brown the aubergine, then the courgettes, then the peppers, each on its own.
Soften the onion and garlic in the pot, add the tomatoes and herbs.
Return all the vegetables and stew gently, partly covered.
Taste, adjust salt, tear in the basil and rest.
Serve warm, or chill overnight and serve the next day at room temperature.

steps.do: Pat the salted aubergine dry with a towel, pressing gently. Heat 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers and a cube dropped in sizzles at once.
steps.look: The oil ripples like a heat haze and moves freely when you tilt the pan. The test cube sizzles loudly.
steps.mistake: Adding the aubergine to oil that is not hot enough, so it soaks up oil like a sponge and turns greasy.
steps.fix: Wait for the shimmer. If the aubergine drinks all the oil immediately, do not add more straight away: keep cooking, and it releases the oil as it browns.

steps.do: Add the aubergine in a single layer with space between pieces, cooking in two batches if needed. Leave it untouched for 2 minutes, then turn and cook 6 to 8 minutes in total until browned on several sides and creamy inside. Lift onto a sheet pan.
steps.look: Deep golden brown faces, a sweet roasted smell, and a cube pressed with a spoon yields completely with no squeak.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan so the aubergine steams grey and stays spongy.
steps.fix: Cook in batches. Grey, steamed pieces can go back in a hot pan alone to take colour.

steps.do: Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and the courgettes in one layer. Cook over medium-high heat 4 to 5 minutes, turning once or twice, until browned on two faces but still holding their shape. Season with a pinch of salt and lift onto the sheet pan.
steps.look: Golden patches on the cut faces, edges just softening, the centre still slightly firm when pressed.
steps.mistake: Cooking courgettes until soft in the skillet; they finish in the stew and will turn to mush.
steps.fix: Pull it earlier than you think. If it has gone soft, add it only in the last 5 minutes of the stew.

steps.do: Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and the peppers. Cook 6 to 7 minutes over medium heat, turning occasionally, until the skins blister and the pieces bend. Season lightly and add to the tray.
steps.look: Blistered, slightly charred spots on the skin and a sweet smell. The pieces flop when lifted.
steps.mistake: Undercooking peppers, which then taste raw and green in the finished dish.
steps.fix: Give them the full time; peppers need longer than courgettes.

steps.do: In the pot, heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil over medium heat and cook the onion with a pinch of salt for 8 minutes, stirring often, until soft and translucent. Add the garlic for 1 minute more.
steps.look: The onion is glassy and slumped with only faint gold at the edges; the garlic smells sweet.
steps.mistake: Browning the onion hard; it should be soft and sweet here, a background flavour.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of water if the onion is colouring too fast.

steps.do: Add the chopped tomatoes and their juice, the herbes de Provence and the bay leaf. Simmer 5 minutes, stirring, until the tomatoes collapse into a loose sauce.
steps.look: The tomatoes break down and the liquid turns glossy and orange red.
steps.mistake: Adding the browned vegetables before the tomatoes have cooked down, so the stew is watery.
steps.fix: Let the sauce thicken for a few more minutes first.

steps.do: Return the aubergine, peppers and courgettes to the pot and fold together gently with a wide spoon. Partly cover and simmer on low heat 20 to 25 minutes, folding once or twice.
steps.look: Small lazy bubbles at the edge only. The vegetables keep their shape and the liquid thickens to a glossy, oil-slicked juice.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard, which breaks the vegetables into a common pulp.
steps.fix: Fold from the bottom with a wide spoon and stir as little as possible.

steps.do: Taste a piece of aubergine and a piece of tomato. Adjust the salt and add black pepper. Remove the bay leaf, tear in the basil and drizzle with a little raw olive oil. Rest 10 minutes off the heat.
steps.look: Every vegetable is still recognisable, each seasoned, the herbs tasting cooked and perfumed rather than grassy.
steps.mistake: Serving it piping hot straight from the stove, when the flavours are at their least settled.
steps.fix: Let it rest, or better still, cool and refrigerate overnight and serve it the next day at room temperature.

science: Each vegetable holds a different amount of water and a different cell structure. Aubergine is a sponge of air pockets that soaks up oil until its cells collapse, then releases it again; salting it first draws out water so it browns rather than steams. Courgette is very wet and goes soft quickly, while peppers have tougher skins that need longer heat to soften and sweeten. Browning needs a surface hotter than boiling water, which only happens when moisture can escape: a crowded pan traps steam and holds the vegetables near 212°F (100°C), too cool for the browning reactions that build roasted flavour. Cooking each in its own batch keeps the pan hot and gives every vegetable its own colour and texture before the gentle stew lets their juices mingle.
plating: Serve in a warm shallow bowl or on a plate as a ring with a hollow in the centre. Spoon it rather than pour it so each vegetable stays distinct, finish with whole small basil leaves, a thread of olive oil and a twist of pepper. As a main course, set it beside a soft pile of polenta or a slice of grilled bread rubbed with garlic.

pairing.drink: A dry Provence rosé. Its red fruit and fresh acidity match the sweet peppers and tomato without overwhelming the herbs, and it is the wine of the same hills.
pairing.brennans: Minuty ‘Prestige’ Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024: a Provence rosé on the list, from the same hills as the dish

variations: Baked tian: slice the same vegetables into 1/8 inch (3 mm) rounds, layer them in overlapping rows over the tomato sauce and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 45 minutes.
With eggs: make four hollows in the finished ratatouille, crack in eggs and cover until the whites set, about 6 minutes.
Cold, as the next day’s lunch: on toast with soft goat’s cheese.
safety: Cool leftovers within 2 hours and refrigerate; they keep 4 days.
Hot oil spits when wet vegetables go in: pat everything dry and lay pieces away from you.

title: Pollo al Ajillo
summary: Spanish garlic chicken: small bone-in pieces browned hard in olive oil with whole garlic cloves, then glazed with dry sherry. It is the course’s first real browning and deglazing lesson, and it shows how to cook garlic slowly so it turns sweet instead of burnt.
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) heavy skillet, stainless or cast iron, with a lid
Wooden spoon or flat spatula for scraping
Cleaver or heavy knife if cutting thighs in half

ingredients.note: ask the butcher to cut each in half across the bone, or use thighs whole
about 12 cloves, lightly smashed with the skin left on

mise: Pat the chicken completely dry with paper towels and season both sides with the salt and pepper. Leave it at room temperature for 20 minutes while you prepare everything else.
Smash each garlic clove once with the flat of a knife so it splits but stays in its skin.
Measure the sherry and stock into one jug.
Chop the parsley. Set a plate lined with paper towels by the stove.

timeline.do: Season the chicken, smash the garlic.
Brown the chicken skin side down with the garlic.
Turn the chicken, then deglaze with sherry.
Simmer uncovered, turning, until glazed and cooked through.
Check the temperature, scatter parsley, rest briefly.
Serve from the pan with bread.

steps.do: Heat the olive oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Lay in the chicken skin side down, spacing the pieces so they do not touch. Work in two batches if they will not fit.
steps.look: An immediate, loud, even sizzle the moment each piece touches the pan.
steps.mistake: Putting the chicken into oil that is not hot, so it sticks and stews without browning.
steps.fix: If the sizzle is weak, lift the pieces out, let the oil heat for another minute and start again.

steps.do: Leave the chicken alone for 6 to 8 minutes, adjusting the heat to keep a steady sizzle, until the skin is deep golden and releases from the pan on its own. Do not tug it free.
steps.look: The skin is evenly deep golden brown and comes away cleanly when nudged with tongs. Rendered fat pools around the pieces.
steps.mistake: Moving or turning the chicken too early, tearing the skin and leaving it stuck to the pan.
steps.fix: If a piece resists, give it another minute; skin that is properly browned lets go by itself.

steps.do: Scatter the smashed garlic cloves into the gaps between the chicken pieces after the first 3 minutes, along with the bay leaves. Turn the garlic now and then so it colours evenly.
steps.look: The cloves sizzle gently, their skins bronze and the kitchen fills with a sweet, nutty garlic smell.
steps.mistake: Using peeled or minced garlic, which burns black in the time the chicken takes to brown.
steps.fix: Keep the skins on. If any clove blackens, pick it out so it does not turn the sauce bitter.

steps.do: Turn the chicken skin side up and cook 3 minutes on the second side. If more than 3 tbsp (45 ml) fat has collected, spoon off the excess, keeping the garlic in the pan.
steps.look: Golden flesh side, clear fat bubbling around the pieces, browned bits stuck to the pan floor.
steps.mistake: Leaving a pool of fat, which turns the sherry glaze greasy.
steps.fix: Tilt the pan and spoon fat into a heatproof bowl, leaving the browned bits behind.

steps.do: Stand back and pour in the sherry and stock. Scrape the pan floor hard with the wooden spoon to lift the browned bits (the fond) into the liquid. Add the herb sprigs.
steps.look: A burst of steam and sizzle, then the liquid turns from pale to amber brown as the fond dissolves. The sharp alcohol smell fades within a minute.
steps.mistake: Pouring the sherry over the skin, which softens the crust you worked to build.
steps.fix: Pour into the gaps between pieces, keeping the skin above the liquid.

steps.do: Simmer uncovered over medium heat 15 to 20 minutes, turning the pieces in the sauce every 5 minutes and finishing skin side up, until the liquid has reduced to a few spoonfuls of glossy glaze.
steps.look: Bubbles turn from thin and fast to slow and syrupy, and the sauce coats the chicken in a shine.
steps.mistake: Reducing until the pan is dry, so the glaze burns and the garlic catches.
steps.fix: Add 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) water and scrape; the glaze should be loose enough to spoon.

steps.do: Check the thickest piece with an instant-read thermometer near, but not touching, the bone. It must read at least 165°F (74°C); thighs are at their best at 175 to 185°F (79 to 85°C), when the connective tissue has softened.
steps.look: Juices run clear when pierced and the meat pulls cleanly from the bone.
steps.mistake: Judging doneness by colour alone, which is unreliable near the bone.
steps.fix: If short of temperature, cover with the lid and cook on low 4 to 5 minutes, then check again.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat, remove the herb stalks, scatter the parsley and rest 3 minutes. Serve from the pan with bread, and show your guests how to squeeze the soft garlic out of its skin onto the bread.
steps.look: The garlic cloves are soft enough to squeeze like paste; the glaze clings to the chicken.
steps.mistake: Leaving the garlic underdone and firm.
steps.fix: If cloves are still firm, simmer them a few minutes more in the glaze with a splash of water while the chicken rests.

science: Browning is the Maillard reaction, in which proteins and sugars react above about 285°F (140°C) to form hundreds of new flavour compounds and a deep brown colour. Skin browns well only when it is dry, because surface water must boil off before the temperature can climb; that is why you pat it dry and leave it untouched. The browned residue on the pan floor, the fond, is concentrated flavour, and liquid dissolves it in seconds: that is deglazing. Garlic left in its skin is insulated, so its sugars caramelise slowly while the inside steams to a soft, sweet paste. Peeled garlic has no such protection and its natural sugars burn quickly, turning acrid.
plating: Bring it to the table in the skillet on a board, the pieces skin side up and glistening, the garlic cloves scattered among them and parsley over the top. For individual plates, set two pieces slightly overlapping, spoon the glaze over, add three garlic cloves and a wedge of bread to the side.

pairing.drink: A chilled glass of fino or manzanilla sherry. The same dry, nutty, saline wine that is in the sauce matches the garlic and cuts the richness of the skin.
pairing.brennans: La Cigarrera Manzanilla Sanlúcar de Barrameda NV (375 ml): the dry manzanilla on the list, the same style as the sherry in the pan

variations: With potatoes: add 1 lb (450 g) small waxy potatoes, halved and browned, with the sherry, and simmer until tender.
Pollo al ajillo with chilli: add one dried guindilla or a pinch of chilli flakes with the garlic.
Shrimp al ajillo: the same garlic oil with peeled shrimp cooked 2 minutes, a direct preview of the scampi to come.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point. Use a thermometer.
Wash hands, board and knife with hot soapy water after handling raw chicken, and never put cooked chicken back on the plate that held it raw.
Pour the sherry away from the flame on a gas stove; alcohol vapour can catch.

title: Chicken Piccata
summary: Thin, flour-dredged chicken cutlets sautéed golden, then served in a sharp pan sauce of white wine, lemon and capers mounted with butter. It is here because the pattern of cutlet, fond, deglaze and butter finish is the backbone of brigade cooking, and because a butter sauce teaches the one moment you must take the pan off the heat.
skills: a lemon and caper pan sauce mounted with butter
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) stainless steel skillet (not non-stick, so a fond forms)
Meat mallet or a small heavy pan for pounding
Plastic wrap or a zip-top bag
Tongs and a fish slice or thin spatula
Wire rack set over a sheet pan, in a 200°F (95°C) oven to hold the cutlets

ingredients.note: 1 tbsp (14 g) for cooking, 3 tbsp (42 g) cold and cubed for the sauce

mise: Lay each breast flat and slice it in half horizontally into two thinner fillets, keeping your flat hand on top and the knife parallel to the board.
Put each piece in the bag or between sheets of plastic wrap and pound from the centre outward to an even 1/4 inch (6 mm). Aim for even thickness, not a large shape.
Season both sides with salt and pepper just before dredging.
Put the flour in the shallow dish. Turn the oven on to 200°F (95°C) with the rack and sheet pan inside.
Mince the shallot, juice the lemon, rinse the capers, cube the cold butter and keep it in the fridge until the end.

timeline.do: Butterfly and pound the chicken. Prepare the sauce ingredients.
Season and dredge; heat the pan.
Sauté the cutlets in two batches, 2 to 3 minutes a side; hold them warm.
Shallot, wine, stock: reduce by half.
Lemon and capers in; butter swirled in off the heat.
Cutlets back through the sauce, parsley on, serve.

steps.do: Dredge each seasoned cutlet in flour, pressing lightly so both sides are coated, then lift and tap it firmly to shake off the excess. Dredge just before cooking, not ahead.
steps.look: A thin, even, dusty film with no clumps or bare patches.
steps.mistake: Dredging minutes ahead, so the flour soaks up moisture and turns gummy.
steps.fix: If the flour has gone pasty, re-dredge in fresh flour.

steps.do: Heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and 1 tbsp (14 g) butter in the skillet over medium-high heat until the butter foam subsides and the fat shimmers.
steps.look: The foam settles, the fat smells nutty and a pinch of flour sizzles immediately.
steps.mistake: Starting cold, which glues the coating to the pan.
steps.fix: Wait for the foam to drop and the sizzle test to pass.

steps.do: Lay in two cutlets, away from you. Cook 2 to 3 minutes undisturbed until the underside is golden, then turn and cook 2 minutes more. Transfer to the rack in the warm oven. Add the last 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil and repeat.
steps.look: Golden brown edge to edge with no pale patches; the cutlet feels firm and springy when pressed. Golden brown bits are forming on the pan floor.
steps.mistake: Overcrowding, which steams the coating pale and soggy.
steps.fix: Cook two at a time. If the fond starts going black rather than brown, lower the heat for the second batch.

steps.do: Check one cutlet at its thickest part with the thermometer: it should read 165°F (74°C). Thin cutlets get there quickly and carry a few degrees more as they rest.
steps.look: Opaque white all the way through with clear juices.
steps.mistake: Leaving thin cutlets in the pan to be safe, so they turn dry and stringy.
steps.fix: Trust the thermometer. If a cutlet is short, it can finish in the warm oven for a few minutes.

steps.do: Pour off all but about 1 tsp (5 ml) of fat. Lower the heat to medium, add the shallot and stir 30 seconds until it softens.
steps.look: The shallot sizzles gently and turns translucent, picking up some of the brown fond.
steps.mistake: Burning the shallot in a pan still too hot from the cutlets.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off the heat for 20 seconds if it is smoking before the shallot goes in.

steps.do: Pour in the wine and scrape the floor of the pan hard with a wooden spoon until all the fond has lifted. Boil until reduced by half, about 2 minutes. Add the stock and reduce by half again, 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.look: The liquid turns light brown, the raw wine smell disappears and the sauce looks slightly syrupy. About 1/2 cup (120 ml) remains.
steps.mistake: Not reducing enough, so the sauce is thin and tastes of raw wine.
steps.fix: Keep boiling and measure by eye: the bubbles become larger and slower as it thickens.

steps.do: Add the lemon juice and capers and simmer 30 seconds. Take the pan completely off the heat. Add the cold butter one cube at a time, swirling the pan constantly until each melts into the sauce before adding the next.
steps.look: The sauce turns opaque, creamy and glossy and coats the back of a spoon. No yellow butter oil separates at the edges.
steps.mistake: Adding the butter over live heat or letting it boil, which splits it into a greasy yellow slick.
steps.fix: If it splits, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) cold water or stock off the heat and whisk hard; it often comes back together.

steps.do: Taste: it should land sharp first, then rich. Adjust with salt or a few drops more lemon. Return the cutlets and any resting juices to the pan, turn them once through the sauce and scatter the parsley.
steps.look: Each cutlet wears a thin glaze and the coating stays on the meat, not in the sauce.
steps.mistake: Leaving the cutlets to soak in the sauce, which softens the crust.
steps.fix: Turn them through once and plate at once.

science: The flour does three jobs: it browns faster than bare chicken, it insulates the thin meat from the full force of the pan, and the starch it leaves behind thickens the sauce when the wine goes in. Pounding to an even thickness means every part reaches a safe temperature at the same moment. The butter finish is an emulsion: cold butter melting slowly into a little reduced liquid disperses as tiny droplets, held in suspension by the milk proteins and the flour starch, which is why the sauce turns creamy rather than oily. Heat is the enemy here. Much above about 140°F (60°C) the emulsion breaks, the fat separates from the water and the sauce turns greasy, which is why the butter goes in off the heat.
plating: Warm the plates. Lay two cutlets slightly overlapping on the left of the plate, spoon the sauce over so a few capers land on top, and set a thin lemon slice and a pinch of parsley on each. Add a neat spoon of buttered pasta, mashed potato or sautéed spinach to the right. Keep the sauce on the meat rather than flooding the plate.

pairing.drink: A crisp, unoaked Italian white such as Verdicchio or Pinot Grigio. Its lemony acidity matches the sauce and its lightness respects the delicate chicken.

variations: Veal piccata: the original, with thin veal scaloppine cooked 1 minute a side.
Fish piccata: sole or flounder fillets dredged and cooked 90 seconds a side.
Chicken francese: dip the floured cutlets in beaten egg before frying for a softer, eggy crust.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C). Use a fresh board after pounding raw chicken, and wash the mallet and bag area well.
Discard any flour left after dredging raw chicken; it is contaminated.
When pouring wine into a hot pan, stand back and pour away from you to avoid steam burns.

title: Shrimp Scampi
summary: Shrimp sautéed briefly, then finished in a sauce of garlic, white wine, lemon and butter and tossed with linguine. Shrimp go from tender to rubbery in under a minute, so this dish is the course’s best teacher of doneness by sight, by curl and by colour.
skills: a garlic, wine and butter sauce
equipment: Large pot, at least 6 quarts (6 litres)
Paring knife or kitchen shears for deveining
Bowl of iced water to keep shrimp cold while you peel

ingredients.note: about 16 to 20 per pound (35 to 45 per kg)

ingredients.item: Kosher salt for the pasta water

ingredients.note: zest finely grated, plus 2 tbsp (30 ml) juice

mise: Keep the shrimp cold in a bowl set over ice while you work.
Peel each shrimp, leaving the tail on if you like. Run a paring knife 1/8 inch (3 mm) deep along the back and lift out the dark vein with the tip of the knife. Rinse and pat completely dry.
Optional but worth it: simmer the shells in 1 cup (240 ml) water for 10 minutes and strain for a quick stock to use in place of some pasta water.
Season the shrimp with 1 tsp (6 g) salt and keep them in the fridge.
Slice the garlic, zest and juice the lemon, chop the parsley, cube the cold butter.
Put the pasta water on to boil.

timeline.do: Water on. Peel and devein the shrimp; make the shell stock if using.
Salt the water and drop the linguine.
Sear the shrimp in batches and lift them out underdone.
Garlic and chilli, then wine; reduce.
Pasta into the pan with butter and pasta water; toss.
Shrimp back for the final minute with lemon and parsley.

steps.do: Salt the boiling water and cook the linguine 2 minutes less than the packet time, stirring in the first minute. Reserve 1 cup (240 ml) pasta water before draining or lifting.
steps.look: A pinpoint of firm white core when you bite a strand.
steps.mistake: Fully cooking the pasta in the water, so it goes soft in the sauce.
steps.fix: Shorten the sauce toss if it is already done.

steps.do: While the pasta cooks, heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add half the shrimp in a single layer and cook 1 minute without moving, until the underside turns pink with golden spots.
steps.look: A brisk sizzle; the undersides turn from grey translucent to coral pink.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan, so the shrimp poach in their own liquid and never colour.
steps.fix: Cook in two batches with space between every shrimp.

steps.do: Turn each shrimp and cook 30 seconds more, then lift them onto a plate while still slightly translucent in the centre. Repeat with the rest.
steps.look: The shrimp are pink outside, bending into a loose C, with a grey translucent centre if you cut one.
steps.mistake: Cooking them through now. They will finish in the sauce and turn rubbery if already done.
steps.fix: Pull them early. Underdone at this stage is correct.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium-low, add the remaining 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil, the garlic and chilli flakes. Cook 1 to 2 minutes, stirring, until the garlic is soft and fragrant but has not taken colour.
steps.look: Garlic slices are pale straw coloured and limp, and the oil smells sweet.
steps.mistake: Browning the garlic in a pan still very hot from the shrimp.
steps.fix: Take the pan off the heat for 30 seconds before adding the garlic; if it browns, start the garlic again.

steps.do: Pour in the wine, raise the heat to medium-high and simmer 2 minutes, scraping up any browned bits, until reduced by about half.
steps.look: The sharp alcohol smell fades and the liquid looks slightly thicker.
steps.mistake: Skipping the reduction, so the sauce tastes of raw wine.
steps.fix: Keep reducing; taste a drop and it should be mellow.

steps.do: Add the drained linguine, 1/2 cup (120 ml) pasta water (or shell stock) and the cold butter. Toss continuously over medium heat 1 to 2 minutes until the butter melts into a creamy sauce that coats the pasta.
steps.look: The sauce turns opaque and glossy, every strand slick, no free butter pooling at the edge.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil hard after the butter goes in, so the sauce splits into oil.
steps.fix: If it looks greasy, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) pasta water and toss hard off the heat.

steps.do: Return the shrimp and their juices to the pan with the lemon zest and juice. Toss over low heat for 1 minute only, until the shrimp are just opaque throughout.
steps.look: Each shrimp is a loose C shape, opaque to the centre, the flesh firm with a slight snap when bitten.
steps.mistake: Cooking until the shrimp curl into tight O rings, which means they are overcooked.
steps.fix: If you overshoot, serve at once; the longer they sit in the heat, the tougher they get.

steps.do: Add the parsley, taste and adjust salt and lemon. Plate straight away.
steps.look: The lemon lands behind the garlic, the sauce clings, and the shrimp sit on top in loose curls.
steps.mistake: Holding the dish while you finish other things.
steps.fix: Have the plates warm and the table set before the shrimp go back in.

science: Shrimp muscle proteins set over a narrow range: they turn opaque at around 120°F (49°C), are perfectly tender near 135 to 140°F (57 to 60°C), and squeeze out water and turn tight and rubbery beyond about 150°F (66°C). Because shrimp are small, they cross that range in seconds, and a tight O shape tells you the muscle has contracted too far. Searing them briefly and finishing them in the gentler heat of the sauce gives control. The sauce is a butter emulsion, kept stable by starchy pasta water, which coats the fat droplets and stops them merging. Garlic cooked low and slow keeps its sweetness; brown it and it turns bitter, a flavour impossible to hide in a sauce this light.
plating: Use warm shallow bowls. Twist the linguine into a nest with tongs, arrange five or six shrimp on and around it in loose curls, tails pointing the same way, and spoon the remaining sauce over. Finish with parsley, a little lemon zest and a lemon wedge on the side.

pairing.drink: A crisp Albariño from Rías Baixas. Its saline edge and citrus match the shrimp and lemon, and its acidity cuts the butter.
pairing.brennans: Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025: the Albariño on the list, saline and citrus for shrimp and lemon

variations: Without pasta: serve the shrimp and sauce in a bowl with crusty bread for mopping.
Gulf shrimp scampi with a pinch of Creole seasoning in place of the chilli flakes.
Langoustine or prawn scampi, the original, split in the shell and grilled with garlic butter.
safety: Keep raw shrimp refrigerated below 40°F (4°C) until cooking, and cook them until opaque throughout, which is about 145°F (63°C).
Thaw frozen shrimp overnight in the fridge or in a sealed bag under cold running water, never at room temperature.
Discard any shrimp that smell of ammonia.

title: Garides Saganaki
summary: A Greek taverna dish of shrimp poached in a thick tomato sauce with ouzo, crowned with melting feta and served bubbling in its pan. After scampi, it shows a second way to protect a delicate protein: rather than searing it, you let it cook gently in a sauce, and judge the sauce’s reduction before the shrimp ever go in.
skills: a quick tomato sauce with ouzo
equipment: 10 to 12 inch (25 to 30 cm) ovenproof skillet or two-handled pan with a lid
Small saucepan if making shell stock
Long matches or a lighter if flaming the ouzo (optional)

ingredients.note: peeled and deveined, tails on, shells kept
or one 28 oz (794 g) can whole tomatoes, crushed
broken into large chunks, not crumbs
season lightly; the feta is salty

mise: Peel and devein the shrimp, leaving tails on. Simmer the shells in 2/3 cup (160 ml) water for 10 minutes, strain and keep the liquor.
Halve the tomatoes and grate the cut sides on the large holes of a box grater over a bowl until only the skin is left in your hand. Discard the skins.
Dice the onion fine, mince the garlic, break the feta into 1 1/4 inch (3 cm) chunks.
Pat the shrimp dry and keep them cold.

timeline.do: Peel the shrimp and start the shell stock. Grate the tomatoes.
Soften the onion; add garlic, chilli and tomatoes.
Simmer the sauce until it is thick and the oil rises.
Shrimp in; ouzo over and cooked off.
Feta on, lid on.
Oregano and parsley over; to the table bubbling.

steps.do: Warm the olive oil in the pan over medium-low heat. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and cook 7 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until soft and translucent with no colour.
steps.look: The onion is glassy and limp and smells sweet. No gold at the edges.
steps.mistake: Cooking over high heat so the onion browns; browned flecks taste bitter against the tomato.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of water to stop browning.

steps.do: Add the garlic and chilli flakes and stir 1 minute until fragrant.
steps.look: The garlic softens and the oil turns faintly red from the chilli.
steps.mistake: Letting the garlic colour.
steps.fix: Move straight on to the tomatoes if it begins to colour.

steps.do: Add the grated tomatoes and the shell liquor. Raise the heat to medium and simmer 12 to 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and sweet.
steps.look: The sauce reduces by about half, darkens, and orange oil rises to the surface. A spoon dragged across the pan leaves a track that holds for a moment.
steps.mistake: Stopping while the sauce is thin. The shrimp and the feta release liquid, and a thin sauce turns into a watery pan.
steps.fix: Keep simmering until the track holds; this is the step that decides the dish.

steps.do: Taste and season the sauce lightly with salt, remembering that the feta will add more. Nestle the shrimp into the sauce in one layer and cook 1 minute.
steps.look: The shrimp begin to turn pink at the edges where they touch the sauce.
steps.mistake: Salting fully before the feta goes in, which makes the finished pan too salty.
steps.fix: If it is over salted, add a little unsalted tomato or water and simmer briefly.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and pour the ouzo over. To flame it, return the pan to the heat, tilt it away from you and touch the edge of the liquid with a long match; let the flame burn out on its own, about 10 seconds. Otherwise simply simmer 1 minute to cook off the alcohol.
steps.look: A soft blue flame that dies down by itself, or a fading anise and alcohol smell as it simmers.
steps.mistake: Pouring ouzo from the bottle over a hot pan, which can draw flame back to the bottle.
steps.fix: Always measure into a cup first and pour off the heat. If the flame lingers, cover the pan with the lid to put it out.

steps.do: Turn the shrimp over, scatter the feta chunks on top and cover with the lid. Cook on low heat 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.look: The feta softens and slumps with glossy shoulders, still in chunks; the shrimp are opaque and curled into loose C shapes.
steps.mistake: Stirring the feta in so it dissolves into a grainy pink sauce.
steps.fix: Leave the feta on top and do not stir. If it dissolved, call it a creamy sauce and serve it proudly, but next time leave it alone.

steps.do: Uncover, scatter the oregano (crumble it between your palms to wake it up) and the parsley, and drizzle with a little more olive oil.
steps.look: A bubbling red pan dotted with white feta and green herbs.
steps.mistake: Leaving the lid on longer, so the shrimp overcook in the steam.
steps.fix: Serve straight away.

steps.do: Take the pan to the table on a board with bread. Taste the sauce with a crumb of feta on the spoon: together they should be well seasoned and bright.
steps.look: Anise in the background, tomato sweet, feta salty, shrimp tender.
steps.mistake: Leaving it to sit before serving.
steps.fix: This dish is at its best within minutes.

science: Poaching in a sauce protects shrimp because the liquid never rises above its simmering point, around 200°F (93°C), and the shrimp cook from all sides at once rather than from one scorching surface. The trade is that the sauce must be reduced before the shrimp go in, since shrimp release water as they cook and the closed lid traps more as condensation. Ouzo carries anethole, the aromatic compound that gives anise its scent; it dissolves in fat and alcohol and bridges sweet tomato and salty feta. Feta is a brined cheese whose structure softens with heat but resists fully melting, which is why it slumps into glossy chunks rather than flowing like mozzarella.
plating: Serve in the pan it was cooked in, set on a wooden board, with bread on the side. For plated portions, spoon sauce into a warm shallow bowl, arrange four or five shrimp tails up, set two feta chunks between them and finish with oregano, parsley and a thread of olive oil.

pairing.drink: Santorini Assyrtiko, bone dry with a mineral, salty edge. It cuts through feta and tomato the way a squeeze of lemon would.
pairing.brennans: Gaia ‘Wild Ferment’ Assyrtiko Santorini 2023: the Santorini Assyrtiko on the list, a Greek white for a Greek pan

variations: Baked: assemble in an ovenproof dish and bake at 400°F (200°C) for 10 minutes until the feta softens.
With orzo: stir 1 cup (180 g) cooked orzo into the sauce before the shrimp.
Mussels saganaki: the same sauce with 2 lb (900 g) cleaned mussels, covered until they open.
safety: Cook shrimp until opaque throughout, about 145°F (63°C).
When flaming, turn off the extractor fan, keep hair and sleeves back and keep the lid nearby to smother the flame.

title: Blackened Redfish
summary: Redfish fillets dipped in butter, packed with a Cajun spice blend and seared on a smoking hot cast-iron pan until the spices form a dark crust while the fish stays moist inside. It is the hottest pan in the course, so it teaches heat safety and the exact line between blackened spice and burnt fish. It is also a dish of your city, popularised in New Orleans in the 1980s.
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) cast-iron skillet (only cast iron takes and holds this heat)
Outdoor burner or grill if you can; otherwise every window open and the extractor on full
Shallow dish for melted butter, another for the spice
Heavy oven mitt or welder’s glove

ingredients.us: 4 fillets, each about 6 oz and 1/2 inch thick
ingredients.note: or black drum, snapper or catfish; thicker than 3/4 inch (2 cm) will burn outside before cooking through
melted; 6 tbsp (84 g) for dipping, 4 tbsp (56 g) to serve

mise: Mix all the dry spices in a small bowl until evenly coloured, then spread them on a plate.
Pat the fillets very dry with paper towels. Keep them in the fridge until 10 minutes before cooking.
Melt the butter gently; pour 6 tbsp (85 g) into a shallow dish for dipping and keep the rest warm.
Open windows, turn the extractor to its highest setting and plan where the smoke will go: if indoors, close the kitchen door to the rest of the house and leave the smoke alarm working.
Clear the stove of anything flammable: towels, paper, plastic.
Lay out the spatula, mitt and a warm platter.

timeline.do: Mix the spice. Dry the fish. Ventilate the kitchen.
Set the dry cast iron over the highest heat.
Dip and coat the fillets.
Sear the first side, about 2 minutes.
Turn and sear the second side.
Plate with butter and lemon.

steps.do: Set the empty, dry cast-iron skillet over your highest heat and leave it for 8 to 10 minutes. Do not add any oil to the pan.
steps.look: The pan begins to smoke faintly and a drop of water flicked in skitters and vanishes in under a second. If you have an infrared thermometer, it reads about 500°F (260°C) or above.
steps.mistake: Not heating long enough; the spice then steams instead of blackening, and the fish sticks.
steps.fix: Give it the full time. Cast iron heats slowly but holds heat once there.

steps.do: Dip one fillet into the melted butter, turning to coat both sides, then lay it on the spice plate and press gently so a thick, even layer sticks. Turn and coat the other side. Repeat with all fillets.
steps.look: A complete, even coat of red spice with no bare patches; the butter helps it cling.
steps.mistake: Coating minutes ahead, so the spice turns pasty.
steps.fix: Coat right before cooking. If the coating is thin, dip again lightly and recoat.

steps.do: Wearing the mitt, lay two fillets in the pan, laying them away from you. Drizzle 1 tsp (5 g) of melted butter over the top of each fillet. Stand back: there will be a burst of smoke and loud sizzling.
steps.look: Immediate loud sizzle and thick smoke. The butter on top bubbles.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan with all four, which drops the temperature.
steps.fix: Cook two at a time; let the pan recover 1 to 2 minutes between batches.

steps.do: Cook without moving for 2 minutes, until the underside is a very dark, mahogany crust, nearly black in places.
steps.look: The edge of the fillet turns opaque about a third of the way up. The crust smells toasty and spicy, not acrid like burnt hair.
steps.mistake: Moving the fish early, which tears the crust.
steps.fix: If it smells acrid and the crust is turning grey-black and dry, the pan is too hot: lower the heat slightly for the next batch.

steps.do: Slide the fish spatula flat under the fillet in one confident push and turn it. Drizzle a little more butter over the cooked side. Cook 1 1/2 to 2 minutes more.
steps.look: Both sides are dark, the fillet is opaque through the edges, and it begins to flake at the sides when pressed gently.
steps.mistake: Using tongs or a thick spatula, which breaks the fish.
steps.fix: If the fillet breaks, put it back together on the plate; the crust hides it.

steps.do: Check the thickest part with the thermometer: 140 to 145°F (60 to 63°C). The flesh should flake with gentle pressure and be opaque white with no glassy centre.
steps.look: Moist, opaque white flakes under a dark crust.
steps.mistake: Cooking until the flesh is dry and chalky.
steps.fix: Thin fillets cook fast: lift them as soon as they reach temperature.

steps.do: Move the fillets to the warm platter. Let the pan recover heat for 1 to 2 minutes and cook the second batch the same way. Turn off the heat and leave the pan on a cold burner well out of reach; it stays dangerously hot for 30 minutes.
steps.look: The second batch sizzles as loudly as the first.
steps.mistake: Putting the next fillets into a pan that has cooled.
steps.fix: Wait for faint smoke again before the second batch.

steps.do: Spoon the remaining warm butter over each fillet and serve at once with lemon wedges.
steps.look: The butter pools glossy on the dark crust; the fish smells of toasted spice and lemon.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit; the crust softens as it waits.
steps.fix: Serve straight from the pan to the plate.

science: Blackening is not burning the fish. It is the butter solids and spices browning and charring on a surface around 500°F (260°C), far hotter than a normal sauté. The milk solids in butter brown fast, and paprika is rich in sugars and pigments that darken into a deeply flavoured crust in seconds. Because the fillet is thin and the heat so intense, the crust forms before the heat has time to travel through and dry out the centre. Cast iron is essential because it is heavy and stores a lot of heat, so it does not cool much when the cold fish lands. A thin pan would drop in temperature and steam the fish. The smoke is butter fat and spice combusting, which is why ventilation matters.
plating: Set the fillet crust side up across the centre of a warm plate, slightly off centre. Spoon a line of melted butter over it, add a lemon wedge at one end and a neat spoon of rice or a crisp green salad at the other. A classic New Orleans plate adds a pat of herb butter melting on top. Keep the crust dry and visible: no sauce over it.

pairing.drink: An off-dry Riesling. A touch of sweetness tames the cayenne, its acidity cuts the butter, and low alcohol does not inflame the heat.
pairing.brennans: C.H. Berres ‘Old Vines’ Riesling 2022: an off-dry German Riesling on the list to calm the cayenne

variations: Blackened chicken: pound boneless thighs to an even 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) and cook 3 to 4 minutes a side to 165°F (74°C).
Blackened tofu: press extra-firm tofu, slice into 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) slabs and use the same method, 2 minutes a side.
Blackened shrimp over grits, a bridge to the last dinner of this level.
safety: This is the most dangerous pan in the level. Cook outdoors if you can. Indoors, ventilate fully and expect the smoke alarm to sound.
Never add water to a smoking hot pan, and never leave it unattended.
Keep a lid or a sheet pan beside the stove to smother a fat fire. Never use water on burning fat. Know where your fire extinguisher is.
The handle of cast iron is as hot as the pan: always use a heavy mitt.
Fish is safe at 145°F (63°C), opaque and flaking easily.

title: Pan-Fried Fish with Chermoula
summary: Skin-on white fish fillets marinated briefly in chermoula, the Moroccan herb, spice and lemon sauce, then pan-fried skin side down until the skin shatters, with more chermoula spooned over at the table. After blackening, this is fish cookery at moderate heat: crisp skin, moist flesh, and the habit of judging doneness by the flake rather than the clock.
skills: a herb, spice and lemon marinade
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) non-stick or well seasoned carbon steel skillet
Food processor, blender or mortar and pestle
Small dry pan for toasting cumin
Paper towels and a sharp knife for scoring

ingredients.item: Skin-on white fish fillets (sea bass, snapper or bream)
ingredients.note: scaled, pin bones removed, about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick

ingredients.item: Fresh coriander, leaves and tender stems

ingredients.note: 1/2 tsp (3 g) for the chermoula, the rest for the fish

mise: Toast the cumin seeds in a small dry pan over medium heat for 60 to 90 seconds, shaking, until they darken a shade and smell nutty. Grind them.

Blend the coriander, parsley, garlic, cumin, paprika, cayenne, preserved lemon, lemon juice, olive oil and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt to a loose, bright green sauce with some texture. Taste: it should be punchy.
Pat the fish fillets very dry, especially the skin. Run the back of a knife along the skin, from tail to head, to squeeze out moisture, then dry again.
Score the skin with three shallow diagonal cuts, just through the skin, about 1/16 inch (2 mm) deep, so it does not curl in the pan.
Spread one third of the chermoula over the flesh side only. Keep the skin side clean and dry. Refrigerate 20 minutes, no longer.
Keep the remaining chermoula aside for the table.

timeline.do: Toast cumin and blend the chermoula.
Dry, score and marinate the fish flesh side only.
Prepare sides; take the fish out of the fridge.
Heat the pan. Salt the skin. Fry skin side down.
Turn for the last minute; check temperature.
Plate skin side up with fresh chermoula and lemon.

steps.do: Take the fish from the fridge, scrape off any chermoula that has strayed onto the skin and pat the skin dry once more. Season the skin with salt just before cooking.
steps.look: The skin looks matte and dry, like paper, not shiny or wet.
steps.mistake: Leaving marinade or water on the skin, which steams it and makes it stick.
steps.fix: Dry the skin again with a fresh paper towel; moisture is the enemy of crisp skin.

steps.do: Heat the neutral oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers but does not smoke, about 2 minutes.
steps.look: The oil moves freely and ripples when the pan is tilted.
steps.mistake: Adding fish to a cold pan, which glues the skin down.
steps.fix: Wait for the shimmer, then test with the tip of a fillet: it should sizzle immediately.

steps.do: Lay each fillet skin side down, placing it away from you. Immediately press the top gently with the fish spatula for 15 to 20 seconds so the whole skin makes contact as it tightens.
steps.look: A steady, crackling sizzle, and the fillet lies flat instead of curling.
steps.mistake: Not pressing, so the fillet curls up and the skin browns only at the edges.
steps.fix: If a fillet curls, press again for a few seconds until it relaxes.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium and cook without moving for 4 to 5 minutes, depending on thickness, until the flesh has turned opaque about three quarters of the way up the side.
steps.look: The opaque line climbs the side of the fillet. The sizzle settles to a steady crackle. The edges of the skin look golden.
steps.mistake: Peeking and moving the fish too early, which tears the skin.
steps.fix: When the skin is crisp it releases by itself; if it sticks, give it another 30 seconds.

steps.do: Slide the spatula under each fillet and turn it. Cook flesh side down for 30 to 60 seconds only, just to finish the top.
steps.look: The skin is deep golden and crackles when tapped. The flesh side takes a light golden colour from the chermoula.
steps.mistake: Cooking a long time on the flesh side, which burns the herbs and dries the fish.
steps.fix: One minute at most; the fish should be nearly cooked before you turn it.

steps.do: Check the thickest fillet with the thermometer. Pull the fish at 140°F (60°C); resting carries it to the safe 145°F (63°C). The flesh should be opaque and part into large flakes when nudged with a fork.
steps.look: Opaque, moist, pearly flakes that separate easily.
steps.mistake: Cooking until the flakes look dry and fall apart.
steps.fix: If it is short of temperature, cover the pan off the heat for 1 minute.

steps.do: Transfer the fillets skin side up to warm plates or a rack. Rest 1 minute. Never put sauce over the skin.
steps.look: The skin stays crisp and glassy.
steps.mistake: Resting skin side down on a plate, which steams the skin soft.
steps.fix: Always rest and serve skin side up.

steps.do: Spoon the fresh chermoula onto the plate beside or under the fish, not on top of the skin. Add a lemon wedge.
steps.look: A vivid green pool against golden skin.
steps.mistake: Drowning the fish in sauce so the skin turns soggy.
steps.fix: Serve extra chermoula in a small bowl at the table instead.

science: Fish skin is mostly collagen and water with a thin layer of fat beneath. To crisp, the water must be driven off and the collagen must shrink and dry, which only happens on a hot, dry surface. That is why the skin is scraped, dried and salted just before it meets the pan, and why it cooks most of the way skin side down: the skin insulates the delicate flesh while the heat climbs. Scoring prevents curling, because collagen contracts sharply when heated. The chermoula marinade stays on the flesh side and only for 20 minutes, because lemon juice is acidic: left longer, acid begins to denature the surface proteins, turning the fish chalky before it is cooked.
plating: Spoon a generous swoosh of chermoula across the plate with the back of a spoon. Set the fillet skin side up across it at an angle so the sauce shows on both sides. Add a neat pile of herbed couscous or roasted potatoes to one side and a lemon wedge. Finish with a few whole coriander leaves and a pinch of flaky salt on the skin.

pairing.drink: A crisp Loire Sauvignon Blanc. Its green, herbal character echoes the coriander and parsley and its acidity matches the lemon.
pairing.brennans: Famille Durand Val de Loire Sauvignon Blanc 2024: the Loire Sauvignon Blanc on the list, herbal enough for the chermoula

variations: The library’s roast version: layer sliced potatoes, peppers and tomatoes with chermoula, roast at 410°F (210°C) for 20 minutes, set the fish on top and roast 12 to 15 minutes more.
Chermoula shrimp: marinate peeled shrimp for 15 minutes and sear 1 minute a side.
Grilled whole fish: stuff the cavity with chermoula and lemon slices and grill over medium coals.
safety: Fish is safe at 145°F (63°C), when it is opaque and flakes easily.
Keep fish refrigerated until 10 minutes before cooking and marinate it in the fridge.
Lay fish into hot oil away from you to avoid splashes.

title: Wiener Schnitzel
summary: A thin veal or pork cutlet passed through flour, egg and fine crumbs and shallow-fried in swirling fat until the crust puffs away from the meat in golden ripples. The breading station is a fundamental of every kitchen, and that rippled, loose crust is its test.
skills: swirling in fat so the crumb puffs
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) heavy skillet with sides at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep
Meat mallet or a heavy small pan
Plastic wrap or a large zip-top bag
Three shallow dishes or plates for the breading station
Wire rack set over a sheet pan
Wide fish slice or slotted spatula

ingredients.item: Veal cutlets (top round) or boneless pork loin cutlets
ingredients.note: about 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) thick before pounding
unseasoned, from white bread or rolls; not panko
enough for 3/4 inch (2 cm) depth in a 12 inch (30 cm) skillet

mise: Lay each cutlet between sheets of plastic wrap and pound from the centre outwards with even, glancing blows to 1/8 inch (3 mm), keeping it in one piece. It will roughly double in size.
Make the breading station left to right: flour on the first plate; eggs beaten with the cream until no streaks of white remain on the second; breadcrumbs on the third. Then the rack and sheet pan.
Season the cutlets on both sides with salt and pepper just before breading.
Keep one hand for dry (flour and crumbs) and one for wet (egg) so your fingers do not become clubbed with breading.
Line a sheet pan with a wire rack for draining. Set lemon and parsley ready.

timeline.do: Pound the cutlets. Set up the breading station.
Heat the fat slowly towards 330°F (165°C).
Bread the first two cutlets, right before frying.
Fry two at a time, about 2 minutes a side, swirling.
Bread and fry the second pair.
Plate at once with lemon.

steps.do: Pour the oil into the skillet and add the clarified butter. Heat over medium heat to 330 to 340°F (165 to 170°C), checking with the thermometer.
steps.look: The fat ripples, and a breadcrumb dropped in sizzles and turns golden in about 30 seconds.
steps.mistake: Fat too cool, so the crumb soaks up grease; fat too hot, so the crust browns before the meat cooks.
steps.fix: Adjust the heat and wait for the thermometer. Keep it steady between batches.

steps.do: Dredge a seasoned cutlet in flour on both sides and shake off all the excess. A thin, even film is all you want.
steps.look: The meat looks dusty and dry with no thick patches.
steps.mistake: Leaving thick flour, which forms a pasty layer between meat and crumb.
steps.fix: Tap firmly and pat off excess with your dry hand.

steps.do: Lay it in the egg, turn to coat, then lift and let the excess drip off for a few seconds.
steps.look: A thin, glossy coat of egg with no bare flour showing.
steps.mistake: Leaving too much egg, which makes a thick, heavy crust.
steps.fix: Let it drip longer, or run the cutlet against the rim of the dish.

steps.do: Lay the cutlet in the breadcrumbs and scatter crumbs over the top. Turn once and lift. Do not press: the crumbs should barely cling, loose and fluffy.
steps.look: An even, loose coating with no bare spots, slightly shaggy rather than packed flat.
steps.mistake: Pressing the crumbs on hard, which glues them to the meat and stops the crust from puffing.
steps.fix: If you pressed, the schnitzel will still be good; next time simply turn it in the crumbs.

steps.do: Lower the cutlet into the fat, laying it away from you. Immediately start swirling the pan gently in a circular motion so waves of hot fat wash over the top of the cutlet.
steps.look: Vigorous bubbling all around the cutlet. Within 30 seconds the crust begins to lift and form ripples and bubbles.
steps.mistake: Leaving the pan still, so the top stays flat and the crust clings.
steps.fix: Keep the pan moving. You can also spoon fat over the top continuously.

steps.do: Fry 1 1/2 to 2 minutes until the underside is deep golden, then turn with the fish slice and fry 1 to 1 1/2 minutes more, still swirling.
steps.look: Both sides deep golden, the crust billowed and wrinkled, separated from the meat like a loose jacket.
steps.mistake: Turning several times, which breaks the delicate puffed crust.
steps.fix: Turn once only.

steps.do: Lift the schnitzel out, let the fat drip off for a few seconds, and lay it on the rack. Pork must reach 145°F (63°C); a cutlet this thin passes it in the pan. Check the first one if unsure.
steps.look: The crust stays crisp and the meat is moist and just white or pale pink at the centre with clear juices.
steps.mistake: Draining on paper towels, which steam the underside soft.
steps.fix: Use the rack. If the second batch must wait, hold the first in a 200°F (95°C) oven for no more than 10 minutes.

steps.do: Bread and fry the remaining cutlets, letting the fat come back to temperature between batches. Serve immediately with lemon wedges, parsley and lingonberry jam.
steps.look: Each schnitzel as puffed and golden as the first.
steps.mistake: Frying the second batch in fat that has cooled, which gives a greasy crust.
steps.fix: Check the thermometer before each batch; wait for 330°F (165°C).

science: The puffed crust, called soufflieren in Vienna, comes from steam. As the cutlet hits hot fat, water in the egg layer turns to steam, and because the crumbs are loose rather than pressed, that steam can lift the egg and crumb layer away from the meat into a bubbled shell. Swirling the fat over the top keeps the upper surface hot so the coating sets in its raised shape. Flour gives the egg something to grip; egg glues the crumbs; fine crumbs brown evenly. Pounding the meat thin lets it cook through in the same 3 to 4 minutes the crust needs to turn golden. Clarified butter adds a nutty taste without milk solids, which would burn at frying temperature.
plating: Lay the schnitzel across a large warm plate so it nearly reaches the rim, which is the Viennese style. Set a lemon wedge and a small mound of lingonberry jam beside it and a scattering of parsley. Serve potato and cucumber salad or parsley potatoes in a separate dish so nothing sits against the crust and softens it.

pairing.drink: Austrian Grüner Veltliner, dry and peppery with bright acidity. It is the wine of Vienna’s own vineyards and cuts the fried crust cleanly.
pairing.brennans: Bründlmayer ‘Terrassen’ Grüner Veltliner 2023 (375 ml): the Grüner Veltliner on the list, the wine of Vienna for its most famous dish

variations: Schnitzel Wiener Art: pork loin in place of veal, the everyday Austrian version.
Chicken schnitzel: butterflied breast pounded to 1/4 inch (6 mm), fried to 165°F (74°C).
Holstein schnitzel: topped with a fried egg, anchovies and capers.
safety: Never fill a skillet more than half full with fat, and never leave hot fat unattended.
Keep a lid or sheet pan beside the stove to smother a fat fire. Never use water.
Pork and veal cutlets must reach 145°F (63°C).
Throw away leftover flour, egg and crumbs that touched raw meat.
Let the fat cool completely before straining or discarding it.

title: Kofta Kebabs with Yoghurt Sauce
summary: Spiced minced lamb kneaded with grated onion and herbs, shaped onto flat skewers and cooked under a fierce overhead grill (broiler), served with a garlicky yoghurt sauce and flatbread. Shaping and cooking mince evenly teaches seasoning by test patty and the safe internal temperature for ground meat.
skills: cooking under a hot grill or over coals
equipment: 8 flat metal skewers, or wooden skewers soaked in water for 30 minutes
Box grater and a clean kitchen towel for squeezing the onion
Sheet pan lined with foil, with a rack if you have one
Overhead grill or a charcoal or gas grill
Small frying pan for the test patty

ingredients.item: Minced lamb or beef, about 20 percent fat

mise: Grate the onion on the fine side of the grater, tip it into a clean towel and twist hard over the sink until no more juice drips. You should have about 1/3 cup (60 g) of dry pulp.
Chop the parsley and mint finely. Mix all the dry spices with the salt and pepper in a small bowl.
Make the yoghurt sauce: stir the yoghurt with the garlic paste, lemon juice, 1 tbsp (15 ml) olive oil and a pinch of salt. Refrigerate.
Toss the sliced red onion with the sumac and a pinch of salt; leave to soften.
If using wooden skewers, soak them in water for 30 minutes so they do not burn.

timeline.do: Grate and squeeze the onion; make the yoghurt sauce and sumac onions.
Knead the meat mixture; fry a test patty and adjust seasoning.
Chill the mixture 30 minutes.
Shape onto skewers. Preheat the grill to high.
Grill 3 to 4 minutes a side.
Rest 2 minutes; serve on flatbread with sauce.

steps.do: Put the mince, squeezed onion, garlic, herbs and spice mix into the bowl. Knead firmly with one hand for 2 to 3 minutes, squeezing the mixture through your fingers.
steps.look: The mixture changes from loose and crumbly to sticky and tacky; it clings to your palm and holds together when you press a lump.
steps.mistake: Mixing briefly with a fork, so the kofta crumbles and falls off the skewer.
steps.fix: Keep kneading. If your hand gets warm, rinse it under cold water and continue.

steps.do: Pinch off a walnut-sized piece, flatten it, and fry it in the small pan over medium heat for 2 minutes a side until cooked through. Taste it.
steps.look: A cooked patty that tastes well seasoned, warm with spice, with no bland finish.
steps.mistake: Tasting raw mince, which is unsafe, or skipping the test and serving bland kofta.
steps.fix: Add salt in 1/4 tsp (1.5 g) steps or more spice, knead again, and fry another test patty.

steps.do: Cover and chill the mixture for at least 30 minutes.
steps.look: Firm, cold meat that is easier to shape and holds onto the skewer.
steps.mistake: Shaping warm mixture, which is sticky and slumps.
steps.fix: If you are short of time, chill for 15 minutes in the freezer.

steps.do: Divide the mixture into 8 equal portions of about 3 oz (85 g). With wet hands, squeeze each around a skewer into a sausage about 5 inches (13 cm) long and 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick, pressing your fingertips along it to make shallow dents.
steps.look: Even cylinders of the same thickness, tight against the skewer, with finger dents along the length.
steps.mistake: Making uneven thickness, so the thin end overcooks before the thick end is done.
steps.fix: Roll gently on the board to even them out.

steps.do: Preheat the overhead grill on high for 10 minutes with the rack about 4 inches (10 cm) below the element. Lay the skewers on the foil-lined sheet pan, ideally on a rack, and brush lightly with oil.
steps.look: The element glows red; the oven is blazing hot.
steps.mistake: Putting the kofta under a grill that is not yet hot, so they stew grey in their fat.
steps.fix: Wait for the full preheat.

steps.do: Grill 3 to 4 minutes until the top is browned and sizzling, then turn each skewer with tongs and grill 3 to 4 minutes more.
steps.look: Deeply browned, sizzling surfaces with crisp edges at the dents; fat bubbles and drips.
steps.mistake: Turning too early, before a crust forms, so the meat tears and sticks.
steps.fix: Wait until the surface is browned; it releases more easily.

steps.do: Check the thickest kofta with the thermometer: minced lamb or beef must reach 160°F (71°C). Pull them when they reach it.
steps.look: Juices run clear; the centre is just cooked through, no pink.
steps.mistake: Judging by the outside, which can look done while the centre is raw.
steps.fix: Return any that are short for 1 to 2 minutes more.

steps.do: Rest 2 minutes. Slide the kofta off the skewers with a fork onto warm flatbread, spoon over the yoghurt sauce and top with sumac onions and a few mint leaves.
steps.look: Juicy, glossy kofta with the cool sauce melting around them.
steps.mistake: Sliding them off immediately, so the juices run out.
steps.fix: Give them the 2-minute rest.

science: Kneading mince with salt does the binding that egg or breadcrumbs do in other recipes. Salt dissolves a muscle protein called myosin, and working the meat draws it out as a sticky film that glues the particles together and holds the kofta onto the skewer. The onion is grated and squeezed because its water would loosen the mixture and make it slump and steam. Fat, about 20 percent, keeps the kofta moist and carries the spices, many of whose flavour compounds dissolve in fat. Ground meat needs to reach 160°F (71°C) because mincing spreads any surface bacteria right through the meat, unlike a whole steak where they sit only on the outside.
plating: Lay a warm flatbread on the plate and spoon a broad stripe of yoghurt sauce down the middle. Set two kofta side by side on the sauce. Pile sumac onions at one end, scatter chopped parsley and mint, and add a lemon wedge. A small chopped salad of tomato and cucumber on the side completes it.

pairing.drink: A Côtes du Rhône red, Grenache led, with warm spice and soft tannin that suits cumin, allspice and lamb.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de Châteaumar ‘Cuvée Vincent’ Côtes du Rhône 2023: the Grenache-led Côtes du Rhône on the list, warm with spice for lamb

variations: Kofta in a pan: shape into small patties and fry 3 minutes a side over medium-high heat.
Kofta with tahini: bake the kofta on a bed of sliced potatoes and tomatoes, covered with tahini sauce, at 400°F (200°C) for 25 minutes.
Chicken kofta with minced thigh, cooked to 165°F (74°C).
safety: Minced lamb and beef must reach 160°F (71°C); minced chicken or turkey 165°F (74°C).
Never taste raw mince: fry a test patty instead.
Wash hands well after kneading raw meat, and keep it cold until shaping.

title: Swedish Meatballs with Cream Sauce
summary: Small, tender meatballs of beef and pork seasoned with allspice and nutmeg, browned in butter and finished in a cream gravy built in the same pan. The panade of soaked breadcrumbs explains why some meatballs stay soft, and the gravy carries the pan sauce lesson into a roux and cream.
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) heavy skillet, stainless or cast iron
Tongs or a spoon for turning
Sheet pan to hold shaped meatballs
mise: Make the panade: stir the breadcrumbs into the milk and leave 10 minutes until soft and pasty.
Soften the onion in 1 tbsp (14 g) butter over low heat for 5 minutes without colour, then cool it completely.
Warm the stock. Measure the cream and soy.
Set a sheet pan beside you and a bowl of cold water for wetting your hands.

timeline.do: Panade soaking; soften and cool the onion.
Mix the meat, test a small patty, adjust seasoning.
Roll the meatballs and chill briefly.
Brown in two batches.
Make the roux and gravy in the same pan.
Simmer the meatballs in the gravy until cooked through.

steps.do: Mash the panade with a fork until smooth. Add both minces, the cooled onion, egg, allspice, nutmeg, salt and pepper. Mix with your hand for about 1 minute, just until evenly combined.
steps.look: A soft, moist, evenly mixed mass that holds together when pressed.
steps.mistake: Kneading hard as you would for kofta, which makes these meatballs dense and springy.
steps.fix: Mix only until you see no streaks; tender is the goal here.

steps.do: Fry a teaspoon-sized test patty in a little butter for 1 minute a side, taste and adjust salt and spice.
steps.look: A warm, savoury taste with the allspice noticeable but not dominant.
steps.mistake: Seasoning by guesswork.
steps.fix: Adjust and test again; seasoning is fixed once rolled.

steps.do: With wet hands, roll the mixture into balls 1 inch (2.5 cm) across, about 1/2 oz (15 g) each. You should get about 28 to 30. Lay them on the sheet pan and chill 10 minutes.
steps.look: Smooth, round balls of equal size with no cracks.
steps.mistake: Making uneven sizes, which cook at different speeds.
steps.fix: Weigh the first few until your eye learns the size.

steps.do: Heat 1 tbsp (14 g) butter with the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat. When the foam subsides, add half the meatballs in one layer. Brown 5 to 6 minutes, shaking the pan and turning them so they colour on all sides. Lift onto a plate and repeat.
steps.look: Even deep brown all over, a steady sizzle, browned bits forming on the pan floor.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan so the meatballs steam grey and stick.
steps.fix: Brown in batches with room around each ball.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium. Leave about 2 tbsp (30 ml) fat in the pan (add butter if needed). Sprinkle in the flour and whisk 1 to 2 minutes into a smooth paste, scraping the browned bits.
steps.look: A bubbling paste the colour of peanut butter that smells toasty.
steps.mistake: Burning the roux on a pan still too hot.
steps.fix: If it smells scorched or goes dark brown, wipe out and start the roux with fresh butter.

steps.do: Pour in the warm stock gradually, whisking constantly to keep it smooth. Bring to a simmer and cook 2 to 3 minutes until it thickens. Whisk in the cream and soy sauce.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, light brown gravy that coats the back of a spoon.
steps.mistake: Adding cold stock all at once, which causes lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk out lumps, or strain the gravy through a sieve before the meatballs go back.

steps.do: Return the meatballs and their juices to the gravy. Simmer gently 5 to 8 minutes, turning, until cooked through. Check one with the thermometer: 160°F (71°C).
steps.look: The gravy bubbles lazily and thickens further; the meatballs are firm but springy.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which can split the cream and toughen the meat.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer. Thin the gravy with a splash of stock if it gets too thick.

steps.do: Taste the gravy and adjust salt and pepper. Scatter parsley or dill and serve with mashed potatoes, lingonberry jam and quick-pickled cucumber.
steps.look: Silky gravy, tender meatballs, a sweet-tart jam beside them.
steps.mistake: Underseasoning the gravy, which tastes flat against the jam.
steps.fix: Add salt a pinch at a time; a few drops of soy also deepen it.

science: A panade is starch soaked in liquid. When minced meat cooks, its proteins tighten and squeeze out juice, which is why plain meatballs can turn dry and bouncy. The soaked breadcrumbs sit between the meat particles, physically stopping the proteins from bonding too tightly, and the gelatinised starch holds onto moisture as the meat firms. Light mixing matters for the same reason: vigorous kneading draws out the sticky myosin that binds kofta, giving a springy texture these meatballs avoid. The gravy is thickened by a roux, flour cooked in fat, which coats each starch granule in fat so it can swell in hot liquid without clumping.
plating: Spoon a smooth mound of mashed potato slightly off centre in a warm shallow bowl and make a hollow with the back of the spoon. Arrange seven meatballs alongside, ladle the gravy over the meatballs and into the hollow, and place a neat spoon of lingonberry jam and a few slices of pickled cucumber on the side. Finish with chopped dill.

pairing.drink: A light, juicy red such as Beaujolais-Villages, low in tannin, with bright berry fruit that echoes the lingonberry and cuts the cream.
pairing.brennans: Louis Jadot Beaujolais-Villages 2021 (375 ml): the Beaujolais-Villages on the list, light and berry-bright against the cream gravy

variations: Minnesota style from the library: a larger batch with more gravy, served over egg noodles.
Köttbullar for a buffet: roll smaller, 3/4 inch (2 cm), and serve on picks with the gravy as a dip.
Mushroom gravy: add 4 oz (115 g) sliced mushrooms to the pan before the roux.
safety: Mixed minced beef and pork must reach 160°F (71°C).
Taste the cooked test patty, never the raw mixture.
Cool leftovers within 2 hours; reheat to 165°F (74°C).
