title: Bangers and Mash with Onion Gravy
summary: Pork sausages cooked low and slow until taut and glossy, a smooth buttery mash and a deep onion gravy. A pub dinner that teaches three separate disciplines: gentle sausage cookery, the right potato and method for mash, and a gravy built on properly browned onions.
equipment: Large heavy skillet for the sausages
Potato ricer, food mill or hand masher (never a food processor)

ingredients.item: Good pork sausages, high meat content
ingredients.note: Cumberland, Lincolnshire or a butcher’s pork sausage

mise: Take the sausages out of the fridge 15 minutes before cooking. Do not prick them.
Peel the potatoes and cut into even 2 inch (5 cm) chunks. Rinse and put them in the large pan with cold water to cover by 1 inch (2.5 cm) and 1 tsp (6 g) salt.
Slice the onions thinly and evenly. Strip the thyme leaves.
Heat the stock and the milk in separate small pans or jugs.

timeline.do: Start the onions on low for the gravy.
Potatoes on, from cold water. Sausages into a cold pan on low.
Flour and stock into the onions; simmer the gravy.
Drain and steam-dry the potatoes; mash with butter, then milk.
Check the sausages; cook the peas.
Mash, sausages, gravy over.

steps.do: Melt the gravy butter in the saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the onions with a pinch of salt and the thyme. Cook 25 to 30 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until soft, sweet and deep golden brown.
steps.look: The onions collapse, turn jammy and take a rich amber colour. They smell sweet, not sharp.
steps.mistake: Turning up the heat to hurry them, so they scorch at the edges while staying pale in the middle.
steps.fix: Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water whenever they stick or brown too fast, and scrape; patience gives the colour.

steps.do: Bring the potatoes to the boil from cold, then lower to a steady simmer and cook 15 to 20 minutes.
steps.look: A knife slides into the largest chunk with no resistance and the edges are just starting to crumble.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which breaks the outside to mush while the centre stays raw.
steps.fix: Simmer gently; test the largest piece, not the smallest.

steps.do: Meanwhile, put the oil and sausages in the cold skillet, then set it over low to medium-low heat. Cook 20 to 25 minutes, turning every few minutes so they brown evenly.
steps.look: A gentle, steady sizzle, never violent. The sausages swell, turn evenly golden brown and glossy, and the skins stay intact.
steps.mistake: High heat, which splits the skins and leaves the outside burnt and the inside raw. Pricking them, which lets the juices escape.
steps.fix: Turn the heat down at the first sign of spitting or splitting. A split sausage still eats well; just lower the heat.

steps.do: Stir the flour into the onions and cook 1 minute. Add the hot stock gradually, stirring, then the Worcestershire and mustard. Simmer 8 to 10 minutes until glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon. Season to taste.
steps.look: A shiny, dark gravy with soft onion strands, thick enough to leave a trail when you draw a finger across the coated spoon.
steps.mistake: Adding all the stock at once to raw flour, giving lumps.
steps.fix: Stir hard; small lumps dissolve as it simmers. Add a splash of water if it gets too thick.

steps.do: Drain the potatoes in the colander, return them to the hot empty pan over low heat and shake for 1 to 2 minutes to steam off excess water.
steps.look: The surfaces turn dry and floury and steam rises.
steps.mistake: Mashing wet potatoes, which gives a watery, heavy mash.
steps.fix: Let them steam-dry; it makes the mash fluffy.

steps.do: Press the potatoes through the ricer back into the pan (or mash thoroughly). Beat in the butter first, a few cubes at a time, then add the hot milk gradually, beating with a wooden spoon until smooth and soft. Season with salt and white pepper.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, fluffy mash that holds soft peaks on the spoon.
steps.mistake: Using a food processor or blender, which ruptures the starch cells and turns mash into glue. Adding cold milk.
steps.fix: If the mash is stiff, add more hot milk a tablespoon at a time. Gluey mash cannot be repaired; next time use a ricer.

steps.do: Check the largest sausage with the thermometer: pork sausages must reach 160°F (71°C). Rest them 2 minutes.
steps.look: Firm, plump sausages with clear juices and no pink at the centre.
steps.mistake: Serving by colour alone; browned outsides can hide raw middles.
steps.fix: Cover the pan and cook on low a few minutes more if short.

steps.do: Cook the peas in boiling salted water for 2 minutes and drain. Plate the mash, rest two sausages against it and pour the gravy over everything.
steps.look: A pillow of mash, glossy sausages, gravy flowing over both.
steps.mistake: Letting the mash sit, which forms a skin.
steps.fix: Keep the mash covered over very low heat with a little extra milk until plating.

science: Floury potatoes have large starch granules and little moisture, so they break into a light, fluffy mash; waxy potatoes hold together and turn pasty. Overworking any cooked potato ruptures the swollen starch cells, releasing free starch that makes mash gluey, which is why a ricer beats a blender. Adding butter before milk lets the fat coat the starch first, keeping the texture silky. Sausages cook gently because the casing traps juice and fat: high heat makes the filling expand faster than the skin can stretch, so it splits. Onions turn sweet and brown slowly as their sugars caramelise and react with amino acids, which takes time at low heat.
plating: Spoon a generous mound of mash into a warm shallow bowl and make a wide well with the back of the spoon. Lean two sausages against the mash at an angle, crossed if you like. Pour the onion gravy into the well and over the sausages, letting it pool. Spoon the peas to one side and finish with a few thyme leaves.

pairing.drink: A pint of English bitter or a light, fruity red such as Côtes du Rhône. Both have enough body for the sausages without overpowering the gravy.

variations: Colcannon mash: fold in 2 cups (150 g) shredded cabbage or kale softened in butter, with chopped spring onions.
Oven method for sausages: roast on a sheet pan at 375°F (190°C) for 25 minutes, turning once.
Toad in the hole: brown the sausages, then bake them in a Yorkshire pudding batter.
safety: Pork sausages must reach 160°F (71°C).
Drain potatoes by pouring away from you; steam scalds.
Never leave a pan of sizzling fat unattended.

title: Dublin Coddle
summary: A pale, gentle stew of pork sausages, bacon, sliced potatoes and onions simmered slowly in stock under a lid. It is here to show that a low, covered simmer builds deep flavour without any browning, and that a pale stew must be seasoned with care.
equipment: Heavy pot or Dutch oven with a tight lid, about 5 quarts (5 litres)

ingredients.note: Irish style breakfast sausages if available
peeled and sliced 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) thick
taste at the end; bacon and stock are salty

mise: Peel and slice the potatoes into even 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) rounds; keep them in cold water so they do not brown.
Slice the onions. Cut the bacon into pieces.
Bring a medium pan of water to the boil for blanching.
Warm the stock. Chop the parsley.

timeline.do: Slice potatoes and onions; boil water.
Blanch the sausages and bacon 2 minutes.
Layer the pot and add the stock.
Lid on, the barest simmer or a 300°F (150°C) oven, for about 1 1/2 hours.
Check the sausages and potatoes, taste and season.
Ladle into warm bowls with parsley and bread.

steps.do: Drop the sausages and bacon into the boiling water and simmer 2 minutes. Lift out with the slotted spoon and drain. If you prefer, cut each sausage in half.
steps.look: The sausages firm and turn pale, and a little grey foam rises on the water.
steps.mistake: Boiling much longer, which drains flavour into water you will throw away.
steps.fix: Two minutes is enough; the job is to firm the sausages and rinse off excess salt.

steps.do: In the pot, make a layer of half the onions, then half the potatoes, then all the sausages and bacon. Season each layer with pepper and a scatter of parsley. Finish with the remaining onions, then the remaining potatoes on top.
steps.look: Neat layers, with potatoes forming a lid over the meat.
steps.mistake: Dumping everything in at random, so the top potatoes stay dry and the meat sits exposed.
steps.fix: Rearrange so the potatoes are on top and the meat is in the middle.

steps.do: Tuck the bay leaf and thyme sprigs in at the side. Pour the warm stock down the side of the pot until it comes about two thirds of the way up; the top layer of potatoes should sit just above the liquid to steam.
steps.look: Liquid visible just below the top potatoes.
steps.mistake: Drowning everything so it boils into a thin soup.
steps.fix: Ladle some stock out if you added too much; you can add it back later if needed.

steps.do: Bring to a simmer over medium heat, then cover tightly and turn the heat to the lowest setting, or move the pot to a 300°F (150°C) oven. Cook 1 1/2 hours without stirring.
steps.look: Under the lid, only a few slow bubbles rise at a time. A gentle, savoury steam.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil, which breaks the potatoes into mush and makes the sausages split.
steps.fix: Turn the heat down, or set the pot slightly off the burner, until the bubbles barely move.

steps.do: After 1 hour, lift the lid and check the liquid level. Add a splash of stock if it has dropped below halfway.
steps.look: Bottom potatoes soft and beginning to thicken the broth; top potatoes steamed and tender.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil dry and catch on the base.
steps.fix: Add hot stock or water and lower the heat.

steps.do: At 1 1/2 hours, check a sausage with the thermometer: 160°F (71°C). The potatoes should be completely tender and the broth slightly thickened by their starch.
steps.look: A knife slides through the top potatoes; the broth is milky and savoury.
steps.mistake: Serving with firm potatoes.
steps.fix: Cover and cook 15 minutes more.

steps.do: Taste the broth and season with salt only if needed, plus more black pepper. Remove the bay leaf and thyme stalks.
steps.look: A savoury, porky, peppery broth.
steps.mistake: Salting at the start, which can leave the finished stew far too salty after the bacon gives up its salt.
steps.fix: If over salted, add a few slices of raw potato and simmer 10 minutes, or add unsalted stock.

steps.do: Ladle into warm, deep bowls, giving everyone potatoes, sausages, bacon and plenty of broth. Shower with the remaining parsley and serve with buttered soda bread.
steps.look: A pale, steaming bowl with bright green parsley on top.
steps.mistake: Serving in shallow plates, which lose the broth.
steps.fix: Use deep bowls; the broth is half the dish.

science: Most stews start by browning meat for flavour, but coddle takes a different route: a long, gentle simmer below boiling extracts flavour into the liquid instead. As the sausages and bacon sit in hot stock, salt, fat and savoury compounds migrate out into the broth and the potatoes absorb them. Keeping the liquid just under boiling, around 185 to 195°F (85 to 90°C), stops the sausage casings from bursting and keeps the potatoes in whole slices while their outer starch slowly thickens the broth. Because there are no browned flavours to lean on, seasoning carries more weight, and pepper and parsley are doing real work.
plating: Use deep, warm bowls. Ladle in potatoes first, then lay a sausage and two pieces of bacon on top, pour broth around to half fill the bowl and scatter a generous handful of parsley over the top. Put a thick slice of soda bread with butter on the side plate.

pairing.drink: A dry Irish stout, roasted and bitter, which cuts the pork fat and suits the plain, savoury broth.

variations: Browned coddle: brown the sausages and bacon lightly before layering, for a deeper, darker stew.
Oven coddle: assemble in a casserole and bake covered at 300°F (150°C) for 2 hours.
With barley: add 1/4 cup (50 g) pearl barley with the stock for a thicker stew.
safety: Pork sausages must reach 160°F (71°C).
Cool leftovers within 2 hours and reheat to 165°F (74°C).
Lift lids away from you so steam goes the other way.

title: Chicken Teriyaki
summary: Boneless chicken thighs with skin rendered crisp in a pan, then lacquered in a reduction of soy, mirin, sake and sugar. Real teriyaki is a pan glaze, not a marinade, and it teaches reduction as a glaze: thick enough to coat, stopped before the sugar burns.
skills: a soy, mirin and sake glaze
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) heavy skillet, stainless, cast iron or non-stick
A smaller pan or a pot lid to press the thighs flat

ingredients.note: ask your butcher to bone them, or bone them yourself
a light seasoning; the sauce is salty

mise: Pat the thighs dry. Trim any loose flaps of fat or skin hanging beyond the meat. With the tip of a knife, make two shallow cuts in the thickest part of the flesh side so the thighs cook evenly.
Prick the skin all over with a fork or the tip of a knife, about 10 times, so fat can escape. Season lightly with salt on both sides.
Stir the soy, mirin, sake, sugar and ginger in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves.
Start the rice. Slice the spring onions. Prepare the vegetables.

timeline.do: Rice on. Trim and prick the thighs; mix the sauce.
Thighs skin side down into the pan; render 8 to 10 minutes.
Turn, cook 3 to 4 minutes; check temperature.
Pour off the fat, wipe the pan, add the sauce and glaze.
Rest and slice.
Serve over rice with the glaze.

steps.do: Put the oil in the cold skillet and lay the thighs in skin side down, flattening them so all the skin touches the pan. Set over medium heat.
steps.look: Within a minute the thighs begin to sizzle quietly as the pan heats.
steps.mistake: Starting in a very hot pan, which shrinks the skin into tight, uneven ridges before the fat renders.
steps.fix: If the skin seizes, press it flat with a smaller pan set on top.

steps.do: Cook 8 to 10 minutes without turning, pressing the thighs flat with a smaller pan or a lid for the first few minutes. Adjust the heat to keep a steady, moderate sizzle.
steps.look: Fat renders out and pools in the pan; the skin turns deep golden brown, flat and crisp, and the flesh goes opaque two thirds of the way up the side.
steps.mistake: Turning early, before the fat has rendered, leaving flabby skin.
steps.fix: Be patient. If the skin is browning too fast before the fat renders, lower the heat.

steps.do: Turn the thighs and cook 3 to 4 minutes on the flesh side. Check the thickest part with the thermometer: at least 165°F (74°C); thighs are juiciest at 175°F (79°C).
steps.look: Firm, springy meat with clear juices.
steps.mistake: Pulling at the first sign of colour on the second side.
steps.fix: Keep cooking in 1 minute bursts until the thermometer agrees.

steps.do: Lift the thighs onto a plate. Pour all the fat out of the pan into a heatproof bowl and wipe the pan with a wad of paper towel held in tongs, leaving the browned bits.
steps.look: A nearly dry pan with a little fond on the base.
steps.mistake: Leaving the fat in, so the glaze slides off the chicken instead of clinging.
steps.fix: Wipe again. Fat and glaze do not mix.

steps.do: Return the pan to medium heat, pour in the sauce and let it bubble 30 seconds. Return the thighs skin side up.
steps.look: The sauce boils immediately with a sweet, savoury smell.
steps.mistake: Adding the sauce to a ripping hot pan, which can scorch the sugar instantly.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off the heat for 20 seconds before the sauce goes in.

steps.do: Simmer 2 to 3 minutes, spooning the sauce over the thighs and turning them twice, until the sauce reduces to a thick, shiny glaze. Finish skin side up.
steps.look: The bubbles grow large, slow and glossy; a drop on the spoon stretches before it falls. The thighs look lacquered.
steps.mistake: Reducing too far, so the sugar burns and turns bitter and sticky.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off as soon as it coats a spoon; it thickens more as it cools. If it went too far, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) water and swirl.

steps.do: Rest the thighs 2 minutes on a board, then slice across the grain into 3/4 inch (2 cm) strips, keeping the shape of each thigh.
steps.look: Moist, opaque slices with the glossy skin intact on top.
steps.mistake: Slicing straight away, so juice floods the board.
steps.fix: Give them the short rest.

steps.do: Spoon rice into bowls, fan a sliced thigh over the top, drizzle the remaining glaze over the meat and finish with spring onions and sesame seeds.
steps.look: Mahogany, glossy skin and a thin drizzle of glaze, not a puddle.
steps.mistake: Pouring glaze all over the rice so it turns syrupy.
steps.fix: Use a spoon to place the glaze on the chicken.

science: Teriyaki means lustre and grilling, and the shine comes from reduction. As the soy, mirin, sake and sugar boil, water evaporates and the sugars concentrate into a syrup that sets into a glossy film on cooling. Sugar also browns fast above about 320°F (160°C), which is why the sauce goes in only after the cooking is done: marinate first and the sugars burn before the skin has rendered. Rendering skin is slow because the fat beneath it must melt and escape before the skin itself can dry and crisp, so a moderate heat and a flat, pressed thigh give the best result. Draining the fat lets the water-based glaze grip the skin instead of sliding off on an oily layer.
plating: Fill a warm bowl two thirds with rice and flatten the top. Fan the sliced thigh across the rice, keeping the skin uppermost and the slices slightly overlapping. Spoon a ribbon of glaze along the slices, scatter spring onions and sesame seeds, and set the green vegetables in a neat pile at one side.

pairing.drink: A chilled junmai sake, or an off-dry Riesling whose sweetness meets the glaze and whose acidity cuts the rendered skin.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Riesling Réserve 2020: the Alsace Riesling on the list, crisp against the sweet glaze

variations: Salmon teriyaki: sear skin-on fillets 4 minutes skin side, 1 minute flesh side, then glaze.
Tofu teriyaki: press and slice firm tofu, dust with cornstarch, fry until crisp, then glaze.
Yakitori style: thread thigh pieces on skewers, grill, and brush with the reduced sauce.
safety: Chicken thighs must reach at least 165°F (74°C).
Pour hot fat into a heatproof container and let it cool before throwing it away; never pour fat down the sink.
Wash boards and knives after trimming raw chicken.

title: Kung Pao Chicken
summary: Diced, velveted chicken stir-fried in a wok with dried chillies, Sichuan peppercorns, aromatics and peanuts, finished in a glossy sauce that is sweet, sour and gently numbing. A classic stir-fry teaches mise en place, because nothing can be cut once the wok is hot.
skills: frying dried chillies and Sichuan pepper
a balanced sweet and sour sauce
equipment: Wok, 14 inch (35 cm) carbon steel, or a 12 inch (30 cm) heavy skillet
Wok spatula or wide metal spatula
Small bowls for each prepared ingredient (the mise en place)
Strong extractor fan or an open window

ingredients.note: plus 1 tsp (5 ml) for the marinade
snipped in half, seeds shaken out

ingredients.item: Spring onions, white and pale green parts

mise: Dice the chicken into even 3/4 inch (2 cm) cubes. Toss with 2 tsp (10 ml) light soy, 1 tsp (5 ml) Shaoxing and 2 tsp (6 g) cornstarch until coated, then stir in 1 tsp (5 ml) oil. Marinate 15 to 30 minutes in the fridge. This is velveting.

Whisk the sauce ingredients (light and dark soy, vinegar, sugar, cornstarch, stock, Shaoxing) in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves. Taste it: sweet and sour should balance, with salt behind. Adjust now, because you cannot adjust once it is in the wok.
Snip the chillies in half crossways with scissors and shake out most of the seeds.

Slice the garlic and ginger, cut the spring onions. Put every ingredient in its own bowl, lined up beside the stove in the order it goes in: chillies and peppercorns, chicken, aromatics, sauce, peanuts.
Turn on the extractor fan; frying chillies gives off pungent fumes.

timeline.do: Rice on. Dice and velvet the chicken.
Mix and taste the sauce. Prepare every aromatic into bowls.
Heat the wok until it smokes faintly.
Chillies and peppercorns, then the chicken.
Aromatics, sauce, peanuts.
Into a warm dish and to the table.

steps.do: Heat the empty wok over high heat until a wisp of smoke rises, about 1 to 2 minutes. Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and swirl to coat the sides.
steps.look: The oil shimmers instantly and streaks across the hot surface.
steps.mistake: Adding oil to a cold wok, so food sticks.
steps.fix: Heat the wok first, then the oil. Hot wok, cool oil, as the saying goes.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium. Add the dried chillies and Sichuan peppercorns and stir 20 to 30 seconds until the chillies darken to deep red and smell toasty.
steps.look: Chillies turn a shade darker, puff slightly and smell fragrant and smoky. The oil takes on a red tint.
steps.mistake: Cooking on high heat so the chillies blacken and turn the dish acrid and bitter.
steps.fix: If any chilli goes black, scoop them all out, wipe the wok and start again; burnt chillies ruin the dish.

steps.do: Turn the heat to high, add the chicken and spread it in a single layer. Leave it for 1 minute to sear, then stir-fry 2 to 3 minutes, tossing, until the pieces are white all over with golden edges.
steps.look: A loud sizzle, chicken pieces separating and turning opaque, golden spots on the edges.
steps.mistake: Stirring constantly from the start, so the chicken never browns and the wok cools.
steps.fix: Let it sit for that first minute. If the wok is small, cook the chicken in two batches.

steps.do: Push the chicken up the side of the wok, add the remaining 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil to the centre, and stir-fry the garlic, ginger and spring onions for 30 seconds until fragrant. Toss everything together.
steps.look: A burst of fragrance, the garlic softening without browning.
steps.mistake: Adding the aromatics too early, so they burn while the chicken cooks.
steps.fix: They go in only for the last minute.

steps.do: Stir the sauce again (the cornstarch settles) and pour it around the edge of the wok. Toss for 20 to 30 seconds until it thickens and turns glossy.
steps.look: The sauce bubbles, thickens in seconds and coats every piece with a shine.
steps.mistake: Forgetting to restir, so lumps of cornstarch form.
steps.fix: If it thickens too much, add a splash of water and toss.

steps.do: Check a large piece of chicken: 165°F (74°C), opaque through.
steps.look: Juicy, opaque meat.
steps.mistake: Overcooking while you check, so the sauce reduces to stickiness.
steps.fix: Pull the wok off the heat while you check.

steps.do: Off the heat, toss in the peanuts. Taste and add a few drops of vinegar if it needs brightness.
steps.look: The peanuts are coated but still crunchy.
steps.mistake: Adding the peanuts early, so they soften.
steps.fix: Peanuts last, off the heat.

steps.do: Tip into a warm serving dish at once and serve with rice. Warn diners that the whole chillies are for flavour, not for eating.
steps.look: Glossy chicken studded with red chillies, green onions and golden peanuts.
steps.mistake: Leaving it in the hot wok, where it keeps cooking.
steps.fix: Transfer immediately.

science: Velveting coats the chicken in a thin film of cornstarch and soy. In the wok, the starch gelatinises into a protective layer that slows moisture loss and gives the meat its silky surface, while also helping the sauce cling. The numbing tingle of Sichuan peppercorns comes from a compound called hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, which stimulates touch receptors in the mouth rather than heat receptors. Frying dried chillies in oil releases their flavour compounds into the fat, but chillies are thin and dry and burn quickly, so the heat is lowered for that step. A stir-fry happens in under five minutes at very high heat, so every ingredient must be ready before cooking starts.
plating: Serve family style in a warm shallow bowl or on a platter, piled high in the centre so the red chillies and green onions show on top. Scatter a few extra peanuts and sliced green onion tops. Rice goes in separate bowls.

pairing.drink: An off-dry German Riesling Spätlese-style or a Kabinett: the touch of sugar soothes the chilli and the acidity matches the black vinegar.
pairing.brennans: J.J. Prüm ‘Wehlener Sonnenuhr’ Riesling Kabinett 2020: the Mosel Kabinett on the list, its touch of sweetness for the chillies

variations: Kung pao shrimp: peeled shrimp, velveted the same way, stir-fried for 1 1/2 minutes.
Kung pao tofu: extra-firm tofu cubes fried crisp before the chillies.
With vegetables: add diced celery or red pepper with the aromatics.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C).
Frying chillies releases fumes that sting eyes and throat: run the fan and do not lean over the wok.
Peanuts are a common, serious allergen: tell anyone you are cooking for that the dish contains them.
Wash hands after handling chillies before touching your eyes.

title: Jeyuk Bokkeum (Spicy Stir-Fried Pork)
summary: Thinly sliced pork shoulder marinated in gochujang, chilli flakes, garlic and ginger, then stir-fried with onion until the edges caramelise. Korean spicy pork introduces fermented chilli paste and the danger that sugar brings to high heat.
skills: stir-frying to caramelise without burning sugar
equipment: Large wok or 12 inch (30 cm) skillet

ingredients.item: Pork shoulder (butt) or pork belly, boneless

ingredients.note: grated, optional; it adds sweetness and tenderises

mise: If the pork is not pre-sliced, wrap it and freeze for 30 to 45 minutes until firm but not hard, then slice across the grain into 1/8 inch (3 mm) slices, about 2 inches (5 cm) long.
In the bowl, stir the gochujang, gochugaru, soy, sugar, mirin, garlic, ginger, grated pear, half the sesame oil and the pepper into a thick red paste.
Add the pork and massage the marinade in with your hand (wear a glove if you like) until every slice is coated. Cover and refrigerate at least 30 minutes, or up to overnight.
Slice the onion, cut the spring onions and chilli. Wash and dry the lettuce leaves.
Start the rice.

timeline.do: Freeze and slice the pork if needed.
Make the marinade and coat the pork; refrigerate.
Rice on if not already. Slice the vegetables.
Heat the pan; stir-fry the pork.
Onions in; then spring onions and chilli.
Sesame oil and seeds; serve with rice and lettuce.

steps.do: Heat the neutral oil in the wok or skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
steps.look: Rippling oil, a faint haze.
steps.mistake: Starting cold, so the pork stews in its marinade.
steps.fix: Wait for the shimmer.

steps.do: Add the pork, spreading it out in as even a layer as you can. Leave it for 1 minute to sear.
steps.look: A loud sizzle; the marinade begins to bubble and darken at the edges.
steps.mistake: Piling all the pork in a heap, which steams it grey.
steps.fix: If your pan is small, cook in two batches.

steps.do: Stir-fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning and spreading the meat, until the pork is cooked through and the edges begin to caramelise. Lower the heat a notch if the marinade on the pan starts to blacken.
steps.look: Pork opaque with dark red, slightly charred edges and a sweet, smoky, spicy smell.
steps.mistake: High heat throughout, so the sugar in the marinade burns black and bitter before the pork cooks.
steps.fix: Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and scrape; it releases the stuck marinade and cools the pan. Lower the heat.

steps.do: Add the sliced onion and stir-fry 2 minutes until it softens but keeps some bite.
steps.look: The onion turns glossy and translucent at the edges, coated in red sauce.
steps.mistake: Adding the onion at the start, so it releases water and the pork boils.
steps.fix: Onion goes in once the pork has browned.

steps.do: Check a thick slice of pork with the thermometer: 145°F (63°C) minimum; thin slices pass this quickly. Then add the spring onions and chilli and toss 30 seconds.
steps.look: Spring onions bright green and just wilted.
steps.mistake: Cooking the spring onions until limp.
steps.fix: They need only 30 seconds.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Drizzle with the remaining sesame oil and scatter the sesame seeds. Taste and add a pinch of sugar or a splash of soy if needed.
steps.look: A glossy, deep red stir-fry smelling of toasted sesame.
steps.mistake: Adding sesame oil over high heat, which burns off its aroma.
steps.fix: Sesame oil is a finishing oil; add it off the heat.

steps.do: Serve with rice and lettuce leaves. To eat as a wrap (ssam), lay a lettuce leaf in your palm, add a spoon of rice and a piece of pork, fold and eat in one bite.
steps.look: Hot, spicy pork against cool, crisp lettuce.
steps.mistake: Serving without anything to temper the heat.
steps.fix: Rice, lettuce and a side of kimchi or cucumber balance the spice.

science: Gochujang is a fermented paste of chilli, glutinous rice, soybeans and salt. Fermentation breaks starches into sugars and proteins into savoury amino acids, so the paste brings sweetness, heat and deep umami at once. That sugar is what caramelises on the pork edges, but sugars burn fast above about 350°F (175°C), so marinated meat demands a slightly lower heat than plain stir-fries and an eye on the pan floor. Slicing the pork thin and across the grain shortens the muscle fibres, making each bite tender and letting it cook through in minutes. Grated pear contains enzymes that soften surface proteins and adds natural sugar.
plating: Pile the pork in the centre of a warm platter, mounded high with the onions woven through. Scatter sesame seeds and a few fine rings of spring onion on top. Serve rice in individual bowls and stack the lettuce leaves beside the platter with small dishes of kimchi.

pairing.drink: An off-dry German Riesling. Its touch of sweetness cools the gochujang heat and its acidity cuts the pork fat. A cold lager also works.
pairing.brennans: Stein ‘Weihwasser’ Riesling Feinherb 2023: the off-dry Riesling on the list, cooling against gochujang heat

variations: Ojingeo bokkeum: the same marinade with squid, cooked for only 2 minutes.
Dak galbi style: boneless chicken thighs with cabbage and sweet potato, cooked to 165°F (74°C).
Milder version: halve the gochugaru and add an extra tbsp of soy and sugar.
safety: Pork must reach at least 145°F (63°C).
Marinate in the fridge, never on the counter, and throw away leftover marinade that touched raw meat.
Partly frozen meat slices more safely; keep your fingers curled under on the guiding hand.

title: Gà Kho Gừng (Caramel Ginger Chicken)
summary: Vietnamese caramel ginger chicken: bone-in chicken braised in a dark caramel with fish sauce, shallots and two additions of ginger, reduced until the sauce turns to a sticky glaze. Kho cooking uses a caramel taken nearly to bitter, which makes this the first meeting with sugar stages.
skills: a dark caramel as a savoury base
equipment: Heavy medium pot or deep skillet, about 3 quarts (3 litres), light coloured inside if possible so you can judge the caramel
Cleaver or heavy knife if chopping bone-in chicken
Small bowl of cold water and a pastry brush

ingredients.note: chopped into 2 inch (5 cm) pieces through the bone, or boneless thighs halved
half smashed, half cut into fine matchsticks

mise: Pat the chicken dry and toss with 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the fish sauce. Leave 15 minutes.
Peel the ginger. Cut half into 1/4 inch (6 mm) coins and smash them with the flat of the knife; cut the other half into fine matchsticks.
Slice the shallots, mince the garlic, slice the spring onions and chilli.
Measure everything and set it by the stove. Caramel moves fast, so the fish sauce, shallots and chicken must be within reach before the sugar goes in.

timeline.do: Toss chicken with fish sauce; prepare ginger and aromatics.
Make the dark caramel.
Shallots, fish sauce, chicken and smashed ginger in.
Simmer uncovered, turning, about 25 minutes.
Julienned ginger and black pepper in.
Spring onions on; serve with rice.

steps.do: Put the sugar and 1 tbsp (15 ml) water in the dry pot and set it over medium heat. Swirl the pot gently to dissolve the sugar; do not stir with a spoon. If crystals form on the sides, brush them down with a wet pastry brush.
steps.look: The sugar dissolves into a clear syrup and starts to bubble.
steps.mistake: Stirring, which can make the syrup crystallise into grainy sugar.
steps.fix: If it crystallises, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and heat gently to redissolve.

steps.do: Keep cooking, swirling, until the caramel turns from pale gold to amber and then to a deep mahogany, like strong tea or dark maple syrup. This takes 4 to 6 minutes; the last stage happens in seconds.
steps.look: Thin wisps of smoke and a smell that is rich and slightly bitter, like the edge of burnt sugar, but not acrid.
steps.mistake: Pulling it at light gold, which makes a sweet sauce without the bitter depth kho needs. Or letting it go black and acrid.
steps.fix: If it smells sharp and burnt and looks black, discard it once cool and start again. Never taste hot caramel.

steps.do: Immediately add the oil and shallots and stir 30 seconds. Then stand back and pour in the remaining 2 tbsp (30 ml) fish sauce; it will hiss and steam.
steps.look: The caramel loosens into a dark sauce; the shallots soften. A savoury, salty-sweet steam.
steps.mistake: Pouring the fish sauce in while leaning over the pot.
steps.fix: Pour at arm’s length and turn your face away. If the caramel seizes into lumps, keep stirring over the heat; it melts back.

steps.do: Add the chicken, smashed ginger and garlic. Turn the pieces to coat them in the caramel for 2 minutes.
steps.look: The chicken takes on a deep amber coat.
steps.mistake: Leaving the chicken still, so the caramel burns on the base.
steps.fix: Keep turning until coated.

steps.do: Add the water or coconut water, bring to a simmer and cook uncovered over medium-low heat for 20 to 25 minutes, turning the pieces every 5 minutes.
steps.look: The liquid bubbles steadily and reduces slowly; the chicken turns a rich brown.
steps.mistake: Covering the pot, which stops the reduction.
steps.fix: Leave it uncovered; reduction is the method.

steps.do: When the sauce has reduced to a few spoonfuls of dark, sticky glaze, add the julienned ginger and black pepper. Cook 3 to 5 minutes more, turning to coat.
steps.look: Large, slow bubbles; the sauce coats the chicken glossily. The fresh ginger smells sharp and bright.
steps.mistake: Reducing until the pan is dry and the sauce burns.
steps.fix: Add 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) water and scrape; you want a glaze, not a crust.

steps.do: Check the thickest piece: 165°F (74°C) minimum, near but not touching the bone; thighs are best at 175°F (79°C).
steps.look: Meat pulls from the bone; juices run clear.
steps.mistake: Undercooking bone-in pieces that look brown outside.
steps.fix: Add a splash of water, cover, and simmer 5 minutes more.

steps.do: Taste the sauce: it should be salty, sweet and faintly bitter, with ginger heat. Adjust with fish sauce or a pinch of sugar. Scatter spring onions and chilli and serve with plenty of rice.
steps.look: Glossy, dark chicken with a sharp ginger finish.
steps.mistake: Serving with too little rice; kho is meant to be salty and eaten with rice.
steps.fix: Serve generous rice and a plain green vegetable.

science: Sugar passes through stages as it heats. Above about 340°F (170°C) the molecules break apart and recombine into hundreds of new compounds: first buttery and sweet, then, as it darkens towards 375°F (190°C), increasingly bitter and roasted. Vietnamese kho deliberately takes the caramel to the dark end because the bitterness balances the salty fish sauce and gives depth and colour without soy. Fish sauce is fermented anchovy and salt, packed with glutamates that taste deeply savoury. The two ginger additions work differently: smashed ginger simmered long mellows and sweetens, while ginger added at the end keeps its sharp heat because its pungent compounds have not had time to break down.
plating: Serve in the pot or a warm clay pot on a board, with the pieces piled and glazed and the fresh ginger matchsticks visible on top. Scatter spring onions and chilli. Rice goes in individual bowls; spoon a little glaze over each person’s rice.

pairing.drink: An aromatic, off-dry Alsace Pinot Gris, with enough weight and sweetness for caramel and fish sauce, or a crisp lager.
pairing.brennans: Albert Boxler Pinot Gris 2020: the Alsace Pinot Gris on the list, weighty enough for caramel and fish sauce

variations: Cá kho: the same caramel method with thick catfish steaks, cooked gently 30 minutes.
Thịt kho: pork belly and boiled eggs in caramel and coconut water, simmered 1 1/2 hours.
Boneless version: halved boneless thighs simmered 15 minutes.
safety: Caramel is far hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Never touch or taste it hot, and keep children away from the stove.
Pour fish sauce into hot caramel at arm’s length; it spits violently.
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C).

title: Chicken Adobo
summary: The Philippine classic: chicken simmered in vinegar, soy, garlic, bay and black pepper, then browned and returned to its reduced, glossy sauce. Adobo reverses the usual order, simmer first and sear last, and teaches how cooked vinegar softens from sharp to rounded.
equipment: Heavy pot or deep skillet with a lid, about 4 quarts (4 litres), stainless or enamel (not bare aluminium or cast iron, which react with vinegar)
Separate skillet for browning, or a sheet pan under the overhead grill (broiler)

ingredients.item: Bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks

ingredients.note: Filipino soy if you can find it

mise: Put the chicken in a bowl with the soy, vinegar, garlic, bay and pepper. Turn to coat, cover and refrigerate 30 minutes (or up to overnight).
Crack the peppercorns under a heavy pan or in a mortar so they split but are not powdered.
Start the rice when the chicken goes on to simmer.

timeline.do: Marinate the chicken in the fridge.
Everything into the pot with water; simmer uncovered 10 minutes without stirring.
Cover and simmer 30 minutes, turning once.
Lift out the chicken and brown it. Reduce the sauce.
Chicken back into the glaze.
Serve over rice.

steps.do: Tip the chicken and all of its marinade into the pot, arrange the pieces skin side down in one layer, and add the water. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat.
steps.look: The liquid comes to a lively boil and the sharp smell of vinegar rises.
steps.mistake: Using a reactive pan, which gives a metallic taste.
steps.fix: Use stainless steel or enamel.

steps.do: Lower to a steady simmer and cook uncovered for 10 minutes without stirring.
steps.look: The harsh vinegar smell softens noticeably over the 10 minutes.
steps.mistake: Stirring or covering straight away, which, by Filipino kitchen tradition, traps the raw vinegar taste.
steps.fix: Leave it alone; let the sharpest acidity cook off in the open first.

steps.do: Turn the pieces skin side up, cover with the lid and simmer gently 25 to 30 minutes until tender.
steps.look: The meat is tender and beginning to pull back from the ends of the drumstick bones.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which toughens the chicken.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer with small, steady bubbles.

steps.do: Check the thickest piece with the thermometer: at least 165°F (74°C); 175 to 185°F (79 to 85°C) is best for thighs and legs. Lift the chicken onto a plate and pat the skin dry with paper towels.
steps.look: Tender, cooked chicken with pale, soft skin.
steps.mistake: Trying to brown wet skin, which spits and will not crisp.
steps.fix: Pat thoroughly dry.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken skin side down for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and crisp, then 1 minute on the other side. (Or cook skin side up under a hot overhead grill for 4 to 5 minutes.)
steps.look: Deep golden, blistered skin with a loud sizzle. The soy in the skin browns fast.
steps.mistake: Walking away; the soy-soaked skin can burn quickly.
steps.fix: Watch it closely and lower the heat if it darkens too fast.

steps.do: While the chicken browns, raise the heat under the pot and boil the sauce hard for 8 to 10 minutes until reduced by about two thirds. Stir in the brown sugar if using, and taste.
steps.look: The sauce darkens and turns glossy, coating a spoon. It tastes salty, tangy and rounded, with no raw vinegar sting.
steps.mistake: Reducing too far, so it becomes intensely salty.
steps.fix: Add a splash of water to bring it back.

steps.do: Return the browned chicken to the pot and turn it in the glaze for 1 minute. Fish out the bay leaves.
steps.look: Glossy, dark chicken with crisp edges.
steps.mistake: Simmering again for long, which softens the crisp skin.
steps.fix: One minute is enough to coat.

steps.do: Serve over plenty of rice with the soft garlic cloves and a spoon of sauce, scattered with spring onions.
steps.look: Rice soaking up the dark sauce.
steps.mistake: Too little rice; adobo sauce is meant for rice.
steps.fix: Serve generous rice.

science: Vinegar is acetic acid in water. That is why the smell changes so clearly in the first ten minutes. The acid also slightly firms the outside of the meat and helps the dish keep well, which suits a hot kitchen. Simmering first and browning last works because the skin, once rendered by the gentle braise, crisps very quickly in a hot pan, and the soy that soaked into it browns fast through the Maillard reaction.

pairing.brennans: Marcel Lapierre Morgon 2023: the Morgon on the list, juicy acidity for a vinegar braise

Pork adobo: 2 lb (900 g) pork belly or shoulder in 2 inch (5 cm) chunks, simmered 1 hour.
Adobong puti: leave out the soy and use salt, for a pale, sharp adobo.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C).
Marinate in the fridge. The marinade is boiled with the chicken, so it is safe to use as the sauce here.
Browning soy-soaked skin spits: lay pieces away from you.

title: Chana Masala
summary: Chickpeas simmered in a North Indian masala of slowly browned onion, ginger, garlic, tomato and ground spices, cooked until the oil separates from the sauce. That masala base, fried until it releases its oil, is the foundation of a great deal of North Indian cooking.
skills: an onion, ginger and tomato masala cooked until the oil separates
equipment: Heavy pot or deep sauté pan, about 4 quarts (4 litres)
Microplane or mortar for ginger and garlic paste

ingredients.note: drained and rinsed; or 1 1/4 cups (250 g) dried, soaked and cooked
for colour; or 1/2 tsp (1 g) cayenne
finely chopped or grated; or one 14 oz (400 g) can crushed

mise: Chop the onions finely and evenly; uneven pieces brown unevenly.
Grate the ginger and garlic to a paste. Slit the chilli.
Measure the ground coriander, cumin, turmeric and chilli powder into one small bowl, and the garam masala and amchur into another.
Grate the tomatoes on a box grater, discarding the skins, or open the can.
Drain and rinse the chickpeas. Chop the coriander. Start the rice.

timeline.do: Chop, grate and measure everything.
Bloom cumin seeds; brown the onions 12 to 15 minutes.
Ginger, garlic and ground spices; then tomatoes until the oil separates.
Chickpeas and water; simmer 15 minutes, mashing a few.
Garam masala and amchur off the heat.
Coriander on; serve with rice or naan.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and bay leaf and fry 20 to 30 seconds until the seeds crackle and darken one shade. This is the tadka.
steps.look: The seeds sizzle, pop and smell toasty and nutty.
steps.mistake: Burning the seeds black, which makes the whole dish bitter.
steps.fix: If they go black, wipe out the pot and start again; it costs only 30 seconds.

steps.do: Add the onions and a pinch of the salt. Cook 12 to 15 minutes, stirring every minute or so, until deep golden brown.
steps.look: The onions go from white to translucent to light gold to an even deep gold, and smell sweet and caramel-like.
steps.mistake: Rushing the onions on high heat or stopping at pale; under-browned onions give a thin, sharp masala.
steps.fix: Lower the heat if edges darken before the centres; add a splash of water if they stick.

steps.do: Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and stir 1 minute until the raw smell disappears.
steps.look: A fragrant steam; the paste turns from bright to pale.
steps.mistake: Burning the garlic paste on the hot base.
steps.fix: Lower the heat slightly before adding.

steps.do: Add the ground spices with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and stir constantly for 30 to 45 seconds.
steps.look: The spices darken slightly and smell toasted; the water stops them scorching.
steps.mistake: Frying dry ground spices too long, which burns them in seconds.
steps.fix: The splash of water is your insurance; add more if they stick.

steps.do: Add the tomatoes and the rest of the salt. Cook 8 to 12 minutes, stirring and scraping often, until the mixture thickens to a paste, pulls away from the sides of the pan, and the oil separates and glistens at the edges.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, brick red masala with small beads of red oil around the rim and on the surface. It no longer tastes of raw tomato.
steps.mistake: Adding the chickpeas while the tomatoes are still watery; the masala then tastes stewed, not fried.
steps.fix: Keep cooking and stirring. The oil separating is the sign that the water has gone and the masala has fried.

steps.do: Add the chickpeas and water, stir and bring to a simmer. Cook 15 minutes over medium-low heat, stirring now and then. Mash about a quarter of the chickpeas against the side of the pan.
steps.look: The sauce thickens and turns creamy as the mashed chickpeas dissolve into it.
steps.mistake: Adding too much water, giving a thin soup.
steps.fix: Simmer uncovered a little longer to reduce, or mash more chickpeas.

steps.do: Take the pot off the heat. Stir in the garam masala and amchur. Taste and adjust the salt; it should be tangy, warm and savoury.
steps.look: A bright, sour lift in the finish and a warm, aromatic smell.
steps.mistake: Adding garam masala early and cooking out its fragrance.
steps.fix: Always add it at the end.

steps.do: Scatter the coriander, set lemon wedges alongside and serve with rice or warm naan.
steps.look: A thick, glossy curry clinging to the chickpeas.
steps.mistake: Serving it too thin.
steps.fix: Let it stand 5 minutes; it thickens as it sits.

science: Many flavour compounds in spices are fat soluble, so blooming whole cumin in hot oil, a tadka, releases them into the fat that then carries them through the dish. Browning onions slowly converts their sugars and amino acids into sweet, deep flavours through caramelisation and the Maillard reaction. The masala is ready when the oil separates because, once the water from the tomatoes and onions has evaporated, there is nothing left to hold the fat in suspension; it pools at the edges, and the remaining solids can then fry rather than boil, deepening in flavour. Mashing some chickpeas releases starch that thickens the sauce from within.
plating: Ladle into a warm bowl, smoothing the top with the back of the ladle. Scatter coriander and a few fine rings of onion or slivers of ginger across one side, and set a lemon wedge on the rim. Serve rice in a separate bowl or naan folded in a basket.

pairing.drink: An aromatic, off-dry white such as Alsace Gewurztraminer or Riesling, or a mango lassi. Sweetness and spice notes in the wine suit garam masala.

variations: Pindi chole: add a tea bag while simmering the chickpeas for a dark colour, and finish with a tadka of ghee and green chilli.
Chana saag: stir in 5 oz (140 g) baby spinach in the last 3 minutes.
Rajma masala: the same base with kidney beans, simmered 25 minutes.
safety: Cool leftovers within 2 hours and reheat until steaming throughout, 165°F (74°C).
If cooking dried kidney beans for the variation, boil them hard for 10 minutes first to destroy a natural toxin; chickpeas do not need this.

title: Thai Green Curry with Chicken
summary: Chicken simmered in a green curry made by frying the paste in cracked coconut cream until the oil separates, then balanced with fish sauce, palm sugar and Thai basil. Frying paste in coconut cream until it splits is the Thai cousin of the Indian masala, and the balance of salty, sweet and hot is a seasoning lesson in itself.
skills: frying curry paste in cracked coconut cream
balancing fish sauce, palm sugar and lime
equipment: Wok or heavy 3 quart (3 litre) saucepan
Can opener and a spoon to scoop the cream

ingredients.note: choose one without stabilisers if you can; it cracks more easily
Thai brands such as Maesri or Mae Ploy; use 3 tbsp (45 g) for milder
sliced 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick, bite sized

ingredients.item: Thai aubergines or 1 small Japanese aubergine
ingredients.note: Thai aubergines quartered, or 1 inch (2.5 cm) pieces

ingredients.item: Palm sugar or light brown sugar

ingredients.note: only if your coconut cream will not split

mise: Open the coconut milk without shaking it. Spoon the thick cream from the top, about 1/2 cup (120 ml), into one bowl and leave the thin milk in the can.
Slice the chicken thin across the grain. Cut the aubergines. Drain the bamboo shoots.
Tear the lime leaves and remove the tough centre rib.
Shave or chop the palm sugar. Pick the basil leaves. Slice the chilli.
Start the rice.

timeline.do: Rice on. Separate the coconut cream; prepare chicken and vegetables.
Crack the coconut cream and fry the paste.
Chicken in, then thin coconut milk, stock, lime leaves, aubergine.
Simmer until chicken and aubergine are tender.
Season with fish sauce and palm sugar; taste and balance.
Basil in off the heat; serve with rice.

steps.do: Put the thick coconut cream in the wok over medium heat. Bring it to a bubble and cook, stirring often, for 3 to 5 minutes until it reduces, turns thick and the oil separates out in clear, shiny pools. This is cracking the cream.
steps.look: The cream bubbles, thickens, then breaks: you see clear oil around white curds and hear a light frying sound instead of a bubble.
steps.mistake: Stopping before it splits, so the paste simmers rather than fries.
steps.fix: Some brands contain stabilisers that stop the oil separating. After 5 minutes, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) neutral oil and carry on.

steps.do: Add the curry paste and fry it in the separated oil for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring and pressing it into the fat.
steps.look: The paste darkens a shade, smells intensely fragrant of lemongrass and chilli, and the oil turns green tinged.
steps.mistake: Rushing this step; raw paste tastes harsh and grassy.
steps.fix: Keep frying until the smell changes from raw to rounded and toasty; lower the heat if it sticks.

steps.do: Add the chicken and stir for 2 minutes until every piece is coated in paste and has turned opaque on the outside.
steps.look: Chicken pieces turning white at the edges, glossy with green paste.
steps.mistake: Adding all the liquid first and poaching the chicken in a bland broth.
steps.fix: Coat the meat in paste first; it seasons the surface.

steps.do: Pour in the thin coconut milk from the can and the stock. Add the lime leaves, aubergine and bamboo shoots. Bring to a gentle simmer.
steps.look: A pale green, oil-flecked curry bubbling gently, the lime leaves giving off a citrus scent.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which can make coconut milk grainy.
steps.fix: Keep a gentle simmer with small bubbles.

steps.do: Simmer 8 to 10 minutes until the aubergine is tender and the chicken is cooked. Check a piece of chicken: 165°F (74°C).
steps.look: Aubergine soft and translucent at the edges; chicken opaque through.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the aubergine into mush.
steps.fix: Thai aubergines need about 8 minutes; check one with a knife.

steps.do: Season with 1 1/2 tbsp (22 ml) fish sauce and the palm sugar. Taste. Green curry should lead with heat and salt, with sweetness behind. Add fish sauce for salt, sugar to round, a few drops at a time.
steps.look: A curry that tastes hot, salty and fragrant with a soft sweet finish.
steps.mistake: Seasoning by measurement alone, without tasting.
steps.fix: Adjust in small amounts and taste between each addition.

steps.do: Take the wok off the heat. Stir in the Thai basil and red chilli; the basil should wilt in the residual heat.
steps.look: Bright green basil just collapsing, with a sweet anise perfume rising.
steps.mistake: Adding basil over the heat and cooking it to a black, limp tangle.
steps.fix: Basil goes in off the heat, at the last moment.

steps.do: Ladle into bowls and serve with jasmine rice on the side.
steps.look: A loose, oil-flecked curry: it should be soupy, not thick.
steps.mistake: Reducing it to a thick gravy.
steps.fix: Thai curries are meant to be spooned over rice; add a splash of stock if it has thickened.

science: Coconut milk is an emulsion of coconut fat droplets in water, held together by proteins. Heating the thick cream drives off water until those proteins can no longer keep the fat dispersed, and it separates into clear oil and solids, which is the cracking. That oil is what fries the paste. Frying matters because many aromatic compounds in chilli, lemongrass, galangal and shrimp paste dissolve in fat and only develop their full, rounded flavour at frying temperatures well above boiling. Simmer the paste in liquid alone and it stays near 212°F (100°C), tasting raw. Basil goes in last because its fragrant oils, especially the anise-scented ones in Thai basil, evaporate quickly with heat.
plating: Serve the curry in a deep bowl with a ladle, a few whole basil leaves and chilli slices floating on top and the green-tinged oil glistening on the surface. Rice goes in a separate bowl or moulded in a small cup and turned out on the plate beside a shallow bowl of curry.

pairing.drink: An off-dry Riesling or Gewurztraminer: a little sweetness calms the chilli, and aromatic grapes echo lime leaf and basil. A cold Thai lager also works.
pairing.brennans: Stein ‘Weihwasser’ Riesling Feinherb 2023: the off-dry Riesling on the list, a little sweetness to calm the chilli

variations: Red curry with duck: red paste, sliced roast duck breast, pineapple and cherry tomatoes.
Vegetable green curry: tofu, green beans and courgette, with soy sauce in place of fish sauce.
Green curry with fish balls or shrimp, added for the last 3 minutes only.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C).
Wash hands after slicing fresh chilli and keep them away from your eyes.
Some curry pastes contain shrimp paste: tell guests if they ask what is in the dish.

title: Maafe (Groundnut Stew)
summary: A Senegalese and West African stew of beef simmered in tomato and thickened with groundnut paste, with sweet potato, carrot and cabbage, cooked until the peanut oil rises and shines on top. It teaches slow simmering until meat is tender and how to read, and skim, the oil a finished stew releases.
equipment: Heavy pot or Dutch oven, about 5 quarts (5 litres), with a lid
Wooden spoon with a flat edge for scraping the base
Ladle and a shallow spoon for skimming

ingredients.note: cut into 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) cubes; or bone-in lamb shoulder
left whole and unbroken; pierce once for more heat

ingredients.item: Natural peanut butter, smooth and unsweetened

mise: Pat the beef dry and season with 1 tsp (6 g) salt and the pepper.
Chop the onion, mince the garlic and grate the ginger.
Peel and cut the carrots and sweet potato into large, even chunks so they hold their shape in the long simmer. Cut the cabbage into wedges, keeping a little core on each so they stay together.
Warm the stock.
Stir the peanut butter in its jar so the oil is mixed back in before measuring.

timeline.do: Season the beef; cut vegetables.
Brown the beef in batches; soften onion, garlic, ginger; fry the tomato paste.
Tomatoes, stock, bay and Scotch bonnet in; simmer 1 hour partly covered.
Whisk in the peanut butter; add carrots and sweet potato. Simmer uncovered.
Cabbage in. Rice on.
Skim some oil, remove the chilli, taste and serve.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the pot over medium-high heat until shimmering. Brown the beef in two batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side, without crowding. Lift each batch onto a plate.
steps.look: Deep brown crust on at least two sides of each cube and brown fond on the pot base.
steps.mistake: Crowding all the beef in at once, which steams it grey.
steps.fix: Brown in batches; the colour is flavour for the whole stew.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and cook 6 to 8 minutes, scraping up the fond, until soft and lightly golden. Add the garlic and ginger and cook 1 minute.
steps.look: Soft, golden onion; the fond dissolving into it.
steps.mistake: Leaving the fond to burn while the onions cook.
steps.fix: Add a splash of water to lift it if it darkens too fast.

steps.do: Stir in the tomato paste and fry 2 minutes, stirring constantly.
steps.look: The paste darkens from bright red to a deeper brick red and smells sweet.
steps.mistake: Adding liquid before the paste has fried, leaving a raw tomato taste.
steps.fix: Give it the full 2 minutes, scraping so it does not burn.

steps.do: Add the crushed tomatoes, stock, bay leaves and the whole Scotch bonnet. Return the beef and its juices. Bring to a boil, then lower to a gentle simmer, partly cover and cook 1 hour.
steps.look: Steady small bubbles; the beef starting to soften.
steps.mistake: Breaking the Scotch bonnet, which can make the stew fiercely hot.
steps.fix: Stir gently around the chilli. If it bursts, taste early and add more stock or tomato to dilute.

steps.do: Ladle about 1 cup (240 ml) of hot broth into a bowl with the peanut butter and whisk until smooth and pourable. Stir it back into the pot.
steps.look: A smooth, creamy orange broth with no lumps of peanut butter.
steps.mistake: Adding cold peanut butter straight to the pot, where it forms lumps that scorch on the base.
steps.fix: Whisk it loose first; any lumps left will melt as you stir.

steps.do: Add the carrots and sweet potato. Simmer uncovered over medium-low heat for 35 to 40 minutes, stirring and scraping the base every 5 minutes.
steps.look: The sauce thickens and darkens to a rich reddish brown; the vegetables become tender.
steps.mistake: Leaving it unstirred, so the peanut sauce catches and burns on the base.
steps.fix: Scrape the bottom often. If it does catch, move the stew to a clean pot without scraping up the burnt layer.

steps.do: Nestle the cabbage wedges into the stew for the last 15 to 20 minutes, spooning sauce over them.
steps.look: Cabbage wedges wilted and tender, holding together.
steps.mistake: Adding cabbage too early, so it disintegrates.
steps.fix: Add it near the end.

steps.do: The stew is done when the beef is fork tender, the sauce clings to a spoon and a layer of reddish oil has risen and shines on the surface. Skim off some of that oil with a shallow spoon if you prefer it lighter, leaving a sheen. Remove the Scotch bonnet and bay leaves.
steps.look: A glossy, thick sauce with beads and a thin layer of red oil on top. The beef breaks apart with a fork.
steps.mistake: Stopping before the oil rises, when the peanut still tastes raw and pasty.
steps.fix: Simmer longer. The oil rising is the sign the peanut has cooked through.

steps.do: Taste and season with salt. Serve over rice with the vegetables arranged around the meat.
steps.look: Rich, savoury, gently hot, nutty but not sweet.
steps.mistake: Undersalting, which leaves peanut stews tasting flat and sweet.
steps.fix: Salt in small additions, tasting each time.

science: Beef chuck is full of collagen, the tough connective tissue that makes it chewy if cooked quickly. In a long simmer at 180 to 200°F (82 to 93°C), collagen slowly converts to gelatin, which makes the meat tender and gives the sauce body. Peanut butter is about half fat. As the stew simmers, water evaporates and the peanut proteins and starches cook and thicken, until the fat can no longer stay suspended and rises as a red-tinted oil, coloured by the tomato. That separation, like the oil in a finished masala, shows the raw paste has cooked into a sauce. Skimming some is a matter of taste.
plating: Spoon rice into a wide, shallow bowl, slightly to one side. Ladle the stew beside and over part of the rice, then arrange a piece of sweet potato, a carrot chunk and a cabbage wedge on top so each vegetable shows. Spoon a little of the glossy red oil over the meat. Add a few slices of fresh chilli for those who want it.

pairing.drink: A fruity, medium-bodied red with soft tannins, such as Barbera: its acidity cuts the peanut richness. A ginger beer also suits it.
pairing.brennans: La Miraja ‘Le Masche’ Barbera d’Asti 2023: the Barbera on the list, its acidity cutting the peanut

variations: Chicken maafe: bone-in thighs browned and simmered only 30 minutes before the peanut goes in.
Vegetable maafe: double the sweet potato, add chickpeas and okra, and use vegetable stock.
Lamb maafe: bone-in lamb shoulder, simmered 1 1/2 hours before the peanut.
safety: Peanuts are a common and serious allergen; tell anyone you cook for that the stew is built on them.
Wear gloves to handle cut Scotch bonnet, and never touch your eyes after handling it.
Cool leftovers within 2 hours and reheat to 165°F (74°C).

title: Beef Fajitas
summary: Skirt steak marinated in citrus, garlic and cumin, seared hard over the highest heat, rested and sliced thin across the grain, with charred onions and peppers and warm tortillas. Skirt steak teaches the single most important carving rule: always slice across the grain.
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) cast-iron skillet, griddle or a very hot outdoor grill
Zip-top bag or shallow dish for marinating
Large board with a groove to catch juices
Clean kitchen towel or tortilla warmer
mise: Pull off any shiny silverskin from the steak with a knife tip and your fingers. Cut the steak into pieces about 6 inches (15 cm) long so it fits the pan. Look at the meat and notice the grain: the long fibres run across the width of the strip, not along it.

Whisk the lime and orange juice, 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil, garlic, cumin, chilli powder, soy, salt and pepper. Put the steak and marinade in the bag, press out the air and refrigerate 1 to 4 hours, no longer.
Slice the onion and peppers into strips of even width.
Prepare the pico de gallo, guacamole, sour cream, lime and coriander in small bowls.
Wrap the tortillas in a clean towel ready to warm.

timeline.do: Trim the steak; marinate in the fridge 1 to 4 hours.
Slice the vegetables; set out the toppings.
Heat the cast iron for 8 to 10 minutes. Pat the steak dry.
Sear the steak 2 to 4 minutes a side; rest it.
Char the onions and peppers; warm the tortillas.
Slice across the grain and serve everything at once.

steps.do: Take the steak out of the marinade, scrape off the garlic and pat it very dry with paper towels. Throw the marinade away.
steps.look: Dry, matte surfaces with no pooling liquid.
steps.mistake: Searing wet meat, which steams instead of browning.
steps.fix: Dry it again; the sear depends on it.

steps.do: Heat the cast iron over high heat for 8 to 10 minutes until it smokes faintly. Add 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil and swirl.
steps.look: The oil shimmers and smokes immediately.
steps.mistake: Cooking skirt on a medium pan, so it greys and toughens before it browns.
steps.fix: Wait for the smoke; skirt wants the hottest pan you can make.

steps.do: Lay the steak in, away from you, and sear without moving for 2 to 3 minutes until deeply browned, then turn and sear 2 to 3 minutes more.
steps.look: A loud sizzle, a dark brown crust with some charred spots, and a savoury, slightly smoky smell.
steps.mistake: Moving it around, which stops the crust forming.
steps.fix: Leave it alone; turn only once.

steps.do: Check the thickest part. The USDA safe minimum for whole cuts of beef is 145°F (63°C) followed by a 3 minute rest. Skirt is traditionally served medium-rare, pulled at 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C) to finish near 135°F (57°C) after resting. Choose the 145°F (63°C) mark for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or with a weakened immune system.
steps.look: The meat feels springy, like the flesh at the base of your thumb when you touch thumb to middle finger, for medium-rare.
steps.mistake: Cooking skirt well done, which makes it tough and chewy.
steps.fix: Pull it a few degrees early; it rises as it rests.

steps.do: Move the steak to the board and rest 5 to 10 minutes, loosely tented with foil.
steps.look: Juices settle; only a little pools on the board.
steps.mistake: Slicing immediately, so the juice floods out.
steps.fix: Use the rest time to cook the vegetables.

steps.do: Add the remaining oil to the hot pan. Add the onion and peppers in an even layer, season with a pinch of salt and cook over high heat for 6 to 8 minutes, tossing only every minute or two, until charred at the edges but still slightly crisp.
steps.look: Blackened edges, softened but not limp strips and a sweet, smoky smell. The browned juices from the steak coat them.
steps.mistake: Stirring constantly, which stops them charring.
steps.fix: Let them sit between tosses; cook in two batches if the pan is crowded.

steps.do: Warm the tortillas one at a time in a dry pan over medium heat for 20 to 30 seconds a side until soft and lightly spotted. Stack them in the towel.
steps.look: Soft, pliable tortillas with a few golden spots.
steps.mistake: Serving cold tortillas, which crack when folded.
steps.fix: Keep them wrapped in the towel; they steam and stay soft.

steps.do: Slice the steak: first cut each piece into 5 inch (13 cm) lengths following the grain, then turn each length 90 degrees and slice it across the grain, on a slight angle, into 1/4 inch (6 mm) strips.
steps.look: Each slice shows short fibre ends on its cut face, and the meat is pink and tender.
steps.mistake: Slicing along the grain, which leaves long fibres and chewy strips however well it was cooked.
steps.fix: If a slice feels stringy, turn the knife 90 degrees; you are going with the grain.

steps.do: Serve the steak and vegetables on a hot platter or straight from the skillet with tortillas, pico de gallo, guacamole, sour cream, lime and coriander, and let everyone build their own.
steps.look: A sizzling platter of pink steak and charred vegetables.
steps.mistake: Letting it all go cold while you set the table.
steps.fix: Set the table and toppings before you slice.

science: Skirt steak comes from the diaphragm, a hard-working muscle with long, coarse fibres running across its width. Those fibres are strong and chewy if you bite along them, but slicing across the grain cuts them into short lengths that your teeth separate easily. The citrus marinade flavours the surface, but acid also begins to break down surface proteins, so beyond four hours the outside turns mushy and grey. Skirt is thin, so it needs extreme heat to brown before the centre overcooks. Resting lets the muscle fibres relax and the juices, which are pushed to the centre by heat, redistribute so they stay in the meat when you slice.
plating: Bring the cast iron to the table on a board, still sizzling: vegetables in a bed on one side, the sliced steak fanned across the top in overlapping rows so the pink centres show. Scatter coriander and set lime wedges at the edge. Put the toppings in small bowls around it and tortillas in a folded towel.

pairing.drink: A Paloma or a classic margarita, whose lime and salt mirror the marinade, or a juicy Zinfandel with enough fruit for the char.
pairing.brennans: Ridge Vineyards ‘Lytton Springs’ Dry Creek Valley 2021 (375 ml): the Zinfandel blend on the list, ripe fruit for charred steak

variations: Chicken fajitas: boneless thighs in the same marinade, cooked to 165°F (74°C).
Shrimp fajitas: marinate 20 minutes only and sear 1 minute a side.
Portobello fajitas: thick mushroom slices seared hard with the peppers.
safety: The USDA safe minimum for whole beef cuts is 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest; medium-rare is a choice, not the safe standard, for vulnerable diners.
Never reuse marinade that touched raw meat as a sauce unless you boil it for at least 1 minute.
Cast iron stays dangerously hot for a long time; always use a mitt and warn diners if it goes to the table.

title: Picadillo Cubano
summary: Cuban picadillo: minced beef browned hard, simmered with a sofrito of onion, pepper and garlic, tomato and dry wine, then balanced with olives, capers, raisins and crisp potato. The sofrito and the balance of salty, sweet and sour make a quick weeknight dish into a lesson in seasoning.

ingredients.item: Minced beef chuck, about 20 percent fat

ingredients.note: peeled, cut in 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) dice

ingredients.item: Green cubanelle or green bell pepper

ingredients.note: mashed to a paste with a pinch of salt
grated, skin discarded; or 1/2 cup (120 ml) tomato sauce

ingredients.item: White rice, black beans and fried sweet plantains

mise: Dice the potato into even 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) cubes, rinse and pat completely dry.
Finely dice the onion and pepper to the same size, about 1/4 inch (6 mm). Mash the garlic.
Grate the tomato. Halve the olives, rinse the capers, measure the raisins.
Keep the beef cold until it goes in the pan, and do not salt it in advance.

timeline.do: Dice the potato and the sofrito vegetables. Rice on.
Fry the potato until golden; lift out.
Brown the beef as one layer; break it up and salt it.
Sofrito into the fat, then cumin and oregano.
Tomato, wine and bay; then olives, capers, raisins.
Vinegar and potatoes in; season and serve.

steps.do: Heat the olive oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Fry the potato in one layer for 8 to 10 minutes, turning every couple of minutes, until golden on the edges and tender inside. Lift onto paper towels and salt lightly.
steps.look: Golden, crisp-edged cubes; a knife slides in easily.
steps.mistake: Stirring constantly, so they never brown, or crowding them.
steps.fix: Leave them for a minute between turns. Cook in batches if needed.

steps.do: Pour off all but 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the oil. Raise the heat to high. Add the beef and press it into one flat layer across the pan. Leave it completely still for 4 to 5 minutes.
steps.look: A loud sizzle; the underside forms a deep brown crust and releases from the pan on its own.
steps.mistake: Stirring and breaking it up immediately, so the meat greys and stews in its juice.
steps.fix: Resist touching it. If the pan is small, brown in two batches.

steps.do: Turn the beef over in large pieces, then break it into small crumbles with the spoon. Season it now with 1 tsp (6 g) salt and the pepper. Cook 2 minutes more.
steps.look: Brown crumbs with crisp edges, fat rendering out.
steps.mistake: Salting the raw mince in a bowl beforehand, which makes it bind into springy pellets.
steps.fix: Salt in the pan, after browning.

steps.do: Push the beef to one side. Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion and pepper to the cleared space in the rendered fat and cook 5 to 6 minutes until soft and slumped. Add the garlic for 1 minute.
steps.look: Soft, translucent onion and pepper; a sweet, fragrant smell.
steps.mistake: Browning the sofrito hard; it should be soft and sweet.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and stir often.

steps.do: Sprinkle the cumin and oregano over the vegetables and stir them into the fat for 30 seconds, then mix everything together.
steps.look: A toasty, warm smell as the spices bloom.
steps.mistake: Adding the spices with the liquid, where they taste raw.
steps.fix: Bloom them in fat first.

steps.do: Add the grated tomato, wine and bay leaves. Simmer 5 minutes until the liquid reduces and the fat rises and shines on top. Fold in the olives, capers and raisins and cook 8 to 10 minutes more.
steps.look: A thick, glossy mixture with no pool of liquid; raisins plumped.
steps.mistake: Leaving it watery, so it slides off the rice.
steps.fix: Simmer longer, uncovered.

steps.do: Check the temperature: minced beef must reach 160°F (71°C), which it will have passed long ago. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the vinegar and the potatoes.
steps.look: The potatoes stay crisp on the outside.
steps.mistake: Adding the potatoes early, so they turn soft.
steps.fix: Potatoes go in at the very end.

steps.do: Taste and balance: it should land savoury first, then sweet, then sour. Add salt for savoury, a few more raisins for sweet, a splash of vinegar or olive brine for sour. Remove the bay leaves.
steps.look: A lively mix where no single note shouts.
steps.mistake: Seasoning only with salt.
steps.fix: Balance with the brine, raisins and vinegar as well.

science: Browning minced meat follows the same rule as any sear: the surface must be dry and hot enough, above about 285°F (140°C), for the Maillard reaction. Spread in a still layer, the meat browns; stirred and crowded, it releases water and drops to boiling point, turning grey. Salting raw mince early dissolves the protein myosin, which then binds the meat into a firm, springy mass, perfect for kofta but wrong for loose picadillo. The sofrito sweats gently because onion and pepper turn sweet when their cell walls soften slowly. Balancing salty olives and capers against sweet raisins and sour vinegar works because each taste makes the others clearer.
plating: Mould white rice in a small bowl and turn it out to one side of a warm plate. Spoon the picadillo beside it in a generous mound, showing the olives and potatoes on top. Add a ladle of black beans in a small dish or on the plate and three slices of fried sweet plantain fanned at the edge.

pairing.drink: A Rioja Crianza, whose red fruit and soft oak suit the cumin and raisins, or a classic daiquiri.
pairing.brennans: López de Heredia ‘Viña Cubillo’ Rioja Crianza 2016: the Rioja Crianza on the list, red fruit for cumin and raisins

variations: Picadillo empanadas: cool the mixture and use it to fill pastry rounds, then bake at 400°F (200°C) for 20 minutes.
Pumpkin picadillo: add diced calabaza in place of potato and simmer until tender.
Mexican style: add chopped tomato, serrano chilli and diced carrot, without olives or raisins.
safety: Minced beef must reach 160°F (71°C).
Fry potatoes dry: water in hot oil spits.
Cool leftovers within 2 hours.
