title: Arroz con Pollo
summary: Latin American chicken and rice: bone-in chicken browned, a sofrito cooked down with tomato and annatto, the rice toasted in the fat and steamed under a lid with stock, olives and peas. A one-pot rice teaches the liquid ratio and the discipline of leaving the lid alone.
skills: cooking rice with stock and saffron or achiote without stirring
equipment: Wide heavy pot or Dutch oven with a tight lid, about 5 quarts (5 litres) and 11 inches (28 cm) across

ingredients.item: Bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks

ingredients.us: 1 tsp annatto, or a large pinch saffron
ingredients.note: saffron crumbled into 2 tbsp (30 ml) warm stock
plus 2 tbsp (30 ml) of their brine

mise: Pat the chicken dry and season all over with 1 tsp (6 g) salt. Leave at room temperature 20 minutes.
Rinse the rice in the sieve under cold water, swirling, until the water runs nearly clear. Drain well for at least 10 minutes so it is not dripping.
Mince the onion, pepper and garlic finely; grate the tomato.
Heat the stock. If using saffron, crumble it into 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the warm stock.
Measure the wine, olives and brine. Leave the peas in the freezer.

timeline.do: Season the chicken; rinse and drain the rice.
Brown the chicken, skin side first.
Sofrito, tomato and annatto in the same fat until the oil runs orange.
Toast the rice 2 minutes; wine; hot stock and olives; chicken on top.
Lid on, lowest heat, 22 to 25 minutes. Do not lift the lid.
Peas on, lid back, off the heat 10 minutes. Check the chicken. Fluff and serve.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the pot over medium-high heat. Add the chicken skin side down and cook without moving for 7 to 8 minutes until the skin is deep brown and releases by itself. Turn and cook 2 minutes more. Lift onto a plate.
steps.look: Even deep golden skin and brown fond on the pot floor.
steps.mistake: Moving the chicken early, tearing the skin.
steps.fix: Wait until it releases on its own.

steps.do: Pour off all but about 3 tbsp (45 ml) of fat. Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion, pepper and garlic and cook 5 minutes until soft and sweet, scraping up the fond.
steps.look: Translucent, soft vegetables with no hard browning.
steps.mistake: Burning the fond while the vegetables cook.
steps.fix: Add a splash of stock to lift the fond if it darkens.

steps.do: Add the tomato, oregano, bay and annatto (if using saffron, it goes in with the stock). Cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the mixture darkens and the oil runs orange at the edges.
steps.look: A thick, jammy sofrito with orange oil pooling at the rim.
steps.mistake: Adding the rice to a watery sofrito, which changes the liquid ratio.
steps.fix: Cook until the tomato water has evaporated.

steps.do: Add the drained rice and stir 2 minutes until every grain is coated with fat and the edges turn slightly translucent.
steps.look: Glossy, orange grains; a faint toasty smell; some grains turning chalky white at the tips.
steps.mistake: Adding wet rice, which steams and clumps.
steps.fix: Drain the rice thoroughly; spread it on a towel if needed.

steps.do: Pour in the wine and stir until it boils away, about 1 minute. Add the hot stock (and saffron), olives and brine. Stir once, taste the liquid: it should taste a little saltier than you would like the rice. Add salt if needed.
steps.look: A lively boil; the liquid tastes well seasoned.
steps.mistake: Underseasoning the liquid; rice cannot be seasoned evenly afterwards.
steps.fix: Adjust now, before the lid goes on.

steps.do: Nestle the chicken pieces skin side up on top of the rice, pressing them in slightly, with any juices from the plate. Bring back to a boil, cover tightly and turn the heat to the lowest setting. Cook 22 to 25 minutes without lifting the lid.
steps.look: Steam escaping gently from under the lid; a quiet bubbling sound.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid to check or stirring the rice, which lets out the steam and leaves the top layer hard and chalky.
steps.fix: Trust the time. If your lid is loose, put a sheet of foil under it.

steps.do: Take the pot off the heat. Lift the lid quickly, scatter the peas over, and replace the lid. Rest 10 minutes.
steps.look: The rice has absorbed all the liquid, with small steam holes on the surface.
steps.mistake: Serving immediately, when the rice is wet at the bottom and firm on top.
steps.fix: The rest evens out the moisture; do not skip it.

steps.do: Check the thickest thigh near the bone: at least 165°F (74°C); thighs are best at 175°F (79°C). If a piece is short, put it on a sheet pan in a 375°F (190°C) oven for 5 to 10 minutes while the rice rests.
steps.look: Juices clear, meat pulling from the bone.
steps.mistake: Serving chicken that is pink at the bone.
steps.fix: Always check; the oven rescue costs only minutes.

steps.do: Fluff the rice gently with a fork from the edges inward, lifting rather than stirring. Remove the bay leaves. Garnish with red pepper strips and coriander.
steps.look: Separate, tender, golden grains, each one distinct.
steps.mistake: Stirring with a spoon, which mashes the grains.
steps.fix: Use a fork and a light hand.

science: Coating rice in hot fat before liquid arrives, the pilaf method, seals the outer starch so water enters more slowly and the grains stay separate instead of turning sticky. Rinsing first removes loose surface starch that would otherwise make the pot gluey. The liquid ratio, about 1 3/4 parts liquid to 1 part rice by volume here, accounts for the wine and tomato and the juice the chicken gives up. Rice cooks in steam as much as in water, so lifting the lid lets the steam escape and the top layer stays hard. During the rest off the heat, moisture moves from the wetter bottom to the drier top, evening out the texture.
plating: Bring the pot to the table and serve from it, chicken on top, peas and red pepper strips bright against the golden rice. For plates, spoon a mound of rice in the centre, set a thigh and a drumstick against it, and scatter coriander and a few olives.

pairing.drink: A Spanish white such as Albariño, or a light red Garnacha. Both have the freshness for saffron or annatto and enough body for chicken.
pairing.brennans: Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025: the Albariño on the list, fresh enough for saffron and chicken

variations: Puerto Rican style: add sofrito made with culantro and ají dulce, and a little sazón with annatto.
Arroz con pollo with beer, a Peruvian style: green rice coloured with puréed coriander and a splash of lager.
Oven method: after adding the stock, cover and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 30 minutes.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point near the bone.

Cooked rice must be cooled quickly and refrigerated within 1 hour of finishing if not eaten, because spores of Bacillus cereus survive cooking and multiply at room temperature. Reheat until steaming hot.
Lift lids away from your face.

title: Shrimp and Grits
summary: Slow-cooked stone-ground grits enriched with butter and sharp cheddar, crowned with shrimp seared in bacon fat and finished in a quick pan sauce made from their own shells. Grits are a porridge for dinner, and the shrimp pan sauce pulls together the browning, deglazing and butter-mounting lessons of the whole level. It is also a dish your restaurant serves in its own New Orleans way.
equipment: Heavy medium saucepan with a lid, about 3 quarts (3 litres), for the grits
Small saucepan for the shell stock

ingredients.note: 3 tbsp (42 g) for the grits, 2 tbsp (28 g) cold for the sauce
cut into 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) pieces; or 4 oz (115 g) andouille, sliced

mise: Peel and devein the shrimp, keeping the shells. Simmer the shells in the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) water for 15 minutes, then strain. You should have about 1 cup (240 ml) of stock.
Pat the shrimp dry, season with 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt and the Creole seasoning, and refrigerate.
Grate the cheese. Cut the bacon. Mince the shallot and garlic. Slice the spring onions. Cube the cold butter for the sauce and keep it chilled.
Put the grits in a bowl and cover with water; skim off any husks that float, then drain. This is optional but cleans stone-ground grits.

timeline.do: Peel the shrimp; simmer the shell stock.
Start the grits; stir every 5 minutes for 45 to 50 minutes.
Render the bacon until crisp.
Sear the shrimp in the drippings; lift out underdone.
Finish the grits with butter and cheese. Build the pan sauce.
Shrimp back for 30 seconds; spoon over the grits.

steps.do: Bring the milk, 2 cups (480 ml) water and 1 tsp (6 g) salt to a simmer in the saucepan over medium heat. Pour in the grits in a slow, steady stream, whisking constantly.
steps.look: The grits swirl evenly through the liquid with no clumps.
steps.mistake: Dumping the grits in at once, which forms lumps that stay raw inside.
steps.fix: Whisk hard; break any lumps against the side of the pan.

steps.do: Lower the heat to the lowest setting so the grits barely bubble. Cover and cook 45 to 50 minutes, stirring well every 5 minutes and scraping the bottom and corners. Add hot water 1/4 cup (60 ml) at a time whenever they get too thick.
steps.look: Slow, lazy bubbles that pop like a volcano; the grits thicken, swell and turn creamy.
steps.mistake: Cooking on higher heat to save time, which scorches the bottom and leaves the grains gritty.
steps.fix: Low and slow. If the bottom scorches, do not scrape it up; spoon the top into a clean pan.

steps.do: Taste a spoonful at 45 minutes: the grains should be soft and creamy with no hard bite. Hold the grits covered on the lowest heat.
steps.look: Creamy grits that slowly fall from a spoon, loose but not runny.
steps.mistake: Stopping when they are still sandy and firm.
steps.fix: Give them 10 more minutes and more water.

steps.do: Meanwhile, cook the bacon in the skillet over medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until crisp and the fat has rendered. Lift the bacon out with the slotted spoon onto paper towels, leaving about 2 tbsp (30 ml) fat in the pan.
steps.look: Crisp, golden brown bacon pieces and clear fat in the pan.
steps.mistake: High heat, which burns the bacon before the fat renders.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; rendering is gentle.

steps.do: Raise the heat to medium-high. Add the shrimp in one layer and sear 1 minute until pink underneath, turn and sear 30 seconds more. Lift them onto a plate while still slightly translucent in the centre.
steps.look: Pink, lightly golden shrimp in loose C shapes.
steps.mistake: Cooking them through now, so they turn rubbery in the sauce.
steps.fix: Pull them early; they finish later.

steps.do: Finish the grits: stir in 3 tbsp (42 g) butter and the cheddar until melted. Taste and season. Keep covered.
steps.look: Glossy, golden grits that hold a soft shape on a spoon.
steps.mistake: Adding cheese over high heat, which can make it stringy and oily.
steps.fix: Stir it in off the heat or on the lowest setting.

steps.do: Lower the heat under the skillet to medium. Add the shallot and garlic and stir 30 seconds. Pour in the shell stock and scrape up all the browned bits. Boil 3 to 4 minutes until reduced by half.
steps.look: The stock turns amber and smells richly of shrimp; about 1/2 cup (120 ml) remains.
steps.mistake: Not reducing, so the sauce is thin and weak.
steps.fix: Keep boiling until the volume halves.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Swirl in the cold butter a cube at a time until the sauce turns glossy and slightly thick. Add the lemon juice. Return the shrimp, bacon and any juices and toss over low heat for 30 seconds until the shrimp are just opaque.
steps.look: A glossy sauce coating loose C-shaped, opaque shrimp.
steps.mistake: Boiling after the butter goes in, which splits the sauce.
steps.fix: If it splits, add a spoon of hot grits liquid or water off the heat and swirl.

steps.do: Spoon the grits into warm, shallow bowls. Arrange the shrimp on top, pour the pan sauce over and scatter the spring onions. Pass hot sauce at the table.
steps.look: A golden pool of grits, pink shrimp, glossy sauce running into the grits.
steps.mistake: Letting the grits stand uncovered until a skin forms.
steps.fix: Stir in a splash of hot milk to loosen them just before plating.

science: Stone-ground grits are coarsely milled whole corn, including some of the germ and bran, so they need a long, slow cook for water to penetrate the hard grains and gelatinise their starch. As starch granules absorb liquid and swell, they release amylose into the liquid, turning it creamy; stirring helps that release and stops the heavy grains settling and scorching. Milk adds body and sweetness. The shell stock is the flavour secret: shrimp shells are full of savoury compounds and the pigment astaxanthin, which gives stock its colour and depth in a quarter of an hour. Mounting the reduced stock with cold butter creates an emulsion that coats the shrimp in a glossy sauce.
plating: Spoon a generous ladle of grits into a warm shallow bowl and tap the bowl so it settles into a smooth, even pool. Arrange five or six shrimp in a loose ring or a neat cluster in the centre, tails pointing up and in the same direction. Spoon the sauce and bacon over the shrimp so it runs into the grits, then scatter spring onions over the top.

pairing.drink: A rich Chardonnay with gentle oak, whose buttery body matches the grits, or a Brandy Milk Punch for a true New Orleans brunch.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans Shrimp & Grits: Brennan's own version of this dish, worth tasting against yours

variations: With andouille: smoked sausage in place of bacon, the older Lowcountry road.
Creole sauce: add 1 cup (240 ml) chopped tomato, celery and green pepper to the pan before the stock.
Grit cakes: chill leftover grits in a pan, cut into squares and pan-fry until crisp.
safety: Cook shrimp until opaque throughout, about 145°F (63°C).
Simmering grits spit and can burn: stir with a long spoon and keep the lid on between stirs.
Keep shrimp refrigerated until cooking and discard any that smell of ammonia.

title: Poires à la Beaujolaise
summary: Whole pears poached at a bare shiver in spiced Beaujolais until they turn deep ruby, then glazed with the poaching wine reduced to a syrup with cassis. Poaching fruit is the gentlest dessert technique, and it teaches the moment a skewer slides into the core with only slight resistance.
skills: reducing the liquor to a syrup
equipment: Saucepan just wide enough to hold 4 pears on their sides, about 3 quarts (3 litres)
Melon baller or small spoon for coring
Parchment paper for a cartouche, and a small plate to weigh it down
Thin metal skewer or cake tester
Small saucepan for reducing the syrup

ingredients.note: pared with a peeler, no white pith

ingredients.item: Crème fraîche or vanilla ice cream

mise: Peel the pears from stalk to base in long, smooth strokes, leaving the stalks on. Rub each one all over with a cut lemon half as you go so it does not brown.
Cut a thin slice off the base of each pear so it stands upright. From the base, scoop out the core with a melon baller or the tip of a small spoon, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep.
Cut a circle of parchment the size of the pan with a small hole in the centre: this is the cartouche.
Pare the orange zest. Measure the sugar and spices.

timeline.do: Peel and core the pears; make the cartouche.
Dissolve sugar in the wine with the spices.
Pears in; poach at a shiver 20 to 35 minutes, turning once.
Lift out the pears. Reduce the syrup with the cassis.
Cool the syrup slightly; glaze the pears.
Serve warm or chilled with crème fraîche. Better still, poach a day ahead.

steps.do: Put the wine, sugar, cinnamon, orange zest, peppercorns, clove and vanilla in the saucepan. Warm over medium heat, stirring, until every grain of sugar has dissolved; check by running the spoon across the base.
steps.look: A clear, dark red liquid with no grit on the base of the pan.
steps.mistake: Leaving undissolved sugar on the base, where it scorches and makes the syrup bitter.
steps.fix: Keep stirring over gentle heat until the spoon feels smooth across the bottom.

steps.do: Bring to a simmer, then lower the pears in on their sides. They should be almost covered; add a little water if needed.
steps.look: Pears bobbing in the wine, mostly submerged.
steps.mistake: Using too large a pan, so the pears are only half covered and colour unevenly.
steps.fix: Use a smaller pan or add water until they are nearly covered.

steps.do: Lay the cartouche on the surface and set a small plate on top to keep the pears submerged. Lower the heat until the liquid barely shivers: an occasional bubble, never a boil.
steps.look: The surface trembles gently with a few small bubbles at the edge.
steps.mistake: Boiling the pears, which knocks them about, leaches the colour back out and cooks the outside to mush before the core is done.
steps.fix: Turn the heat down or move the pan half off the burner.

steps.do: Poach 20 to 35 minutes depending on ripeness, turning the pears once halfway. Start testing at 20 minutes by sliding the skewer into the thickest part, near the core.
steps.look: The skewer slides in with only slight resistance at the centre, like testing a cooked potato that still holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Overcooking until the pears slump and the skewer falls through, or pulling them while the core is still hard.
steps.fix: Test each pear separately; lift each out as soon as it is ready.

steps.do: Lift the pears out with the slotted spoon and stand them in a shallow dish.
steps.look: Evenly ruby pears that hold their shape.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in while you reduce the syrup, which overcooks them.
steps.fix: Always lift them out before boiling the syrup.

steps.do: Strain out about 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of the poaching liquid into the small saucepan, add the cassis and boil 8 to 12 minutes until reduced to about 1/2 cup (120 ml) and syrupy. Keep the rest of the liquid for storing the pears.
steps.look: Large, glossy bubbles; the syrup coats the back of a spoon and a drop on a cold plate holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Reducing too far, so it sets hard and sticky as it cools.
steps.fix: Pull it while it still flows; it thickens as it cools. If too thick, add a splash of the poaching liquid.

steps.do: Cool the syrup for 5 minutes, then spoon it over the pears, letting it run down from the stalk, until they shine.
steps.look: A glossy, deep red coat on every pear.
steps.mistake: Pouring very hot syrup that runs straight off.
steps.fix: Let it cool slightly so it clings.

steps.do: Serve warm, or for the best colour, put the pears back in the remaining poaching liquid, cool, cover and refrigerate overnight; the colour travels deeper inside. Glaze again before serving and add a spoon of crème fraîche.
steps.look: Overnight pears are deep ruby right to the core when sliced.
steps.mistake: Serving straight away when the colour is still only skin deep, if you have time to wait.
steps.fix: Poach a day ahead whenever you can.

science: Poaching cooks fruit gently in a liquid held below boiling, around 175 to 185°F (80 to 85°C), so the pectin that glues the pear cells together softens slowly and evenly without the fruit falling apart. The sugar matters as much as the heat. A syrup of about a fifth sugar by weight balances the sugar inside the fruit, so water is not drawn out of the pear into the liquid; too weak a syrup and the flesh turns woolly. The red colour comes from anthocyanins in the wine, which seep into the flesh over time; boiling knocks them back out, while an overnight rest in the cooled liquid carries them deeper.
plating: Stand each pear upright on a chilled shallow plate, slightly off centre. Spoon the glossy syrup over the top so it runs down and pools around the base. Add a neat quenelle of crème fraîche beside it, shaped between two spoons, and a thin crisp biscuit or a sprig of mint at the stalk.

pairing.drink: A glass of the same young Beaujolais, lightly chilled, or a fortified Banyuls whose red fruit and warmth echo the spiced wine.
pairing.brennans: Louis Jadot Beaujolais-Villages 2021 (375 ml): the Gamay on the list, the same grape as the poaching wine

variations: Pears in white wine with vanilla and lemon for a pale, golden version.
Pears poached in port with star anise.
Peaches poached in rosé for summer, peeled after poaching.
safety: The reduced syrup is very hot and sticky; never taste it straight from the pan.
Peel away from your hand, and keep the peeler at a shallow angle.

title: Lemon Posset with Shortbread Fingers
summary: A British dessert of cream boiled with sugar and set by lemon juice alone, served with crisp shortbread fingers. Three ingredients set by acid sit beside a shortbread that teaches the first pastry skill, rubbing cold butter into flour.
equipment: Heavy medium saucepan, at least 2 quarts (2 litres), because boiling cream rises
Four small glasses or ramekins, about 5 oz (150 ml) each
8.5 x 4.5 inch (21 x 11 cm) loaf tin, lined with parchment

ingredients.item: Heavy (double) cream, at least 36 percent fat

ingredients.note: zest of 1, then 1/4 cup (60 ml) strained juice
cold, cut in 1/2 inch (1 cm) cubes

mise: Zest one lemon finely, avoiding the bitter white pith. Juice both and strain the juice; measure 1/4 cup (60 ml).
Set the glasses on a small tray that fits in the fridge.
Cube the butter and keep it cold. Line the loaf tin. Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C) when you start the shortbread.

timeline.do: Zest and juice the lemons; boil the cream 3 minutes.
Lemon in off the heat; stand 10 minutes; strain into glasses.
Chill at least 4 hours.
Rub in and bake the shortbread 35 to 40 minutes.
Cut while hot; cool in the tin.
Serve the possets cold with the shortbread.

steps.do: Put the cream, sugar and lemon zest in the saucepan. Bring to the boil over medium heat, stirring so the sugar dissolves.
steps.look: The cream rises in the pan with large bubbles.
steps.mistake: Using a small pan, so the cream boils over.
steps.fix: Use a tall pan, at least four times the volume of the cream, and stay with it.

steps.do: Once boiling, lower the heat just enough to stop it rising over, and keep it at a rolling boil for 3 minutes, stirring constantly.
steps.look: A steady boil; the cream thickens very slightly and coats the spoon more heavily.
steps.mistake: Pulling it off as soon as it boils; without the 3 minutes it may not set firmly.
steps.fix: Time it: 3 full minutes.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Stir in the lemon juice.
steps.look: The cream thickens noticeably within seconds as the acid works.
steps.mistake: Adding the lemon while it is still on a hard boil, which can make it grainy.
steps.fix: Always off the heat.

steps.do: Leave the mixture to stand 10 minutes, then pour it through the fine sieve into the jug to remove the zest.
steps.look: A smooth, pale yellow cream, slightly thickened.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve, leaving zest strands in the set cream.
steps.fix: Always strain for a silky set.

steps.do: Pour into the glasses, leaving 1/2 inch (1 cm) at the top. Cool 20 minutes, then refrigerate at least 4 hours, uncovered for the first hour, then covered.
steps.look: After chilling, the surface is glossy and the posset holds when you tilt the glass.
steps.mistake: Moving the glasses while setting, which wrinkles the surface.
steps.fix: Set them somewhere they will not be disturbed.

steps.do: For the shortbread, mix both flours, the sugar and salt in the bowl. Add the cold butter and rub it in with your fingertips, lifting the mixture and letting it fall, until it looks like fine breadcrumbs with no large pieces of butter.
steps.look: Even, sandy crumbs that hold together when squeezed in your fist.
steps.mistake: Using warm palms instead of cool fingertips, so the butter melts and turns greasy.
steps.fix: If it turns greasy, chill the bowl 10 minutes and continue.

steps.do: Tip the crumbs into the lined loaf tin and press firmly and evenly with the back of a spoon. Mark into 8 fingers with a knife and prick each finger twice with a fork.
steps.look: A flat, even layer about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.mistake: Pressing unevenly, so the thin parts burn.
steps.fix: Level it with the flat bottom of a glass.

steps.do: Bake at 300°F (150°C) for 35 to 40 minutes until an even pale sand colour, firm at the edges.
steps.look: A uniform pale gold; the kitchen smells of butter.
steps.mistake: Baking hotter to save time, which browns the edges while the centre stays raw.
steps.fix: Low and slow; shortbread should be pale.

steps.do: Sprinkle with the extra sugar, cut along the marks while hot, and cool completely in the tin. Lift out by the parchment.
steps.look: Clean, crisp fingers that snap.
steps.mistake: Cutting cold, which shatters the shortbread.
steps.fix: Cut while warm.

science: Posset sets with no gelatine or egg. Boiling the cream drives off some water and concentrates the fat and milk proteins. Orange and cardamom posset: half orange juice, half lemon, with 2 crushed cardamom pods in the cream.

title: Panna Cotta
summary: Italian cooked cream set with the least gelatine that will still hold, perfumed with vanilla and turned out so it trembles on the plate. Gelatine is measured to the gram here because the goal is the softest set that still stands.

equipment: Four 5 oz (150 ml) ramekins, dariole moulds or glasses
Thin knife and a bowl of hot water for unmoulding

ingredients.note: or 3 sheets of silver-grade leaf gelatine, about 7.5 g, which sets to roughly the same strength
split and scraped; or 1 tsp (5 ml) vanilla bean paste
to grease the moulds, if unmoulding

mise: Weigh the gelatine. Sprinkle powdered gelatine evenly over the cold water in a small bowl and leave 5 to 10 minutes until it swells into a firm, spongy mass. If using sheets, soak them in a bowl of cold water for 5 minutes until floppy, then squeeze out the water.
Wipe the inside of each mould with a very thin film of oil on a paper towel if you plan to unmould. Set them on a small tray.
Split the vanilla bean and scrape out the seeds.
Toss the berries with the sugar and lemon juice and leave them to macerate in the fridge.

timeline.do: Weigh and bloom the gelatine; oil the moulds.
Warm the cream, milk, sugar and vanilla to steaming.
Gelatine in off the heat; strain; cool, stirring.
Pour into moulds; chill at least 5 hours.
Unmould onto chilled plates.
Berries beside; serve.

steps.do: Put the cream, milk, sugar, vanilla seeds and pod and salt in the saucepan. Warm over medium heat, stirring, until steaming and small bubbles appear at the edge, about 180°F (82°C). Do not boil.
steps.look: Wisps of steam and tiny bubbles around the rim; the sugar fully dissolved.
steps.mistake: Boiling the cream, which gives a cooked taste and a skin.
steps.fix: Pull it off the heat at the first bubbles at the edge.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Add the bloomed gelatine and whisk for 1 minute until completely dissolved.
steps.look: No granules or clear strands visible when you lift the whisk; the liquid is smooth.
steps.mistake: Adding gelatine to boiling liquid, which weakens its set, or not dissolving it fully, leaving rubbery lumps.
steps.fix: If you see granules, warm gently for 30 seconds while whisking, never boiling.

steps.do: Pour through the fine sieve into the jug. Remove the vanilla pod.
steps.look: Smooth, speckled cream with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve.
steps.fix: Always strain.

steps.do: Leave the jug to cool for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until it is just warm and slightly thickened, about 75°F (24°C). This keeps the vanilla seeds suspended.
steps.look: The cream coats the back of a spoon slightly more thickly and the seeds stay spread through it.
steps.mistake: Pouring it hot, so the seeds sink and the fat rises, leaving a waxy layer on what becomes the base.
steps.fix: Stir until it cools; you can set the jug in a bowl of iced water to speed it up, stirring constantly.

steps.do: Stir once more and pour into the moulds. Cover with plastic wrap without touching the surface and refrigerate at least 5 hours, or overnight.
steps.look: A smooth, flat surface with seeds evenly spread.
steps.mistake: Moving the tray around while it sets.
steps.fix: Find a level, quiet spot in the fridge.

steps.do: To test the set, tilt a mould: the panna cotta should come away slightly from the side and wobble as one piece.
steps.look: A gentle tremble across the whole surface, like a soft jelly.
steps.mistake: Unmoulding too early, so it collapses.
steps.fix: Give it another hour.

steps.do: To unmould, run a thin knife around the very top edge to break the seal. Dip the mould in hot water up to the rim for 3 to 5 seconds. Lay a chilled plate upside down on top, hold both firmly and turn over with one decisive shake. Lift the mould.
steps.look: It slides free with sharp edges and trembles on the plate.
steps.mistake: Dipping too long, so the outside melts into a puddle.
steps.fix: If it will not release, dip for 2 more seconds. If the surface is melted, return it to the fridge for 15 minutes to firm.

steps.do: Spoon the macerated berries and their juice beside the panna cotta and serve chilled.
steps.look: The panna cotta keeps trembling when the plate is moved.
steps.mistake: Leaving it on a warm plate for a long time.
steps.fix: Unmould onto chilled plates just before serving.

science: Gelatine is collagen extracted from animal tissue. Bloomed in cold water, its protein strands absorb water and swell; heated, they unwind and disperse; cooled, they reconnect into a mesh that traps liquid as a gel. The set depends on concentration. Around 1 percent of the liquid weight, as here with 5 g in about 500 g of cream and milk, gives a gel that just holds its shape and melts at body temperature, which is why panna cotta dissolves on the tongue. More gelatine makes it rubbery. Boiling damages the gelatine strands and weakens the set. Pouring the cream cool and slightly thickened keeps the vanilla seeds and fat evenly distributed.
plating: Turn the panna cotta out slightly off centre on a chilled white plate. Spoon a small pile of berries to one side with a drizzle of their juice running towards it, and set one perfect berry and a tiny mint leaf on top. Leave space on the plate so the tremble is the star.

title: Ginger Milk Curd
summary: A Cantonese pudding of hot sweetened milk poured onto fresh ginger juice, which sets in minutes into a silky curd with no gelatine or egg. An enzyme in ginger does the setting, so the lesson is that temperature, not time, decides whether it works.
skills: heating milk to the right temperature
equipment: Clean muslin, cheesecloth or a thin kitchen towel for squeezing
Four small heatproof bowls, about 5 oz (150 ml) each

ingredients.note: old, knobbly ginger with tan skin; young ginger has too little enzyme

ingredients.item: Whole milk, at least 3.5 percent fat
ingredients.note: not ultra-pasteurised (UHT) if you can avoid it

mise: Scrub the ginger and grate it finely, skin and all, on the Microplane.
Gather the pulp in the muslin and squeeze hard over a bowl to collect about 1/4 cup (60 ml) of juice. Let it stand 1 minute; a white starch will settle at the bottom.
Set the four bowls on a tray where they can sit undisturbed.
Spoon 1 tbsp (15 ml) of juice into each bowl, stirring the juice first so each gets some of the settled starch.

timeline.do: Grate and squeeze the ginger; portion the juice.
Heat the milk with sugar to 167°F (75°C).
Cool to 158 to 167°F (70 to 75°C); stir the juice; pour from a height.
Leave untouched 10 minutes to set.
Test with a tilt.
Serve warm.

steps.do: Heat the milk and sugar in the saucepan over medium-low heat, stirring, until the sugar dissolves and the thermometer reads 167°F (75°C).
steps.look: The milk steams and the surface shivers, but not a single bubble breaks.
steps.mistake: Boiling the milk, which is too hot and destroys the enzyme.
steps.fix: If it boils, let it cool back down to the target range; it will still work once in range.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and pour the milk into the jug. Check the temperature: you want 158 to 167°F (70 to 75°C) at the moment of pouring.
steps.look: The thermometer settles in the range.
steps.mistake: Pouring too hot (above about 176°F, 80°C), which kills the enzyme, or too cool (below about 149°F, 65°C), when the enzyme works too slowly to set.
steps.fix: Wait a minute if too hot; warm gently if too cool.

steps.do: Stir the ginger juice in the first bowl so the settled white starch is lifted back into it.
steps.look: Cloudy, evenly mixed juice.
steps.mistake: Leaving the starch on the bottom; it carries much of the enzyme.
steps.fix: Stir each bowl just before you pour into it.

steps.do: Hold the jug about 8 inches (20 cm) above the bowl and pour 1/3 cup (100 ml) of milk in one quick, steady stream so it lands hard in the centre and mixes itself with the juice.
steps.look: The milk swirls vigorously in the bowl and settles.
steps.mistake: Pouring slowly from close up, which does not mix the juice in, or pouring in two goes.
steps.fix: One confident pour per bowl, then move to the next.

steps.do: Repeat with the other bowls, stirring each juice before pouring. Do not stir after pouring, and do not move the bowls.
steps.look: A still, smooth surface in each bowl.
steps.mistake: Stirring or jostling the bowls, which breaks the forming gel so it never sets.
steps.fix: Leave them completely alone.

steps.do: Wait 10 minutes. Test by tilting one bowl to about 45 degrees.
steps.look: The surface holds firm and does not flow; a spoon pressed on it leaves a dent, like soft tofu.
steps.mistake: Testing too early and disturbing the set.
steps.fix: If it is still liquid after 15 minutes, the milk was the wrong temperature or the ginger was too young; note it and try again with older ginger.

steps.do: Serve warm, as it is traditionally eaten, with a spoon. A few drops of whey may appear around the edge; that is normal.
steps.look: A silky, quivering curd with a warm, spicy ginger bite.
steps.mistake: Chilling it, which makes it weep more whey.
steps.fix: Eat within the hour.

science: Ginger contains a protease, a protein-cutting enzyme called zingibain, which acts on milk the way rennet does in cheesemaking. Milk’s casein proteins float in clusters protected by a hairy outer layer of kappa-casein. The enzyme snips off that outer layer, and the bared clusters stick together into a gel that traps the milk. Enzymes are proteins with a working temperature: zingibain works fastest at around 140 to 160°F (60 to 70°C) and is destroyed above roughly 176°F (80°C). Below about 149°F (65°C) it works too slowly to set the milk before it cools. That is why the thermometer is the most important tool in this recipe.
plating: Serve in the bowl it set in, on a small saucer with a spoon. Do not garnish heavily: one thin sliver of candied ginger or a tiny pinch of finely grated fresh ginger on the centre is enough, so the smooth surface stays the focus.

pairing.drink: A cup of hot jasmine or oolong tea, the classic partner, or a light, sweet Moscato.

variations: Double-skin milk pudding: a steamed milk and egg white pudding, another Cantonese classic.
Ginger curd with brown sugar syrup drizzled over at the table.
Pineapple and kiwi also contain proteases; compare how they react with milk as an experiment, not a dessert.
safety: Hot milk scalds: pour carefully and keep hands clear of the stream.
Use pasteurised milk.

title: Muhallabia
summary: A Levantine milk pudding thickened with cornstarch and ground rice, perfumed with rose water and mastic and scattered with pistachios. A starch-thickened pudding shows that cornstarch must truly boil to thicken and lose its raw, chalky taste.

equipment: Balloon whisk and a heatproof spatula
Four small bowls or glasses, about 5 oz (150 ml) each

ingredients.note: optional; sold at Middle Eastern grocers

mise: Freeze the mastic tears for 15 minutes, then grind them in the mortar with 1 tsp (4 g) of the sugar to a fine powder. Cold resin grinds cleanly; warm resin gums up.
In a small bowl, whisk the cornstarch and ground rice into 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the cold milk until completely smooth, with not one lump.
Chop the pistachios finely. Set out the bowls.

timeline.do: Grind the mastic; make the slurry.
Bring the remaining milk and sugar to a bare simmer.
Whisk in the slurry; cook, stirring, until it bubbles and thickens, about 6 minutes.
Off the heat: mastic and rose water; pour into bowls at once.
Chill 3 hours.
Pistachios and rose petals on top; serve.

steps.do: Pour the remaining 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) milk and the rest of the sugar into the saucepan and bring to a bare simmer over medium heat, stirring so the sugar dissolves and nothing catches.
steps.look: Steam and small bubbles at the edge of the pan.
steps.mistake: Leaving it unstirred, so the milk catches on the base.
steps.fix: Stir often across the bottom.

steps.do: Whisk the slurry once more (the starch settles fast), then pour it into the hot milk in a thin stream, whisking hard and continuously.
steps.look: The milk turns slightly cloudy and begins to thicken almost at once.
steps.mistake: Adding the slurry without restirring, so a lump of starch drops to the bottom.
steps.fix: Whisk any lumps out at once; if they persist, strain the pudding before pouring into bowls.

steps.do: Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with the whisk or spatula, reaching into the corners, for about 6 minutes, until it thickens and one or two slow bubbles heave up and pop on the surface.
steps.look: Thick enough to coat the back of a spoon heavily; a finger drawn across it leaves a clean line. Slow, thick bubbles break the surface.
steps.mistake: Stopping when it first thickens, before it bubbles. It will taste chalky and loosen in the fridge.
steps.fix: Keep stirring until the slow bubbles appear, then cook 1 minute more.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Stir in the mastic sugar and the rose water.
steps.look: A floral, resinous perfume rises.
steps.mistake: Adding rose water during boiling, which drives off its scent.
steps.fix: Add flavourings off the heat.

steps.do: Pour immediately into the bowls while it still flows. Tap each bowl on the counter to level the surface.
steps.look: Smooth, glossy surfaces.
steps.mistake: Waiting, so it begins to set in the pan and has to be spooned out in lumps.
steps.fix: Pour at once. Never stir it once it has started to set.

steps.do: Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface of each to stop a skin forming, or leave uncovered if you like the skin. Cool 20 minutes, then refrigerate at least 3 hours.
steps.look: Set firm with a gentle wobble.
steps.mistake: Leaving it uncovered in the fridge, where it absorbs other smells.
steps.fix: Cover once cool.

steps.do: Just before serving, scatter the chopped pistachios and rose petals over the top.
steps.look: Bright green pistachios on a white pudding.
steps.mistake: Adding nuts too early, which soften.
steps.fix: Garnish at the last moment.

science: Cornstarch is made of tightly packed starch granules. In cold milk they simply float, which is why the slurry is made cold: added dry to hot milk, the outsides would swell instantly into lumps around dry centres. As the milk heats, the granules absorb water and swell, and they burst and release their starch molecules only near boiling, around 194 to 203°F (90 to 95°C). That burst gives full thickening and removes the raw taste. Stop at a mere simmer and the granules stay partly intact, the pudding tastes chalky, and its structure is weak. Once set, the starch network is fragile; stirring breaks it permanently, so it is poured while still fluid.
plating: Serve chilled in the bowls it set in. Scatter the pistachios in a neat crescent across one side rather than all over, add a few rose petals beside them and a single drop of rose water in the centre if you like.

title: Tembleque
summary: A Puerto Rican coconut pudding thickened with cornstarch, cooked until it truly bubbles, set in a mould and turned out under a heavy dusting of cinnamon. It repeats the starch set of muhallabia with coconut milk in place of cow’s milk, and adds unmoulding a whole pudding.
skills: a coconut milk and cornstarch pudding
equipment: 2 cup (500 ml) mould or four 4 oz (125 ml) ramekins
mise: Shake the can well and pour out 1/2 cup (120 ml) into a bowl. Whisk in the cornstarch and salt until no grain is left on the bottom of the bowl.
Rinse the mould or ramekins with cold water and shake out the excess, leaving them wet. A wet mould releases cleanly.
Have the plastic wrap and a spatula ready by the stove.

timeline.do: Slurry made; mould wetted.
Heat the rest of the coconut milk with sugar and cinnamon to steaming.
Slurry in; stir constantly until it bubbles and holds a furrow for a full minute.
Into the wet mould; cover the surface.
Chill at least 4 hours.
Unmould and dust heavily with cinnamon.

steps.do: Pour the remaining coconut milk into the saucepan with the sugar and cinnamon stick. Heat over medium heat, stirring, until it steams and the sugar dissolves. Remove the cinnamon stick.
steps.look: Steam rising, fine bubbles at the edge, a warm cinnamon scent.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil hard, which can make the coconut fat separate.
steps.fix: Keep it just below a simmer.

steps.do: Whisk the slurry again and pour it into the pan in a thin stream, whisking constantly.
steps.look: The mixture begins to thicken within a minute.
steps.mistake: Pouring without whisking, which forms lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk hard; a few small lumps will smooth out as you stir.

steps.do: Switch to the spatula and stir constantly over medium-low heat, reaching into the corners of the pan, until the pudding is very thick. Keep going until slow bubbles burst through the surface.
steps.look: Thick, glossy pudding with large, slow bubbles popping like a volcano.
steps.mistake: Pulling it off at the first thickening; it tastes chalky and slumps when unmoulded.
steps.fix: Keep cooking until the bubbles come.

steps.do: Hold it at that slow bubble for 1 more minute, stirring. Drag the spatula through the centre: the furrow should hold its shape.
steps.look: A clean furrow that stays open; the pudding pulls away from the sides of the pan.
steps.mistake: Stopping stirring, so the coconut fat settles and scorches on the base.
steps.fix: Stir right into the corners the whole time.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and stir in the vanilla. Pour immediately into the wet mould and smooth the top with the spatula.
steps.look: A level, glossy surface.
steps.mistake: Waiting, so it sets in the pan.
steps.fix: Pour at once.

steps.do: Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface. Cool 20 minutes, then refrigerate at least 4 hours.
steps.look: After chilling, the pudding is firm and pulls slightly from the edges of the mould when tilted.
steps.mistake: Unmoulding too early.
steps.fix: If it still feels soft in the centre, chill another hour.

steps.do: To unmould, run a thin wet knife around the edge. Set the serving plate upside down on top, hold both together and turn over with a firm shake. Lift the mould.
steps.look: The tembleque slides out in one piece and wobbles: its name comes from the Spanish word for trembling.
steps.mistake: Not wetting the mould or the knife, so it sticks and tears.
steps.fix: If it sticks, dip the mould in warm water for 5 seconds and try again.

steps.do: Dust heavily and evenly with ground cinnamon through a small sieve. Serve chilled, cut into wedges or spooned.
steps.look: A smooth white pudding under a russet blanket of cinnamon.
steps.mistake: Dusting hours ahead, which turns the cinnamon damp and patchy.
steps.fix: Dust just before serving.

science: Like muhallabia, tembleque relies on cornstarch granules swelling and bursting as the liquid nears boiling, around 194 to 203°F (90 to 95°C). That is when the starch molecules spill out and form a network strong enough to hold a moulded shape after chilling. Coconut milk complicates it: its fat separates and settles when heated, and fat on the pan base scorches quickly, so constant stirring is essential. Stopping at the first thickening leaves granules unburst, so the pudding tastes floury and slumps. A wet mould leaves a thin film of water between pudding and mould so it slides free instead of bonding to the surface.

optional, for frying the nuts and raisins

Crush the cardamom pods, remove the seeds and grind them fine.
Crumble the saffron into the 1 tbsp (15 ml) warm milk and leave to steep.
Sliver the nuts.

Bring the milk to a boil; add rice; simmer, stirring and scraping, about 35 to 40 minutes.

steps.do: Rinse the saucepan with cold water and leave a film of water in it: this helps stop the milk sticking. Pour in the milk and bring it to a boil over medium heat, stirring often.

steps.mistake: Walking away; milk boils over in seconds.
steps.fix: Lower the heat the moment it rises and stir it down.

steps.do: Add the drained rice. Lower the heat so the milk simmers gently with steady small bubbles.
steps.look: A gentle, rolling simmer with a thin skin forming and being stirred back in.
steps.mistake: Simmering too hard, which scorches the milk solids on the base.
steps.fix: Lower the heat to the point where the bubbles barely break.

steps.do: Simmer 35 to 40 minutes, stirring every 2 to 3 minutes and scraping the base and sides with the spatula. Scrape the creamy deposits from the sides of the pan back into the milk; they add flavour.
steps.look: The milk reduces by about half, turns ivory and creamy, and the rice grains swell and soften.
steps.mistake: Letting the milk catch and burn on the base, which gives the whole pudding a scorched taste.
steps.fix: Stir often across the base. If it catches, pour into a clean pan without scraping the burnt layer.

steps.do: Check the rice by crushing a grain between your fingers.
steps.look: The grain squashes completely with no hard centre.
steps.mistake: Adding sugar before the rice is fully soft.
steps.fix: Keep simmering until it is tender.

steps.do: Stir in the sugar and cook 5 minutes more, stirring constantly.
steps.look: The kheer loosens slightly as the sugar melts, then thickens again.
steps.mistake: Adding sugar too early, which slows the rice softening.
steps.fix: Sugar goes in only once the rice is soft.

steps.do: Test the thickness: drag a spoon through it. It should leave a trail that slowly closes.
steps.look: A thick, creamy pudding, loose enough to pour slowly.
steps.mistake: Over-reducing, so it turns stiff, especially once cooled.
steps.fix: Add a splash of milk; kheer thickens a lot as it cools.

steps.do: Take it off the heat. Stir in the ground cardamom, the saffron and its milk, and most of the nuts.
steps.look: Golden streaks of saffron and a warm, floral cardamom scent.
steps.mistake: Adding cardamom early and cooking off its perfume.
steps.fix: Add the aromatics at the end.

steps.do: If you like, fry the remaining nuts and the raisins in the ghee for 1 to 2 minutes until the nuts are golden and the raisins puff. Serve the kheer warm or chilled, scattered with them.
steps.look: Golden nuts and plump raisins on a creamy pudding.
steps.mistake: Serving cold kheer without loosening it; it sets thick in the fridge.

title: Mango Sticky Rice

equipment: Steamer: a bamboo or metal steamer basket over a wok or pot, or a sieve set over a pot with a lid

Large heatproof bowl with a lid or plate
Sharp knife and board for the mango

ingredients.note: divided: 1 cup (240 ml) for the rice, the rest for the sauce
fragrant and yielding slightly when pressed, chilled

ingredients.item: Toasted mung beans or toasted sesame seeds

mise: Rinse the rice in several changes of cold water, rubbing gently, until the water runs nearly clear. Cover with plenty of fresh water and soak at least 4 hours or overnight.
Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, shaking, until golden, if using.
Chill the mangoes.
Wet the cheesecloth and wring it out.

timeline.do: Rinse and soak the rice at least 4 hours.
Drain the rice; set the steamer over boiling water.
Steam 20 to 25 minutes, turning once.
Warm the sweet coconut milk; pour over the hot rice; cover 20 minutes.
Make the salted coconut sauce; cut the mango.
Plate warm rice with cold mango and sauce.

steps.do: Drain the soaked rice. Fill the pot or wok with 2 inches (5 cm) of water and bring it to a boil. Line the steamer with the damp cloth, spread the rice over it in an even layer about 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep and fold the cloth over the top.
steps.look: Steam rising strongly through the basket.
steps.mistake: Letting the rice touch the water, so it boils and turns to paste.
steps.fix: The water must stay below the basket; top up only with boiling water.

steps.do: Cover and steam over medium-high heat for 20 to 25 minutes. Halfway through, lift the cloth and flip the rice over as one cake so it cooks evenly.
steps.look: The grains turn from opaque white to translucent and glossy.
steps.mistake: Letting the pot boil dry.
steps.fix: Check the water level at the halfway turn and top up with boiling water.

steps.do: Taste a few grains.
steps.look: Chewy and tender all the way through, sticky, with no hard white centre.
steps.mistake: Stopping while the centres are still chalky.
steps.fix: Steam 5 minutes more and taste again.

steps.do: While the rice steams, warm 1 cup (240 ml) coconut milk with the 1/3 cup (65 g) sugar and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt in a saucepan over medium-low heat, stirring until dissolved. Do not boil.
steps.look: Steaming, smooth, sweet coconut milk.
steps.mistake: Boiling it, which can split the coconut fat.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as the sugar dissolves.

steps.do: Tip the hot rice into the bowl and pour the warm coconut milk over. Stir gently to coat every grain, cover and leave 20 to 30 minutes.
steps.look: The rice drinks the coconut milk and turns glossy and plump, with no liquid left in the bowl.
steps.mistake: Pouring cold milk over cold rice; it will not absorb.
steps.fix: Both must be hot; the absorption happens during the rest.

steps.do: For the sauce, warm the remaining coconut milk with 1 tbsp (12 g) sugar and 1/4 tsp (1.5 g) salt. Stir in the cornstarch slurry and simmer 1 minute, stirring, until slightly thickened. Cool.
steps.look: A pourable sauce, thicker than the milk, tasting noticeably salty against the sweet.
steps.mistake: Leaving out the salt; the dessert then tastes cloying.
steps.fix: Taste and add another pinch of salt if it tastes only sweet.

steps.do: Cut the mango: stand it on its end, slice down either side of the flat stone to remove the two cheeks, then scoop each cheek out of its skin with a large spoon and slice crossways into 1/2 inch (1 cm) slices.
steps.look: Neat, glistening slices, kept in the cheek shape.
steps.mistake: Cutting into the stone, which is fibrous and hard.
steps.fix: Feel for the stone with the knife and follow its curve.

steps.do: Serve the rice warm with the cold mango alongside, the sauce spooned over the rice and a scatter of mung beans or sesame.
steps.look: Warm, chewy rice, cold sweet mango and a salty-sweet sauce.
steps.mistake: Refrigerating the rice before serving, which makes it hard.
steps.fix: Serve the rice warm or at room temperature on the day.

science: Glutinous rice contains almost no amylose, the straight-chain starch, and is nearly all amylopectin, a branched starch that turns sticky and chewy when cooked. Boiled, it absorbs too much water and collapses to paste. Soaking hydrates the grains in advance, so steam alone can cook them through, keeping each grain whole. The sweetened coconut milk is absorbed after steaming while the starch is still hot and open. Salt makes sweetness taste rounder and less flat because it suppresses bitterness and boosts our perception of other flavours, which is why Thai desserts so often carry a salty coconut cream.

pairing.drink: A late-harvest Riesling or a Moscato, whose tropical fruit matches the mango, or a cup of jasmine tea.
pairing.brennans: Dönnhoff ‘Oberhäuser Brücke’ Riesling Auslese Goldkapsel 2023 (375 ml): the Auslese on the list, tropical sweetness for ripe mango

Black sticky rice with coconut cream, steamed 10 minutes longer.
With durian or ripe peach when mangoes are out of season.

title: Chè Chuối (Banana and Coconut Tapioca)
summary: A Vietnamese sweet soup of bananas poached in coconut milk with tapioca pearls and pandan, finished with toasted sesame and peanuts. It teaches how tapioca starch cooks and how coconut desserts are seasoned with salt.
equipment: Mortar and pestle or a zip-top bag and rolling pin for the peanuts

ingredients.note: Asian finger bananas are traditional; cut in 1 1/4 inch (3 cm) pieces
about 1/8 inch (2 to 3 mm), not instant

mise: Peel and cut the bananas, toss them with 2 tbsp (24 g) of the sugar and leave 20 minutes; they release juice and firm up.
Toast the sesame seeds in the dry pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, shaking, until golden. Crush the peanuts coarsely.
Knot the pandan leaf so it releases its scent.
Bring a medium pan of water, about 4 cups (1 litre), to the boil for the tapioca.

timeline.do: Sugar the bananas; toast sesame; crush peanuts.
Boil the tapioca until a white dot remains; cover off the heat; rinse.
Warm coconut milk, water, pandan, salt and sugar; poach the bananas.
Tapioca and coconut cream in; warm through without boiling.
Serve warm or cold with sesame and peanuts.

steps.do: Pour the tapioca pearls into the boiling water and stir immediately so they do not stick together. Boil 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often.
steps.look: The pearls turn from white to translucent from the outside in, until only a small white dot remains in the centre.
steps.mistake: Not stirring at the start, so the pearls fuse into a lump.
steps.fix: Stir hard for the first minute. Break up clumps with the spoon.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat, cover it and leave 5 minutes.
steps.look: The white dots disappear and the pearls are clear all through.
steps.mistake: Boiling until the centres are clear; by then the outsides have dissolved into slime.
steps.fix: Let the covered pan finish the centres.

steps.do: Drain the pearls in the sieve and rinse under cold water, stirring with your fingers, to wash off surface starch. Leave them in a bowl of cold water.
steps.look: Separate, glossy, translucent pearls.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in the sieve, where they stick into one mass.
steps.fix: Keep them in cold water until needed.

steps.do: In the second saucepan, bring the coconut milk, water, pandan, salt and remaining sugar to a bare simmer over medium-low heat.
steps.look: Small bubbles at the edge, a sweet pandan scent.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which splits the coconut milk.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low.

steps.do: Slide in the bananas and their juice and poach gently 5 to 7 minutes.
steps.look: The banana edges turn slightly translucent and a skewer goes in with no resistance, but the pieces keep their shape.
steps.mistake: Stirring vigorously, which breaks the banana into mush.
steps.fix: Move the pan gently rather than stirring.

steps.do: Drain the tapioca and add it with the coconut cream. Warm 1 to 2 minutes, stirring gently, until heated through. Do not let it bubble. Take off the heat and remove the pandan.
steps.look: A creamy, ivory soup with pearls suspended in it.
steps.mistake: Boiling the coconut cream, which splits it into an oily slick.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as it is hot.

steps.do: Taste: it should be sweet with a clear salty edge. Add a pinch more salt if it tastes flat. Ladle into small bowls warm or let it cool and serve cold, scattered with sesame and peanuts.
steps.look: Glossy bananas, clear pearls, a sprinkle of golden sesame and peanuts.
steps.mistake: Serving without the salt.
steps.fix: Salt is what makes it taste of coconut rather than sugar.

science: Tapioca pearls are pure starch from cassava, with no protein or fibre to hold them together. As they cook, the outer layer gelatinises and turns clear first, while the centre stays raw and white. Boiling until the centre clears dissolves the outside into slime, so the pearls come off the heat with a white dot and finish in the retained heat. Rinsing removes loose surface starch that would make the soup gluey. Coconut cream is fat suspended in water by a thin layer of coconut protein; boiling denatures that protein, the droplets merge and the fat separates, so it goes in last. Sugaring the bananas first draws out water and firms them.
plating: Ladle into small glass bowls so the pearls show. Arrange three or four banana pieces on top, scatter the sesame and peanuts in a line across one side and add a tiny knot of pandan leaf or a mint leaf as garnish.

pairing.drink: Vietnamese iced coffee with condensed milk, or a cup of jasmine tea.

variations: Chè bắp: sweet corn in place of banana.
Chè chuối nướng style: grill the bananas first for a caramelised edge.
With sweet potato cubes poached alongside the banana.
safety: Peanuts and sesame are common allergens: tell guests.
Refrigerate leftovers and eat within 2 days; tapioca hardens when chilled, so warm it gently to soften.

title: Thiakry
summary: A Senegalese dessert of fine millet couscous, steamed twice until tender, cooled and folded into sweetened soured milk and crème fraîche with vanilla, raisins and nutmeg. Cheesecloth or muslin if your sieve has large holes
Clean kitchen towel to seal any gap between pot and steamer
Large wide bowl or tray for working the grain

ingredients.note: from West African grocers; fine wheat couscous works differently, see variations

ingredients.item: Thick plain whole-milk yoghurt or lait caillé (soured milk)

ingredients.note: seeds scraped; or 1 tsp (5 ml) vanilla extract

mise: Spread the millet in the wide bowl. Sprinkle over half the water and the oil and rake it through with spread fingers until every grain is damp and separate, with no clumps.
Fill the bottom of the couscoussier or pot with 2 inches (5 cm) of water and bring to the boil. If your sieve has large holes, line it with damp cheesecloth.
If there is a gap between pot and steamer, wrap a damp twisted towel around the join so steam goes up through the grain.

timeline.do: Moisten the millet; bring the steamer water to the boil.
First steaming, 15 to 20 minutes.
Break up, moisten again, second steaming 15 to 20 minutes.
Spread out and cool completely, fluffing.
Whisk the cream; fold in cold millet and raisins; chill 1 hour.
Grate nutmeg over and serve cold.

steps.do: Tip the moistened millet into the steamer basket without packing it down. Set it over the boiling water and steam, uncovered, for 15 to 20 minutes, timing from when steam rises through the surface of the grain.
steps.look: Steam visibly escaping through the whole surface of the millet.
steps.mistake: Pressing the grain down, so steam cannot pass through and it cooks unevenly.
steps.fix: Loosen it gently with a fork.

steps.do: Tip the millet back into the wide bowl. Break up every lump with a fork, then sprinkle with the remaining water and a pinch of salt, raking with your fingers.
steps.look: Separate, slightly swollen grains with no clumps.
steps.mistake: Leaving lumps, which stay raw in the middle.
steps.fix: Rub lumps gently between your palms.

steps.do: Return the millet to the steamer and steam a second time for 15 to 20 minutes.
steps.look: Fluffy, swollen grains.
steps.mistake: Skipping the second steaming.
steps.fix: Two steamings are essential for millet.

steps.do: Test a few grains by crushing them between your teeth.
steps.look: Tender all the way through, no chalky or gritty centre.
steps.mistake: Serving millet with a hard core, which stays hard however long it sits in the yoghurt.
steps.fix: Steam 5 to 10 minutes longer if needed.

steps.do: Spread the millet out on a tray and cool it completely to room temperature, fluffing it with a fork every 10 minutes to release steam and keep the grains separate.
steps.look: Cold, dry, separate grains.
steps.mistake: Folding warm grain into the cold dairy, which can split the soured milk and makes the dessert grainy and dry as the grain keeps absorbing.
steps.fix: Be patient; put the tray in the fridge for the last 10 minutes if needed.

steps.do: Whisk the yoghurt, crème fraîche, sugar, vanilla seeds and orange blossom water until smooth and pourable, like thick cream.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, sweet cream.
steps.mistake: Leaving it too thick; it will thicken more as the millet absorbs liquid.
steps.fix: Thin with 1 to 2 tbsp (15 to 30 ml) milk.

steps.do: Fold the cold millet and the raisins into the cream until evenly coated. Cover and chill 1 hour so the raisins plump and the flavours meld.
steps.look: A loose, creamy porridge; the grains suspended in cream.
steps.mistake: Serving straight away when the raisins are still hard.
steps.fix: Give it the hour.

steps.do: Spoon into bowls, grate fresh nutmeg over and serve cold.
steps.look: Creamy, tangy, gently sweet, with soft millet and plump raisins.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit at room temperature for long.
steps.fix: Keep it cold until serving.

science: Millet is a hard, small grain. Its starch must absorb water and gelatinise, and steam does this gently, cooking the grain through while keeping it separate. One steaming hydrates only the outside; breaking up and moistening between steamings lets more water reach the core. Gelatinisation needs heat, so cold yoghurt cannot finish an undercooked grain; the core stays chalky. The grain must be fully cooled because warm starch keeps absorbing liquid fast, drying the cream, and heat makes the casein proteins in soured milk tighten and separate into grainy curds. Cold into cold keeps the cream smooth.
plating: Spoon into small glass bowls or cups, smoothing the top. Grate nutmeg in a fine, even dusting over the surface, then add three or four plump raisins and a thin curl of orange zest in the centre.

pairing.drink: Bissap, the chilled hibiscus drink of Senegal, or a glass of sweet Muscat.

Dégué: the same dessert made with larger millet pellets, popular in Burkina Faso and Mali.
safety: Keep the finished dessert refrigerated and eat within 2 days.

title: Brigadeiros
summary: Brazil’s party sweet: condensed milk, cocoa and butter cooked until the mass pulls away from the pan, then cooled, rolled into balls and coated in chocolate sprinkles. It is a pure lesson in heat control and in reading thickness as the pan is tilted.
skills: cooking condensed milk until it pulls from the pan
equipment: Heavy non-stick saucepan, about 2 quarts (2 litres)

ingredients.note: plus extra for your hands and the plate

mise: Butter a plate or shallow dish.
Sift the cocoa to remove lumps.
Tip the sprinkles into a small bowl. Set out the paper cases.

timeline.do: Butter the plate; sift the cocoa.
Cook the mixture on medium-low, stirring constantly, 10 to 14 minutes.
Spread on the buttered plate; cool completely, about 1 hour.
Butter your palms; roll into balls; roll in sprinkles.
Set in paper cases and serve.

steps.do: Put the condensed milk, cocoa, butter and salt in the cold saucepan. Stir over medium-low heat until the butter melts and the cocoa is fully blended.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, dark brown liquid.
steps.mistake: Starting on high heat, which scorches the milk sugars on the base.
steps.fix: Keep the heat at medium-low throughout.

steps.do: Keep stirring constantly, scraping the bottom and sides of the pan in a figure-of-eight motion, for 10 to 14 minutes.
steps.look: The mixture thickens, bubbles slowly and becomes glossier and heavier on the spatula.
steps.mistake: Stopping stirring; condensed milk catches and burns in seconds.
steps.fix: Never leave it. If it scorches, transfer without scraping the base.

steps.do: Test it: drag the spatula across the base of the pan. When the mixture parts and you can see the pan bottom for a full second before it flows back, and the whole mass slides as one when you tilt the pan, it is done. If you have a thermometer, it reads about 225°F (107°C).
steps.look: A thick, shiny mass that pulls away from the sides and moves together as one when the pan is tilted.
steps.mistake: Stopping too soon, so the brigadeiros will not hold a shape; or going too far, so they turn stiff and fudge-like.
steps.fix: Too soft: return to the heat 1 to 2 minutes. Too firm: warm with 1 tbsp (15 ml) milk and stir until smooth, then retest.

steps.do: Scrape the mixture onto the buttered plate and spread it out a little. Cool completely at room temperature, about 1 hour, or 30 minutes in the fridge once warm rather than hot.
steps.look: Cool to the touch, firm enough to scoop but still pliable.
steps.mistake: Trying to roll it warm; it sticks to your hands and will not hold a shape.
steps.fix: Wait until it is completely cool.

steps.do: Rub a little butter on your palms. Scoop a teaspoon of the mixture, about 1/2 oz (15 g), and roll it between your palms into a smooth ball about 3/4 inch (2 cm) across.
steps.look: Smooth, round, glossy balls of even size.
steps.mistake: Rolling with dry hands, so the mixture sticks and the balls are ragged.
steps.fix: Re-butter your palms every few balls.

steps.do: Drop each ball into the sprinkles and roll it around until fully coated, pressing lightly. Set each in a paper case.
steps.look: An even coat of sprinkles all over.
steps.mistake: Letting the balls sit before coating, so the sprinkles do not stick.
steps.fix: Coat each ball straight after rolling.

steps.do: Serve at room temperature. They keep, covered, for 2 days at cool room temperature or 5 days in the fridge.
steps.look: Soft, fudgy centres under a crunchy chocolate coat.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the fridge, when they are hard.
steps.fix: Bring chilled ones to room temperature for 20 minutes.

science: Sweetened condensed milk is milk with most of its water removed and a large amount of sugar added. Cooking it drives off more water, raising the sugar concentration, which raises the temperature at which the mass boils, much as in candy making. Around 225°F (107°C), there is little enough water that the mixture holds its shape when cooled: soft enough to bite, firm enough to roll. The milk proteins and sugars also brown gently, adding a caramel note under the cocoa. Constant stirring matters because the dense, sugary mass sits on the pan base where it is hottest; left still, the sugars burn.
plating: Set the brigadeiros in their paper cases in neat rows on a flat platter or board, or stack a few in a small pyramid. For a party, alternate chocolate sprinkles with some rolled in desiccated coconut or chopped nuts for contrast.

pairing.drink: A small, strong coffee, or a tawny or vintage port, whose dried fruit and warmth suit chocolate and caramel.
pairing.brennans: Dow’s Vintage Port 2000 (375 ml): the vintage port on the list, dark fruit for chocolate and caramel

variations: Beijinho: no cocoa, a little coconut stirred in, rolled in desiccated coconut with a clove on top.

Gourmet brigadeiros: stir in 1 oz (30 g) chopped dark chocolate at the end and roll in cocoa nibs.

title: Crêpes
summary: French crêpes made from a rested, lump-free batter, cooked paper thin in a well seasoned pan and folded around lemon and sugar. It refines the thin pancake with the first lessons in batter rest and pan temperature, and the first crêpe is always the test that tunes the pan.
skills: the first crêpe as a test
equipment: 8 to 9 inch (20 to 23 cm) crêpe pan or non-stick skillet
Blender or a mixing bowl and whisk
Ladle or a 1/4 cup (60 ml) measure
Thin, flexible spatula or palette knife
Plate and a clean kitchen towel to stack the crêpes
Paper towel for buttering the pan

ingredients.note: plus 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) to loosen after resting
plus 1 tbsp (14 g) for the pan

mise: Melt the butter and let it cool slightly.

Put the milk, eggs, flour, sugar, salt and melted butter in the blender, liquids first, and blend 20 seconds until smooth. Scrape down and blend 5 seconds more. By hand: whisk the eggs and half the milk into the flour to a thick smooth paste, then whisk in the rest of the milk and the butter, and pass it through the sieve.
Cover and rest the batter at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 24 hours in the fridge.
Set a plate and towel by the stove for the finished crêpes.

timeline.do: Blend the batter; rest at least 30 minutes.
Stir and loosen the batter; heat the pan.
Cook the test crêpe and adjust heat and batter.
Cook the rest, about 2 minutes each, stacking under a towel.
Fill with lemon and sugar and fold into quarters.
Serve warm.

steps.do: Stir the rested batter. It should be the thickness of single (light) cream and run freely off a spoon. Add milk a tablespoon at a time if it has thickened.
steps.look: A smooth, thin, pourable batter with no lumps and a few small bubbles.
steps.mistake: Using batter that is too thick, which makes heavy, pancake-like crêpes.
steps.fix: Thin it with milk until it coats a spoon thinly.

steps.do: Heat the pan over medium-high heat for 2 minutes. Wipe it with a paper towel dipped in melted butter: a thin film, not a pool.
steps.look: A sheen of butter that sizzles gently; a drop of water dances across the surface.
steps.mistake: Too much butter, which fries the batter into a lacy, greasy edge and stops it spreading.
steps.fix: Wipe out excess with a dry paper towel.

steps.do: Lift the pan off the heat, pour in about 3 tbsp (45 ml) of batter for an 8 inch pan, or 1/4 cup (60 ml) for a 9 inch (23 cm) pan, at one side, and immediately tilt and swirl the pan in a circle so the batter runs to the edges in a thin, even layer.
steps.look: The batter spreads to a complete, thin circle and sets almost at once.
steps.mistake: Pouring into the centre of a level pan and hoping, or pouring too slowly, so it sets thick in one place.
steps.fix: Pour and swirl in one movement. Fill any holes with a drop of batter.

steps.do: Return to the heat and cook 45 seconds to 1 minute, until the edges look lacy and dry and start to lift away from the pan and the underside is golden in patches.
steps.look: Edges curling up and turning golden; the surface no longer looks wet.
steps.mistake: Flipping too early, so the crêpe tears.
steps.fix: Wait until the edge lifts by itself and the centre is matte.

steps.do: Slide the spatula under the edge, lift and flip the crêpe (or pick up the edge with your fingertips, carefully, and turn it). Cook the second side 15 to 20 seconds.
steps.look: The second side has only faint pale spots; the first side is lace-mottled gold.
steps.mistake: Cooking the second side too long, which makes the crêpe dry and brittle.
steps.fix: A few seconds is enough. The paler side goes on the inside when filled.

steps.do: Judge the first crêpe honestly: it is the test. Too pale and thick: the pan is too cool or the batter too thick. Burnt spots: the pan is too hot. Adjust the heat and the batter, then continue.
steps.look: From the second crêpe on, each is thin, even and golden.
steps.mistake: Carrying on without adjusting.
steps.fix: Eat the first crêpe yourself, as French cooks do, and fix the pan.

steps.do: Stack each finished crêpe on the plate under the towel. Butter the pan lightly every two or three crêpes and stir the batter each time, as the flour settles.
steps.look: A neat stack of soft crêpes that peel apart easily.
steps.mistake: Forgetting to stir the batter, so the later crêpes are thinner and the last are thick.
steps.fix: Stir before every pour.

steps.do: To serve, lay a crêpe paler side up, squeeze over a little lemon juice and sprinkle with 1 tsp (4 g) sugar. Fold in half, then in half again into a triangle.
steps.look: A soft triangle with a glossy, sugary interior and crisp lacy edges.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, which makes them soggy.
steps.fix: A light squeeze and a light sprinkle is all.

A very thin film of fat matters: too much and the batter fries at the edges and will not spread; too little and it sticks. The first crêpe calibrates the pan, setting the oil film and showing you the true temperature.
plating: Fold two crêpes into triangles and overlap them on a warm plate, points facing the same way. Crêpes Suzette: warm folded crêpes in butter, sugar, orange juice and zest.
Savoury buckwheat galettes: replace half the flour with buckwheat flour, leave out the sugar and fill with ham, Gruyère and an egg.

title: Kaiserschmarrn

steps.look: A smooth, glossy, pale yellow batter.
steps.mistake: Leaving lumps of flour, which stay as raw pockets.
steps.fix: Whisk longer, or press lumps against the side of the bowl.

steps.do: Whip the egg whites until foamy, then add 1 tbsp (12 g) sugar and keep whipping until they form soft to medium peaks that bend over at the tip when the whisk is lifted.
steps.look: Glossy, white, smooth foam that holds a peak which curls over at the top.
steps.mistake: Over-whipping until dry and grainy, which makes them hard to fold and they collapse.
steps.fix: If grainy, add a little unwhipped white and whisk briefly to smooth them.

steps.do: Stir one large spoonful of whites into the batter to loosen it. Then add the remaining whites and fold gently with the spatula: cut down through the centre, sweep along the bottom and up the side, turning the bowl a quarter turn each time, until no white streaks remain.
steps.look: A light, airy batter with no streaks, noticeably increased in volume.
steps.mistake: Stirring or beating, which knocks out the air and gives a flat, dense pancake.
steps.fix: Fold slowly and stop as soon as the streaks are gone.

steps.do: Melt 1 1/2 tbsp (21 g) butter in the skillet over medium heat until foaming. Pour in the batter and level it gently. Scatter the drained raisins over the top.
steps.look: The batter sets around the edge within a minute and the butter sizzles underneath.
steps.mistake: Pan too hot, so the base burns before the inside cooks.
steps.fix: Lower the heat to medium-low.

steps.do: Cook 3 to 4 minutes until the underside is golden brown when lifted at the edge and the edges are set. Then put the skillet in the oven for 6 to 8 minutes.
steps.look: The pancake puffs up and the top sets and turns pale golden; a skewer comes out clean.
steps.mistake: Taking it out while the centre is still wet.
steps.fix: Give it 2 more minutes in the oven.

steps.do: Using a mitt (the handle is very hot), return the pan to the stove over medium heat. With two forks or spatulas, tear the pancake into rough, bite-sized pieces about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) across.
steps.look: Ragged, irregular pieces with soft, fluffy insides.
steps.mistake: Cutting neat squares; the ragged edges are what catch the caramel.
steps.fix: Tear, do not cut.

steps.do: Add the remaining butter and 1 tbsp (12 g) sugar. Toss the pieces for 2 to 3 minutes until the edges caramelise and turn crisp and golden.
steps.look: Shiny, caramelised edges, and a sweet buttery smell.
steps.mistake: Burning the sugar on too high a heat.
steps.fix: Keep tossing on medium; lower the heat if it smokes.

steps.do: Pile onto warm plates, dust heavily with icing sugar through the sieve, and serve with the warm plum compote.
steps.look: A golden, sugar-dusted heap with crisp edges and fluffy middles.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit, so it loses its crispness.
steps.fix: Serve straight from the pan.

science: Egg whites are about 90 percent water and 10 percent protein. Whisking unfolds those proteins, which then link up around air bubbles to form a stable foam. Any fat, even a trace of yolk, coats the proteins and prevents them from bonding, which is why the bowl must be grease free. Sugar added once the whites are foamy stabilises the foam and makes it glossy. Folding keeps those bubbles intact; in the heat of the pan and oven they expand and the proteins set around them, giving a puffed, airy pancake. Tearing exposes rough surfaces where the butter and sugar caramelise, adding crisp edges to soft insides.
plating: Pile the torn pieces high in the centre of a warm plate in a loose, generous heap, raisins showing. Dust heavily with icing sugar through a sieve held high so it falls like snow. Spoon the warm plum compote into a small bowl on the side or in a pool beside the heap.

pairing.drink: A sweet Austrian wine such as a Burgenland Auslese, or a coffee with whipped cream in the Viennese style.
pairing.brennans: Kracher ‘Cuvée’ Auslese Burgenland 2017: the Burgenland Auslese on the list, an Austrian sweet wine for an Austrian pudding

variations: Apfelschmarrn: fold thinly sliced apples into the batter.
Without raisins, served with lingonberry jam.
Stovetop only: cut the pancake into quarters, flip each quarter and cook 3 minutes more before tearing.
safety: The skillet handle is dangerously hot after the oven: keep a mitt on it or a towel over the handle the whole time.
Cook until no wet batter remains inside the pieces; eggs should reach 160°F (71°C).
