title: Chocolate Chip Cookies
summary: Classic American chocolate chip cookies made by creaming softened butter with two sugars, resting the dough, and baking to crisp edges and a soft, slightly underdone centre. The first bake on a tray teaches creaming, why rested dough spreads less, and how far a hot tray keeps cooking after it leaves the oven.
equipment: Stand mixer with paddle, or a hand mixer and a large bowl
Two sheet pans lined with parchment
3 tbsp (45 ml) cookie scoop or two spoons
Oven thermometer, if your oven runs hot or cold

ingredients.note: about 65°F (18°C): it should dent when pressed but not look greasy
half chips, half a bar chopped into 1/2 inch (1 cm) pieces

mise: Take the butter and egg out of the fridge 1 hour ahead. The butter is ready when a finger leaves a dent without sinking in.
Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt together in a bowl.
Chop the chocolate bar. Line the sheet pans with parchment.
Clear space in the fridge for the dough bowl.

timeline.do: Soften butter and egg; weigh dry ingredients.
Cream, add egg, fold in dry and chocolate.
Rest the dough in the fridge at least 1 hour, ideally overnight.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Scoop the dough.
Bake one tray at a time, 11 to 13 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes on the tray, then on a rack. Serve warm.

steps.do: Beat the softened butter with both sugars on medium speed for 3 to 4 minutes, scraping down the bowl once, until noticeably paler and fluffy.
steps.look: The mixture lightens from tan to pale beige, increases in volume and looks like soft, fluffy frosting.
steps.mistake: Using melted or very soft butter, which cannot hold air, or cold butter, which stays in lumps.
steps.fix: If the butter is too warm and greasy, chill the bowl 10 minutes and beat again. If lumpy and cold, keep beating; friction warms it.

steps.do: Add the egg and vanilla and beat 1 minute until fully combined and smooth. Scrape the bowl.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy mixture, not curdled.
steps.mistake: Adding a cold egg, which makes the creamed butter seize and look curdled.
steps.fix: Beat a little longer; a slight curdle usually smooths once the flour goes in.

steps.do: On low speed, or by hand with the spatula, mix in the flour mixture just until no dry flour shows.
steps.look: A soft, thick dough with no streaks of flour.
steps.mistake: Mixing on high for a long time, which develops gluten and makes tough cookies.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as the flour disappears.

steps.do: Fold in the chocolate with the spatula.
steps.look: Chocolate evenly scattered through the dough.
steps.mistake: Overmixing at this stage.
steps.fix: A few turns are enough.

steps.do: Cover the bowl and refrigerate at least 1 hour, up to 72 hours. Longer rests give deeper, toffee-like flavour.
steps.look: Firm, cold dough that holds a scoop.
steps.mistake: Baking straight away, which spreads thin and flat.
steps.fix: Even 30 minutes helps; overnight is best.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the centre. Scoop the dough into 12 balls of about 1 3/4 oz (50 g) each and set 6 on each tray, at least 3 inches (7.5 cm) apart.
steps.look: Evenly sized, round balls with chocolate showing on the surface.
steps.mistake: Crowding the tray, so the cookies merge.
steps.fix: Bake six to a tray.

steps.do: Bake one tray at a time for 11 to 13 minutes, turning the tray halfway.
steps.look: Golden brown edges, puffed centres that look pale and slightly underdone and soft when gently pressed.
steps.mistake: Baking until the centre looks fully done; it will be hard once cool.
steps.fix: Pull them when the edges are golden and the centres still look shiny and soft. The hot tray finishes them.

steps.do: As soon as they come out, sprinkle a few flakes of sea salt on each. Leave them on the hot tray for 5 minutes, then move to the rack with a spatula.
steps.look: The centres sink slightly and set; the edges firm up.
steps.mistake: Moving them straight away, so they break.
steps.fix: Wait the full 5 minutes.

steps.do: Bake the second tray. Serve warm or at room temperature; store airtight for up to 3 days.
steps.look: Crisp edges, soft, chewy middles, pools of melted chocolate.
steps.mistake: Putting the second batch on a hot tray, which melts the dough before it bakes.
steps.fix: Let the tray cool, or use a fresh tray and parchment.

science: Creaming beats air into butter. The sharp edges of sugar crystals cut tiny pockets into the solid fat, and those air cells expand in the oven, lightening the cookie. That only works when butter is cool and pliable, around 65°F (18°C); melted butter cannot trap air. Brown sugar contains molasses, which holds moisture and makes cookies chewy, while white sugar crisps the edges. Resting the dough lets the flour absorb liquid and the butter firm up, so the cookies spread less and brown more evenly, and enzymes break some starch into sugars for deeper flavour. Baking soda raises the pH, speeding browning. A hot tray keeps cooking the cookies after the oven, so they come out looking underdone.
plating: Stack three cookies slightly offset on a small plate or a sheet of parchment on a board, with a cold glass of milk or a coffee beside them. Break one in half and lay it on top so the melted chocolate shows.

pairing.drink: A cold glass of milk, an espresso, or a tawny or vintage port, whose dried fruit and nuttiness suit chocolate and brown sugar.
pairing.brennans: Dow’s Vintage Port 2000 (375 ml): the vintage port on the list, dried fruit for chocolate and brown sugar

variations: Brown butter cookies, the library’s version: brown the butter, cool it to soft, then whisk rather than cream; the result is chewier and nuttier.
Oatmeal raisin: replace 1/2 cup (60 g) flour with rolled oats and the chocolate with raisins and 1/2 tsp (1 g) cinnamon.
Double chocolate: replace 1/4 cup (25 g) flour with cocoa powder.
safety: Raw cookie dough contains raw egg and raw flour, which can carry harmful bacteria. Do not taste it.
Sheet pans stay very hot; use a mitt and set them on a heatproof surface.

title: Anzac Biscuits
summary: Australian and New Zealand oat and coconut biscuits made by the melting method: butter and golden syrup are melted, foamed with bicarbonate of soda and stirred into the dry ingredients. A melted-butter biscuit is the counterpoint to creaming, and it shows how bicarbonate reacts with syrup and how minutes in the oven decide chewy against crisp.
equipment: Two sheet pans lined with parchment

ingredients.note: such as Lyle’s; or light corn syrup with 1 tsp (5 ml) honey

mise: Heat the oven to 320°F (160°C) with a rack in the centre. Line the trays.
Mix the oats, flour, coconut, sugar and salt in the large bowl.
Measure the bicarbonate into a small cup and boil the kettle.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; mix the dry ingredients.
Melt butter and syrup; foam with bicarbonate; mix the dough.
Roll 12 balls; flatten on the trays.
Bake 12 minutes for chewy, up to 18 for crisp.
Cool on the tray 10 minutes.
Serve, or store airtight for a week.

steps.do: Melt the butter and golden syrup in the saucepan over low heat, stirring, until just melted and smooth. Do not let it bubble.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, golden liquid.
steps.mistake: Boiling it, which starts to caramelise the syrup and makes harder biscuits.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as the butter melts.

steps.do: Pour the boiling water onto the bicarbonate and stir to dissolve, then tip it straight into the warm butter mixture and stir.
steps.look: The mixture foams up pale and roughly doubles in volume.
steps.mistake: Letting the foam sit and collapse before using it.
steps.fix: Use the foam immediately; it is the leavening.

steps.do: Pour the foaming mixture into the dry ingredients and stir with the wooden spoon until every bit is moistened.
steps.look: A stiff, slightly greasy, crumbly dough that holds together when squeezed.
steps.mistake: Adding the butter mixture cold, so it does not bind.
steps.fix: If the dough is too crumbly to hold, add 1 tsp (5 ml) warm water.

steps.do: Roll the dough into 12 balls, each about the size of a walnut, roughly 1 1/2 tbsp (25 g). Set 6 on each tray, 2 inches (5 cm) apart, and flatten each lightly with your palm to 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) thick.
steps.look: Even, round discs with rough edges.
steps.mistake: Pressing very thin, which makes them burn at the edges.
steps.fix: Keep them a little thick; they spread in the oven.

steps.do: Bake one tray at a time: 12 minutes for chewy biscuits, or 15 to 18 minutes for crisp ones.
steps.look: Spread and deep golden; the edges darker than the centres, which still look soft.
steps.mistake: Baking until the centres feel firm in the oven, which makes them rock hard once cool.
steps.fix: Judge by colour: deep gold at the edge. They harden as they cool.

steps.do: Leave on the tray for 10 minutes to firm, then move to the rack to cool completely.
steps.look: Biscuits that are soft when hot and set as they cool.
steps.mistake: Moving them while hot, so they fold or break.
steps.fix: Give them the 10 minutes.

steps.do: Store airtight. Chewy ones keep their chew 3 to 4 days; crisp ones stay crisp for a week.
steps.look: A caramel, oaty, coconut biscuit with a crisp edge.
steps.mistake: Storing them with soft cakes, which makes them go soft.
steps.fix: Store on their own in a tin.

science: There is no egg here, so texture comes from sugar, syrup and baking time. Golden syrup is largely invert sugar, glucose and fructose, which holds onto water and keeps the centre chewy. Bicarbonate of soda is an alkali: when it meets the slightly acidic syrup and hot water it releases carbon dioxide, which is the foam you see and the only lift the biscuits get. It also raises the pH of the dough, and alkaline conditions speed the Maillard browning, which is why Anzacs turn such a deep amber. More minutes in the oven drive off more water, so the same dough can be chewy or crisp.
plating: Stack five or six biscuits in a leaning tower on a small wooden board or plate, with a cup of tea beside them. For a dessert plate, set two biscuits against a scoop of vanilla ice cream with a drizzle of golden syrup.

pairing.drink: A cup of strong black tea or a flat white, or a small glass of Australian fortified Muscat.

variations: Ginger Anzacs: add 1 tsp (2 g) ground ginger and 2 tbsp (24 g) chopped crystallised ginger.
Macadamia Anzacs: add 1/3 cup (45 g) chopped macadamias.
Anzac slice: press the dough into a lined 8 inch (20 cm) square tin and bake 20 minutes, then cut into bars.
safety: The foaming butter mixture is hot: stir it carefully.
Tell guests the biscuits contain coconut, oats and wheat.

title: Cantucci di Prato
summary: Tuscan almond biscuits from Prato: a firm egg dough shaped into logs, baked, sliced on the diagonal and baked again until dry right through. Twice-baking explains how dryness keeps a biscuit crisp for weeks.
equipment: Large mixing bowl and a spatula
mise: Heat the oven to 340°F (170°C) with a rack in the centre. Line the sheet pan.
Zest the orange. Separate one egg, keeping the white for the glaze.
Mix the flour, sugar, salt and zest in the bowl.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; mix the dry ingredients.
Make the dough; shape two logs; glaze.
First bake, 25 to 30 minutes.
Cool the logs 15 minutes; slice at 45 degrees.
Second bake at 300°F (150°C), 15 to 20 minutes.
Cool completely; they crisp as they cool.

steps.do: Add the whole egg and the yolk to the dry ingredients and work them in with the spatula, then your hand, until a stiff, sticky dough forms with no dry flour left.
steps.look: A thick, tacky dough that holds together in a ball.
steps.mistake: Adding water or extra egg because it looks dry at first; it comes together as you work it.
steps.fix: Keep pressing and folding for a minute before deciding it needs anything.

steps.do: Add the almonds and knead them in until evenly spread through the dough.
steps.look: Almonds visible throughout.
steps.mistake: Using toasted almonds, which can burn in the double bake.
steps.fix: Use raw almonds; they toast as the biscuits bake.

steps.do: Dust your hands with flour, divide the dough in two and shape each half into a log about 10 inches (25 cm) long and 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) wide on the tray, 3 inches (7.5 cm) apart. Flatten the tops slightly.
steps.look: Two even logs of the same width and height.
steps.mistake: Making uneven logs, so slices bake unevenly.
steps.fix: Pat and roll them straight with floured hands.

steps.do: Brush the logs with the beaten egg white.
steps.look: A thin, even, glossy coat.
steps.mistake: Pooling egg white along the base, which burns.
steps.fix: Brush lightly; wipe pools from the parchment.

steps.do: Bake 25 to 30 minutes until firm and pale golden.
steps.look: The logs have spread slightly, turned light gold and feel firm when pressed, with a few cracks on top.
steps.mistake: Underbaking, so the logs squash when sliced.
steps.fix: Give them 5 more minutes if they feel soft.

steps.do: Cool on the tray for 15 minutes. Lower the oven to 300°F (150°C).
steps.look: Warm logs, firm enough to cut.
steps.mistake: Cutting hot logs, which squash, or cold logs, which shatter at the almonds.
steps.fix: Cut them warm, neither hot nor cold.

steps.do: Move the logs to a board. With the serrated knife, cut each log on a 45 degree angle into slices about 5/8 inch (1.5 cm) thick, using a gentle sawing motion.
steps.look: Clean, even slices with whole almonds cut through.
steps.mistake: Pressing straight down, which cracks the slices.
steps.fix: Saw gently and let the knife do the work.

steps.do: Lay the slices cut side down on the tray and bake again 15 to 20 minutes, turning them over halfway, until dry all the way through.
steps.look: Pale golden cut surfaces; they feel dry and firm, though they may still flex slightly while hot.
steps.mistake: Pulling them when the cut faces are still soft and damp; they go stale fast.
steps.fix: Bake longer than looks necessary; judge by the snap once cool.

steps.do: Cool completely on the rack. Test one: it should snap cleanly.
steps.look: A crisp snap, a dry, crunchy biscuit.
steps.mistake: Storing while warm, which traps steam and softens them.
steps.fix: Cool fully, then store airtight for up to a month.

science: Cantucci keep for weeks because of water. Biscuits go stale or soft when they hold moisture, and mould needs water to grow. The first bake sets the egg proteins and cooks the dough through; slicing exposes the moist interior; the second, low bake is a drying bake, driving water from the cut faces until the biscuit is almost completely dry. With little water left, there is nothing to make it soft. The Prato tradition uses no chemical leavening, so the dough rises only slightly from the eggs and stays dense and even, perfect for dunking. A low second bake dries without overbrowning.
plating: Stand a handful of cantucci upright in a small glass, or lay five in a fan on a small plate beside a little glass of sweet wine or an espresso. In Tuscany, they are dunked.

pairing.drink: Tuscan Vin Santo for dunking, as in Prato, or a sweet Moscadello di Montalcino; an espresso works too.
pairing.brennans: Castello Banfi ‘Florus’ Moscadello di Montalcino 2011: the Moscadello di Montalcino on the list, a Tuscan sweet wine for a Tuscan biscuit

variations: Chocolate and hazelnut: replace the almonds with toasted hazelnuts and add 2 tbsp (14 g) cocoa.
Pistachio and cranberry, with lemon zest in place of orange.
Anise biscotti: add 1 tsp (2 g) anise seeds and a splash of anise liqueur.
safety: Use a serrated knife with a sawing motion and keep your guiding hand flat on top of the log, fingers clear.
Almonds are a tree nut: tell guests.

title: Fudgy Brownies
summary: Dense, fudgy brownies made with gently melted dark chocolate, butter and cocoa, eggs and sugar beaten for a shiny crackled top, and very little flour, baked until just underdone and cooled completely. Melting chocolate so it never seizes and judging an underbake by skewer are skills used to the top of the course.
skills: beating eggs and sugar for a crackled top
equipment: 8.5 x 4.5 inch (21 x 11 cm) metal loaf tin, lined with a parchment sling overhanging the long sides
Saucepan and a heatproof bowl that sits on top without touching the water
Sharp knife and a jug of hot water for cutting
mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the centre. Line the loaf tin with a parchment sling.
Chop the chocolate into small, even pieces so it melts evenly.
Take the eggs out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead, or stand them in warm water for 5 minutes.
Whisk the flour, cocoa and fine salt together.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; line the tin; bring eggs to room temperature.
Melt chocolate and butter gently; cool 5 minutes.
Whisk eggs and sugars a full 2 to 3 minutes; combine; fold in dry.
Bake 25 to 30 minutes, until a skewer shows moist crumbs.
Cool completely in the tin, about 2 hours.
Lift out and cut with a hot, wiped knife.

steps.do: Put 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water in the saucepan and bring it to a bare simmer. Set the bowl with the chocolate and butter over it; the bowl must not touch the water. Stir gently until melted and smooth. Take the bowl off the heat and cool 5 minutes.
steps.look: A glossy, smooth, flowing mixture with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Letting steam or a drop of water into the chocolate, or overheating it, which makes it seize into a thick, grainy paste.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low and wipe the base of the bowl. If it seizes, stir in 1 tbsp (15 ml) boiling water vigorously; it may smooth out for baking.

steps.do: In a separate bowl, whisk the egg, yolks, both sugars and vanilla hard for 2 to 3 minutes (1 to 2 minutes with a mixer) until thick, pale and glossy.
steps.look: The mixture lightens in colour and falls from the whisk in a thick ribbon; the sugar has largely dissolved.
steps.mistake: Stirring briefly, which gives a dull, matte top with no crackle.
steps.fix: Keep whisking; this step makes the shiny crust.

steps.do: Pour the warm chocolate into the eggs in a steady stream, whisking constantly, until evenly combined and glossy.
steps.look: A thick, shiny, dark batter.
steps.mistake: Adding hot chocolate, which can scramble the eggs.
steps.fix: Let the chocolate cool to warm first; it should feel only warm on your lip.

steps.do: Sift the flour and cocoa mixture over the top and fold it in with the spatula, just until no streaks remain.
steps.look: A thick, glossy batter that falls from the spatula in ribbons.
steps.mistake: Overmixing, which develops gluten and makes them cakey.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as the flour disappears.

steps.do: Scrape into the tin and level it. Sprinkle the flaky salt over the top.
steps.look: An even, glossy surface.
steps.mistake: Leaving it uneven, so one end overbakes.
steps.fix: Smooth with the back of the spatula.

steps.do: Bake 25 to 30 minutes. At 25 minutes, insert the skewer into the centre and pull it out.
steps.look: The top is shiny and crackled; the edges are set; the skewer comes out with dark moist crumbs and a little smear, not wet batter and not clean.
steps.mistake: Baking until the skewer comes out clean, which means you have baked cake.
steps.fix: If wet batter clings, bake 3 minutes more and test again.

steps.do: Set the tin on the rack and cool completely, about 2 hours. The centre sets as it cools.
steps.look: Firm to the touch and slightly sunken in the centre.
steps.mistake: Cutting warm, so they ooze and fall apart.
steps.fix: Be patient. To hurry, chill 30 minutes once at room temperature.

steps.do: Lift out by the parchment sling. Cut into 8 bars with a sharp knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between every cut.
steps.look: Clean, sharp edges with a dense, fudgy interior and a papery top.
steps.mistake: Cutting with a cold, dirty knife, which drags.
steps.fix: Dip and wipe after every cut.

science: Chocolate is cocoa solids and sugar suspended in cocoa butter. A single drop of water makes the sugar and solids clump together into a stiff paste: the chocolate has seized; too much heat does the same as it scorches. Melting it gently over steam avoids both. The shiny, crackled crust comes from dissolved sugar: beating the eggs and sugar for a few minutes dissolves the sugar into the eggs, and in the oven it rises to the surface and dries into a thin, glossy meringue-like skin. Fudginess comes from a high ratio of fat and sugar to flour and from underbaking: the centre stays moist, and carryover heat and cooling set it.
plating: Serve one bar on a small plate, slightly warm if you like (10 seconds in the microwave), with a quenelle of vanilla ice cream or crème fraîche beside it and a light dusting of cocoa on the plate. The crackled top should face up.

pairing.drink: A glass of cold milk, an espresso, or a Banyuls or ruby port, whose red fruit sweetness is made for dark chocolate.
pairing.brennans: Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva NV: the Banyuls on the list, made for dark chocolate

variations: Espresso brownies: dissolve 1 tsp (1 g) instant espresso powder in the vanilla.
Pecan brownies: fold in 1/2 cup (55 g) toasted pecans, a New Orleans favourite.
Swirled: dot the top with 2 tbsp (32 g) peanut butter or raspberry jam and marble with a skewer before baking.
safety: Raw brownie batter contains raw egg and raw flour: do not taste it.
Steam from the bain-marie burns: lift the bowl with a cloth.

title: Victoria Sponge
summary: The British teatime cake: two light sponges made with equal weights of butter, sugar, egg and flour, sandwiched with raspberry jam and whipped cream and dusted with caster sugar. It is the purest test of creaming, where the air beaten in becomes the rise.
equipment: Two 6 inch (15 cm) round cake tins, at least 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) deep, greased and base lined with parchment
Stand mixer or hand mixer and a large bowl
Whisk and a bowl for the cream

ingredients.metric: about 113 g out of the shell
ingredients.note: at room temperature; weigh them out of the shell, and if they come to more or less, match the butter, sugar and flour to their weight

mise: Take the butter and eggs out of the fridge 1 hour ahead.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C), or 325°F (160°C) with a fan, with a rack in the centre.
Grease the tins with butter, line the bases with parchment circles and grease the paper.
Weigh the eggs in their shells and subtract about 7 g per egg for the shell; weigh the butter, sugar and flour to match. Sift the flour, baking powder and salt together.
Beat the eggs lightly in a jug.

timeline.do: Soften butter and eggs; prepare tins; heat oven.
Cream butter and sugar a full 5 minutes.
Add eggs gradually; fold in flour and milk.
Bake 20 to 22 minutes.
Cool 5 minutes in the tins, then completely on a rack.
Whip the cream; sandwich with jam and cream; dust with sugar.

steps.do: Beat the butter and sugar on medium-high speed for a full 5 minutes, scraping down the bowl twice.
steps.look: The mixture turns from yellow to very pale, almost white, and is light, fluffy and noticeably larger in volume.
steps.mistake: Stopping after a minute, when it has barely changed colour; the sponge will be dense.
steps.fix: Time it. Five minutes is not too long.

steps.do: Add the beaten egg a little at a time, about a tablespoon at once, beating well after each addition. If the mixture starts to look curdled, add a spoonful of the flour.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, thick batter after each addition.
steps.mistake: Adding the eggs all at once or cold, so the mixture curdles and loses its air.
steps.fix: Add a spoon of flour and beat; it usually comes back. Cold eggs are the usual cause.

steps.do: Sift the flour mixture over the batter in two additions, folding gently with the spatula after each, cutting through the middle and lifting from the bottom. Fold in the milk and vanilla.
steps.look: A soft batter that drops easily from the spatula, called a dropping consistency.
steps.mistake: Beating the flour in, which knocks out air and develops gluten.
steps.fix: Fold just until no flour shows. If the batter is too stiff to drop, add another teaspoon of milk.

steps.do: Divide the batter evenly between the tins, weighing them for accuracy. Level the tops with the back of a spoon.
steps.look: Two tins holding equal weights of batter, level surfaces.
steps.mistake: Uneven amounts, so the layers bake differently.
steps.fix: Use the scale.

steps.do: Bake on the centre rack for 20 to 22 minutes. Do not open the door for the first 15 minutes.
steps.look: Golden brown, risen and level; the sides just shrinking away from the tins; the top springs back when pressed lightly with a fingertip; a skewer comes out clean.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven early, which can make the sponges sink.
steps.fix: If a fingertip leaves a dent, bake 2 to 3 minutes more.

steps.do: Cool in the tins for 5 minutes, then run a knife around the edge, turn out onto the rack, peel off the paper, and turn them top side up. Cool completely.
steps.look: Smooth, golden sponges with straight sides.
steps.mistake: Filling while warm, which melts the cream.
steps.fix: Wait until completely cool.

steps.do: Whip the cream with 1 tsp (4 g) sugar to soft peaks that just hold their shape.
steps.look: Soft, billowy cream that holds a gentle peak which flops at the tip.
steps.mistake: Over-whipping into grainy, buttery cream.
steps.fix: Stop early; if slightly over, fold in a spoon of unwhipped cream.

steps.do: Choose the less handsome sponge for the base and set it top side down on a plate. Spread the jam to within 1/4 inch (6 mm) of the edge, then spread the cream over it. Set the second sponge on top, top side up, and press lightly.
steps.look: Neat layers of red jam and white cream visible at the side.
steps.mistake: Spreading the cream right to the edge so it squeezes out.
steps.fix: Leave a margin; the weight of the top layer spreads it.

steps.do: Dust the top with caster sugar. Serve within 2 hours, or refrigerate.
steps.look: A golden cake with a sparkling sugar top and straight sides.
steps.mistake: Leaving a cream-filled cake out for hours.
steps.fix: Refrigerate if not eating within 2 hours; bring out 15 minutes before serving.

science: Creaming is the engine of this cake. Beating butter with sugar crystals drives tiny air bubbles into the fat; the longer you cream, the more and finer the bubbles. In the oven, baking powder releases carbon dioxide into those existing bubbles, and steam from the eggs and butter expands them further, so the sponge rises on the air you beat in. Adding egg gradually keeps the butter and egg emulsified; too much at once and the water in the egg overwhelms the fat, it curdles and air escapes. Folding the flour gently keeps the bubbles and limits gluten, keeping the crumb tender. Equal weights give a balanced, reliable cake.
plating: Set the whole cake on a cake stand or a plain plate with a doily. Cut into four wedges with a long, sharp knife, wiping it between cuts so the cream stays clean. Lay a wedge on its side on a small plate so the jam and cream layers show, with a few fresh raspberries beside it.

pairing.drink: A pot of English breakfast tea, or a glass of English sparkling wine, whose bright acidity suits jam and cream.
pairing.brennans: Ridgeview ‘Bloomsbury’ Brut Sussex NV: the English sparkling wine on the list, bright acidity for jam and cream

variations: With buttercream: beat 4 tbsp (56 g) butter with 1/2 cup (60 g) icing sugar instead of whipped cream; it keeps at room temperature.
Lemon sponge: add lemon zest to the batter and fill with lemon curd and cream.
Strawberry sponge: fresh sliced strawberries over the cream in summer.
safety: A cream-filled cake must be refrigerated if it will not be eaten within 2 hours.
Raw batter contains raw egg and flour: do not taste it.

title: Tarta de Santiago
summary: The almond cake of Santiago de Compostela: eggs and sugar whisked to the ribbon stage, ground almonds folded in, baked and dusted with icing sugar around a stencil of the cross of Saint James. An almond cake raised only by whisked eggs shows a second way, after creaming, to put air into a cake.
skills: whisking eggs and sugar to the ribbon
ground almonds in place of flour
equipment: 7 inch (18 cm) springform tin, buttered and base lined with parchment
Stand mixer with whisk or a hand mixer
Paper stencil of the cross of Saint James (print and cut one out), about 4 inches (10 cm) tall
mise: Take the eggs out of the fridge at least 1 hour ahead, or stand them in warm water for 10 minutes. Warm eggs whip to far greater volume.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the centre. Butter the tin and line the base.
Mix the ground almonds, lemon zest, cinnamon and salt in a bowl, breaking up any lumps with your fingers.
Print and cut out the stencil.

timeline.do: Warm the eggs; prepare tin and stencil; heat the oven.
Whisk eggs and sugar to the ribbon, 5 to 7 minutes.
Fold in almonds in three additions; add sherry.
Bake 30 to 35 minutes.
Cool completely in the tin.
Stencil the cross with icing sugar; serve in slim wedges.

steps.do: Whisk the eggs and sugar on medium-high speed for 5 to 7 minutes until very thick, pale and roughly tripled in volume.
steps.look: The mixture turns from yellow to pale cream, and when the whisk is lifted, it falls in a thick ribbon that sits on the surface for 3 seconds before sinking. This is the ribbon stage.
steps.mistake: Stopping too early, when the ribbon sinks at once; the cake will be flat and dense.
steps.fix: Keep whisking. Test by drawing a figure of eight with the falling batter: it should hold its shape briefly.

steps.do: Sprinkle a third of the almond mixture over the foam and fold it in gently with the spatula, cutting down through the centre, sweeping across the bottom and up the side, turning the bowl as you go.
steps.look: The almonds disappear into the foam with minimal loss of volume.
steps.mistake: Stirring or beating, which collapses the foam you just built.
steps.fix: Fold slowly and gently. A little deflation is normal.

steps.do: Fold in the remaining almonds in two more additions, then fold in the sherry. Stop as soon as no dry almond remains.
steps.look: A thick, mousse-like batter with no streaks.
steps.mistake: Overfolding, so the batter turns runny and flat.
steps.fix: Stop when evenly mixed.

steps.do: Pour into the tin and gently level the top. Tap the tin once on the counter to release any large bubbles.
steps.look: An even surface.
steps.mistake: Banging the tin hard, which knocks out the air.
steps.fix: One gentle tap only.

steps.do: Bake 30 to 35 minutes until deep golden, risen and firm to the touch.
steps.look: An even, deep golden top; the edges pulling away from the tin; a skewer in the centre comes out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter.
steps.mistake: Underbaking, so the centre collapses; or overbaking, so it turns dry.
steps.fix: If the top browns too fast before the centre sets, lay a sheet of foil loosely over it.

steps.do: Cool completely in the tin on a rack, at least 45 minutes. The cake sinks a little and firms as it cools.
steps.look: A firm, slightly sunken cake with a thin, crisp crust.
steps.mistake: Releasing the cake while hot, which can tear it.
steps.fix: Leave it until fully cool, then run a knife around the edge and open the springform.

steps.do: Set the cake on a plate. Lay the stencil in the centre of the cake. Dust the whole surface heavily with icing sugar through the sieve held high.
steps.look: A thick, even white coat on the cake and stencil.
steps.mistake: Dusting while the cake is warm, so the sugar melts.
steps.fix: Wait until completely cool.

steps.do: Lift the stencil straight up with both hands in one smooth movement.
steps.look: A crisp, dark golden cross showing through the white sugar.
steps.mistake: Sliding the stencil sideways, which smudges the design.
steps.fix: Lift straight up. If it smudges, dust lightly again and use the stencil once more.

science: Whole eggs can trap a lot of air when whisked with sugar, but only if they are warm: warmth makes the proteins more flexible and the sugar dissolves more easily, so they unfold and wrap around bubbles quickly. At the ribbon stage, the foam is stable enough to carry heavy ground almonds without collapsing. In the oven, the air bubbles expand and the egg proteins set around them, holding the rise without baking powder or creaming. Almonds bring fat and protein rather than starch, so the crumb is moist, dense and tender. As the cake cools, the structure contracts slightly and firms, which is why it is left in the tin.
plating: Serve the whole cake on a plain plate so the cross shows. Cut slim wedges with a sharp knife, wiping it between cuts, and lay each on its side on a small plate with a spoon of lightly whipped cream and a small glass of sherry beside it.

pairing.drink: A glass of cream or pale cream sherry, nutty and gently sweet, the Spanish choice with almond cake; or a sweet Galician aguardiente for the brave.
pairing.brennans: Barbadillo ‘Pale Cream’ Sherry NV: the pale cream sherry on the list, the Spanish match for almond cake

variations: Orange and almond: replace the lemon zest with orange zest and add a splash of orange liqueur.
With a short pastry base, as in some Galician bakeries: blind bake a thin base and pour the batter over.
Individual cakes in a muffin tin, baked 18 to 20 minutes.
safety: Almonds are a tree nut: tell guests the whole cake is built on them.
Raw batter contains raw egg: do not taste it.

title: Malva Pudding
summary: A South African baked pudding: a light, apricot-scented sponge baked until deep brown, then soaked while hot with a hot butter and cream syrup until it drinks every drop. It teaches how a hot sponge absorbs a hot syrup, and how beating egg and sugar to a pale foam lightens a simple batter.
skills: pouring a hot cream syrup over a hot cake
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) square baking dish or a 1 1/2 quart (1.5 litre) oval dish, buttered
Stand mixer or hand mixer and a large bowl
Small jug or measuring cup for the milk mixture
mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the centre. Butter the dish.
Sift the flour, baking soda and salt together.
Stir the milk, melted butter and vinegar together in a jug; it may look slightly curdled, which is fine.
Measure the sauce ingredients into the small saucepan.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; butter the dish; sift the dry ingredients.
Beat egg, sugar and jam until pale and thick.
Fold in dry ingredients and milk mixture alternately.
Bake 30 to 35 minutes until deep brown.
Heat the sauce; poke the hot pudding; pour the sauce over.
Rest 15 minutes; serve warm with ice cream or custard.

steps.do: Beat the egg, sugar and apricot jam on medium-high speed for 4 to 5 minutes until pale, thick and roughly doubled.
steps.look: A pale, creamy foam that falls in a thick ribbon from the beaters.
steps.mistake: Stopping after a minute, which gives a dense, heavy sponge.
steps.fix: Keep beating; this foam is what makes it light.

steps.do: Add a third of the flour mixture and fold it in gently, then half the milk mixture, then another third of flour, the rest of the milk, and the last of the flour, folding after each until just combined.
steps.look: A smooth, loose batter with no pockets of flour.
steps.mistake: Beating hard, which knocks out the air.
steps.fix: Fold with the spatula and stop as soon as it is smooth.

steps.do: Pour into the dish and level it. Bake 30 to 35 minutes.
steps.look: Risen, deep golden brown all over, springing back when pressed; a skewer in the centre comes out clean.
steps.mistake: Pulling it pale; it needs a deep colour for the caramel flavour.
steps.fix: Bake a few minutes longer until deeply browned.

steps.do: Five minutes before the pudding is ready, heat the sauce ingredients over medium heat, stirring, until the butter melts and the sugar dissolves. Bring just to a simmer.
steps.look: A smooth, golden, steaming sauce.
steps.mistake: Boiling the sauce hard, which can split the cream.
steps.fix: Keep it just below a boil.

steps.do: As soon as the pudding comes out, poke holes all over it with a skewer, about 3/4 inch (2 cm) apart, right to the bottom.
steps.look: Dozens of holes across the whole surface.
steps.mistake: Poking only the top, so the sauce sits on the surface.
steps.fix: Push the skewer all the way down.

steps.do: Pour the hot sauce slowly and evenly over the hot pudding. It will look like far too much.
steps.look: The sauce pools, then sinks in and is gradually absorbed.
steps.mistake: Pouring cold sauce or letting the pudding cool first, so it does not absorb.
steps.fix: Hot sauce onto hot pudding is the rule.

steps.do: Rest 15 minutes until the pudding has drunk almost all the sauce, leaving a shallow, glossy moat at the edges.
steps.look: A dark, glossy, sticky top and a soft, saturated sponge.
steps.mistake: Serving immediately, when the sauce is still on top.
steps.fix: Wait the full 15 minutes.

steps.do: Serve warm in squares with vanilla ice cream or custard, spooning any sauce from the dish over the top.
steps.look: A soft, caramel-soaked sponge with a slight crust at the edges.
steps.mistake: Serving it cold, when the butter in the sauce firms.
steps.fix: Rewarm leftovers gently, covered, in a low oven.

science: Baking soda is an alkali that needs an acid to release carbon dioxide; here the vinegar and the apricot jam supply it, and the beaten egg and sugar foam adds air of its own. Baking until deep brown matters because the Maillard reaction and caramelisation on the crust bring the toffee flavour that defines malva. The soaking works because both sponge and sauce are hot: the sponge’s air cells are open and its starch is still soft and swollen, so it draws the liquid in by capillary action, the way a hot sponge soaks up water. Let it cool and the crumb tightens and absorbs far less.
plating: Cut a generous square and lift it onto a warm shallow bowl, glossy top up. Spoon a little of the remaining sauce over and around it, set a scoop of vanilla ice cream against one side so it begins to melt into the sauce, and finish with a thin strip of orange zest or a single mint leaf.

pairing.drink: A cream liqueur, or a sweet South African Muscat or a Sauternes. Brennan’s own float made with Amarula, the South African cream liqueur, vanilla ice cream and root beer is a natural partner.
pairing.brennans: Floating in South Africa: Brennan's Amarula float, a South African cream liqueur beside a South African pudding

variations: Sticky toffee pudding, a close cousin: add chopped dates soaked in boiling water to the batter and use a toffee sauce.
Orange malva: add orange zest to the sponge and orange juice in place of the water in the sauce.
Brandy sauce: replace 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the water with brandy, as some Cape cooks do.
safety: The sauce is hot and fatty: pour it slowly and keep your hand back.
Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours; the sauce contains cream.

title: Peach Cobbler
summary: A Southern cobbler of ripe peaches macerated with sugar, lemon and spice, topped with a rubbed-in buttermilk biscuit dough and baked until the biscuits are golden and the fruit bubbles thickly at the centre. It puts the rubbing-in skill from the shortbread to work over juicy, thickened fruit.
skills: baking until bubbling at the centre
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) square or 9 inch (23 cm) round baking dish, about 1 1/2 quarts (1.5 litres)
Saucepan of boiling water and a bowl of iced water for peeling
Slotted spoon and a paring knife

ingredients.note: fragrant and yielding slightly; or 1 1/2 lb (680 g) frozen sliced peaches, thawed and drained
adjust to the sweetness of the peaches

mise: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) with a rack in the centre. Set the baking dish on the sheet pan.

To peel the peaches, cut a shallow X in the base of each, lower into boiling water for 30 to 45 seconds, then into iced water. The skins slip off. Halve, stone and slice into 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) wedges.
Cube the butter and put it back in the fridge, or the freezer for 10 minutes.
Whisk the biscuit flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda and salt in a bowl.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; peel and slice the peaches.
Macerate the peaches 20 minutes.
Fruit into the dish; bake alone 10 minutes. Make the biscuit dough.
Top with biscuits; bake 25 to 30 minutes until bubbling in the centre.
Cool at least 10 minutes so the juices thicken.
Serve warm with vanilla ice cream.

steps.do: Toss the peaches with the sugar, lemon juice, cornstarch, cinnamon, nutmeg and a pinch of salt. Leave 20 minutes.
steps.look: The peaches release a syrupy juice that pools in the bowl and the cornstarch dissolves.
steps.mistake: Leaving out the cornstarch, so the cobbler floods with thin juice.
steps.fix: Check the cornstarch is fully dissolved in the juice before baking.

steps.do: Tip the peaches and all their juice into the dish and bake alone for 10 minutes while you make the topping.
steps.look: The juices begin to bubble at the edges.
steps.mistake: Putting raw dough on cold fruit, which leaves the underside of the biscuits doughy.
steps.fix: The head start heats the fruit so the biscuit bottoms cook through.

steps.do: Add the cold butter cubes to the flour mixture and rub them in with your fingertips or the pastry blender until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs with some pea-sized pieces of butter left.
steps.look: Crumbly mixture with visible flakes and small lumps of butter.
steps.mistake: Rubbing until fine and warm, so the butter melts and the biscuits are heavy.
steps.fix: Work fast with cold fingertips; chill the bowl 5 minutes if the butter softens.

steps.do: Pour in the buttermilk and stir with a fork just until a shaggy, sticky dough forms. Do not knead.
steps.look: A rough, lumpy dough with no dry flour at the bottom of the bowl.
steps.mistake: Overmixing into a smooth dough, which makes tough biscuits.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as it holds together.

steps.do: Take the dish out of the oven. Drop the dough over the hot fruit in 6 to 8 rough spoonfuls, leaving gaps between them for steam to escape. Sprinkle with the turbinado sugar.
steps.look: Rustic mounds of dough on bubbling fruit, with fruit showing between them.
steps.mistake: Spreading the dough in a solid sheet, which steams underneath and stays raw.
steps.fix: Leave gaps; they let the fruit bubble up and the biscuits bake.

steps.do: Bake 25 to 30 minutes until the biscuits are deep golden and the fruit bubbles thickly, not just at the edges but in the centre too. A biscuit should read about 200°F (93°C) in the middle if you check.
steps.look: Golden, crisp-topped biscuits; thick, glossy juices bubbling slowly in the centre of the dish.
steps.mistake: Pulling it when only the edges bubble; the cornstarch has not thickened the centre, so it runs.
steps.fix: Bake until the centre bubbles. If the biscuits brown too fast, cover loosely with foil.

steps.do: Cool on a rack for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20, so the juices set into a syrup.
steps.look: Juices that thicken as they cool.
steps.mistake: Serving immediately, when the filling is runny and very hot.
steps.fix: Wait; it is better warm than hot.

steps.do: Spoon into bowls with a biscuit on top and a scoop of vanilla ice cream beside it.
steps.look: Glossy peaches, a tender, flaky biscuit, ice cream melting into the juices.
steps.mistake: Burying the biscuit under the ice cream, so it goes soggy.
steps.fix: Put the ice cream beside the biscuit.

science: Sugar draws juice out of the peaches by osmosis, which is the macerating, and dissolves into it. Cornstarch thickens that juice, but only once it reaches a boil, around 203°F (95°C), when the starch granules burst; that is why the cobbler must bubble in the centre, not just at the edges. Lemon juice brightens flavour and keeps the peaches from browning. The biscuit topping is tender because the cold butter pieces stay solid until the oven, where they melt and release steam, leaving flaky layers. Buttermilk is acidic, so it reacts with baking soda for extra lift, while baking powder supplies the rest.
plating: Spoon a portion into a warm shallow bowl so the fruit and juice settle first, then set a whole biscuit on top, golden side up. Place a scoop of vanilla ice cream beside the biscuit and spoon a little extra syrup over the fruit. A sprig of mint or a fresh peach slice finishes it.

pairing.drink: A late-harvest white or a peach-forward cocktail. Brennan’s own OBX, built on gin, peach and lemon, echoes the fruit.
pairing.brennans: OBX: Brennan's gin, peach and lemon cocktail, which echoes the fruit

variations: Georgia batter cobbler, the library’s version: pour a thin batter over melted butter, spoon the peaches on top without stirring and bake; the batter rises up around the fruit.
Blackberry and peach cobbler: replace a third of the peaches with blackberries.
Bourbon peach cobbler: add 1 tbsp (15 ml) bourbon to the fruit.
safety: Fruit fillings bubble far hotter than they look: let the cobbler cool at least 10 minutes before serving.
Lower peaches into boiling water with a slotted spoon, never by hand.

title: Smulpaj (Swedish Crumble Pie)
summary: Swedish crumble pie: sliced apples tossed with sugar and a little starch, covered with a loose crumble of oats, flour, butter and cardamom, and baked until the juices bubble up through the golden top. It takes rubbing in to a free crumble and adds the warmth of Swedish cardamom.
equipment: 8 or 9 inch (20 or 23 cm) pie dish or shallow baking dish
Mortar and pestle or spice grinder for cardamom
Peeler, corer and a sharp knife

ingredients.item: Tart, firm apples (Granny Smith, Braeburn or a mix)
ingredients.note: or 3 cups (450 g) blueberries or bilberries

ingredients.item: Granulated or light brown sugar for the crumble

ingredients.note: best from the seeds of about 8 green pods, freshly ground

ingredients.item: Vanilla ice cream or vanilla custard sauce

mise: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) with a rack in the centre.
Split the cardamom pods, tip out the black seeds and grind them finely. The scent of freshly ground cardamom is far stronger than bought powder.
Peel, quarter and core the apples and cut into slices 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
Cube the butter and keep it cold.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; grind cardamom; slice apples.
Toss the fruit straight into the dish.
Rub the crumble to rubble; scatter loosely over the fruit.
Bake 35 to 40 minutes until juices bubble through.
Cool 10 minutes.
Serve warm with vanilla sauce or ice cream.

steps.do: Toss the apple slices with the sugar, cornstarch and lemon juice directly in the pie dish and spread them in an even layer.
steps.look: Glossy, evenly coated slices, packed fairly level.
steps.mistake: Leaving the cornstarch in dry clumps, which turn into gluey lumps.
steps.fix: Toss until no white powder remains visible.

steps.do: In a bowl, mix the flour, oats, sugar, cardamom and salt. Add the cold butter and rub it in with your fingertips until the mixture forms a rough rubble with some pea-sized clumps and visible pebbles of butter.
steps.look: A loose, uneven crumble that holds in small clumps when squeezed.
steps.mistake: Rubbing it to fine sand or working it until it becomes a dough, which bakes into a hard lid.
steps.fix: If it turns pasty, chill 10 minutes and break it up again with your fingers.

steps.do: Scatter the crumble loosely over the fruit to the edges. Do not press it down.
steps.look: An even, loose, bumpy layer with a few gaps.
steps.mistake: Pressing the crumble flat, which makes it dense instead of crisp.
steps.fix: Air between the crumbs is what crisps them.

steps.do: Set the dish on the sheet pan and bake 35 to 40 minutes.
steps.look: A golden brown top, and thick juices bubbling up through the crumble at the edges and in the centre.
steps.mistake: Pulling it when the top is golden but the juices are not bubbling; the apples will be firm and the juice thin.
steps.fix: Bake until you see bubbles. Cover loosely with foil if the top browns too quickly.

steps.do: Test the apples by pushing a knife through the crumble into the centre.
steps.look: The knife slides in with no resistance.
steps.mistake: Serving with crunchy apples.
steps.fix: Bake 5 to 10 minutes more.

steps.do: Cool 10 minutes so the juices thicken.
steps.look: Juices settle into a glossy syrup.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the oven, when it is scalding.
steps.fix: Wait 10 minutes.

steps.do: Serve warm with vanilla custard sauce poured over or a scoop of vanilla ice cream.
steps.look: Crisp, fragrant crumble, soft tart apples, cold cream.
steps.mistake: Making it hours ahead and serving cold; the crumble softens.
steps.fix: Rewarm briefly in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 10 minutes.

science: Rubbing cold butter into flour coats some of the flour in fat and leaves small pebbles of butter. In the oven, those pebbles melt, fry the surrounding flour and oats and leave little air pockets, which is why a loose crumble turns crisp and an over-worked one turns hard. Oats add chew and a toasty flavour. Cardamom’s aroma comes from volatile oils inside its seeds, mostly a compound called cineole, which fade within weeks once ground, so fresh grinding gives a far stronger scent. The cornstarch thickens the apple juices once they reach a boil; that is why the bubbling at the edges signals doneness.
plating: Spoon a generous portion into a warm shallow bowl, crumble side up, letting some juice run out around it. Pour a ribbon of vanilla custard sauce across one side, or set a scoop of ice cream against it, and dust lightly with a pinch of ground cardamom mixed with sugar.

pairing.drink: A glass of sweet cider or an apple brandy. Brennan’s Apple Crumble cocktail, with bourbon, cider, maple and cinnamon, is the dessert in a glass.
pairing.brennans: Apple Crumble: Brennan's bourbon, cider, maple and cinnamon cocktail, the dessert in a glass

variations: Blåbärspaj: blueberries or bilberries in place of apples, with 1 tbsp (8 g) more cornstarch.
Rhubarb smulpaj in spring, with 2 tbsp (24 g) extra sugar.
Quick vaniljsås: warm 1 cup (240 ml) half milk, half cream with 2 yolks, 2 tbsp (24 g) sugar and vanilla, stirring, until it coats a spoon at 170 to 175°F (77 to 80°C), then strain.
safety: Fruit fillings bubble far hotter than they look: cool before serving, especially for children.
Keep your fingers clear when coring apples: cut them in quarters first and core each quarter flat on the board.

title: Key Lime Pie
summary: The Florida Keys pie: a pressed graham cracker crust filled with condensed milk, egg yolks and key lime juice, baked briefly until just set, chilled and topped with softly whipped cream. Acid thickening returns from the posset, now in a baked custard with a pressed crumb crust.
skills: a custard set by lime acid and a short bake
equipment: 7 inch (18 cm) pie plate or tart tin with a removable base
Zip-top bag and rolling pin, or a food processor, for the crumbs
Flat-bottomed glass or measuring cup for pressing
Microplane zester and a citrus juicer

ingredients.note: about half a 14 oz (397 g) can
from about 10 key limes, or 2 Persian limes, or bottled key lime juice
for zest and thin slices to garnish

mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the centre.
Crush the crackers into fine, even crumbs with no large pieces.
Zest the limes before juicing them. Juice and strain.
Separate the eggs; keep the whites for another use.

timeline.do: Make and bake the crust 10 minutes; cool slightly.
Lower the oven to 325°F (160°C). Whisk the filling.
Bake the filling 12 to 15 minutes until just set.
Cool 30 minutes on a rack.
Chill at least 3 to 4 hours.
Whip the cream; top, garnish and slice.

steps.do: Stir the crumbs, melted butter, sugar and salt together until the mixture looks like wet sand and holds together when squeezed.
steps.look: Evenly moistened crumbs with no dry patches.
steps.mistake: Too little butter, so the crust crumbles apart when sliced.
steps.fix: Add 1 tsp (5 g) more melted butter if it will not hold when squeezed.

steps.do: Tip into the pie plate and press firmly and evenly over the base and up the sides with the bottom of a glass, about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.look: A compact, even shell with a neat top edge.
steps.mistake: Leaving it thick in the corner where base meets side, which bakes hard.
steps.fix: Press the corner with your thumb to even it out.

steps.do: Bake the crust 10 minutes until fragrant and a shade darker. Cool on a rack for 10 minutes. Lower the oven to 325°F (160°C).
steps.look: A lightly toasted, firm crust that smells of biscuit.
steps.mistake: Overbaking, so it turns bitter and hard.
steps.fix: Ten minutes is enough; it bakes again with the filling.

steps.do: Whisk the yolks and lime zest for 1 minute until pale. Whisk in the condensed milk until smooth, then whisk in the lime juice.
steps.look: The mixture thickens noticeably in the bowl as the lime juice goes in: this is the acid setting the milk.
steps.mistake: Adding the juice to the yolks alone, before the condensed milk, which can curdle the yolks.
steps.fix: Follow the order: yolks, milk, then juice.

steps.do: Pour the filling into the warm crust and smooth the top. Bake 12 to 15 minutes.
steps.look: The edges are set and the centre wobbles slightly, like a jelly, when the plate is nudged. For the yolks to be fully safe, the centre should reach 160°F (71°C) on a probe.
steps.mistake: Baking until firm all over or browned, which makes it grainy and cracked.
steps.fix: Probe the centre; if short of 160°F (71°C), bake 2 to 3 minutes more and check again. Or use pasteurised yolks.

steps.do: Cool on the rack for 30 minutes, then refrigerate uncovered for 1 hour, then covered for at least 3 hours more.
steps.look: Firm, smooth filling that slices cleanly.
steps.mistake: Slicing before it is fully chilled, so it runs.
steps.fix: Give it the full chill; overnight is fine.

steps.do: Just before serving, whip the cream with the powdered sugar to soft peaks. Spread or pipe it over the pie, leaving a border of filling showing if you like.
steps.look: Soft, billowy cream that holds gentle peaks.
steps.mistake: Over-whipping, so the cream turns grainy.
steps.fix: Stop when it just holds a peak that curls at the tip.

steps.do: Grate a little lime zest over the cream and add thin lime slices. Cut with a sharp knife dipped in hot water and wiped between cuts.
steps.look: Clean slices showing a pale yellow filling and crisp crust. A true key lime pie is pale yellow, never green.
steps.mistake: Adding green colouring, which is not traditional.
steps.fix: Let the natural pale yellow speak for itself.

science: Key lime filling begins to set before it reaches the oven. Sweetened condensed milk is concentrated milk proteins and sugar; the citric acid in lime juice lowers the pH, and the milk proteins, mainly casein, lose their electrical charge and bond into a thickened network, the same chemistry as a lemon posset. The egg yolks add richness and, as they heat, their proteins coagulate around 150 to 160°F (66 to 71°C), firming the custard. A brief, gentle bake sets the yolks without curdling or browning. The crust is held together by melted butter, which solidifies as it cools and binds the crumbs.
plating: Cut a neat wedge and lay it on its side on a chilled plate so the layers show. Pipe or spoon a small rosette of extra whipped cream at the wide end, top it with a twist of lime slice, and grate fresh lime zest across the plate. A few crumbs of graham cracker scattered beside it add crunch.

pairing.drink: A demi-sec Champagne, whose sweetness meets the condensed milk and whose acidity matches the lime.
pairing.brennans: Laurent-Perrier ‘Harmony’ Demi Sec NV (375 ml): the demi-sec Champagne on the list, sweetness for condensed milk and acidity for lime

variations: Meringue top, the other Keys tradition: whip the 2 leftover whites with 1/4 cup (50 g) sugar and brown it in the oven.
Key lime tartlets in four 4 inch (10 cm) tins, baked 8 to 10 minutes.
Lemon or grapefruit pie with the same method.
safety: The filling contains egg yolks. Bake until the centre reaches 160°F (71°C), or use pasteurised eggs, especially for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or with a weakened immune system.
Keep the pie refrigerated and eat within 3 days.

title: Leche Flan
summary: The Filipino caramel custard: a dark dry caramel poured into moulds, then a rich custard of egg yolks, condensed and evaporated milk, strained twice and baked gently in a water bath until it barely trembles. It unites caramel and a gently set custard, the two pillars of classic desserts.
skills: baking or steaming gently in a water bath
equipment: Four 6 oz (180 ml) ramekins, or a small loaf tin or llanera mould
Small heavy stainless saucepan with a light interior (to judge caramel colour)
Mixing bowl and a spoon or whisk (stir, do not beat)
Roasting tin or deep baking dish for the water bath

ingredients.note: keep the whites for another use
about half a 14 oz (397 g) can
about half a 12 oz (354 ml) can

mise: Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C) with a rack in the centre.
Set the ramekins in the roasting tin, close to the stove, before you start the caramel: you must pour it the moment it is ready.
Boil a kettle of water for the water bath.
Separate the eggs, letting no white into the yolks.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; set out ramekins; boil the kettle.
Make the dry caramel; pour and tilt to coat the bases.
Stir the custard gently; strain twice; pour over set caramel.
Bake in a water bath 35 to 40 minutes.
Cool in the bath, then chill at least 6 hours or overnight.
Run a knife around, invert onto plates, let the caramel flow.

steps.do: Sprinkle the sugar in an even layer over the base of the dry saucepan. Set over medium heat and leave it until the edges begin to melt.
steps.look: The sugar at the edges turns to clear liquid, then pale gold.
steps.mistake: Stirring at the start, which makes the sugar clump and crystallise.
steps.fix: If clumps form, keep heating gently; they will melt. Swirl rather than stir.

steps.do: As the sugar melts, swirl the pan gently to move the dry sugar into the liquid. Keep heating until all the sugar has melted and turned a deep amber, like the colour of maple syrup or a copper coin.
steps.look: A clear, deep amber caramel with a rich, slightly bitter, toasty smell and a few wisps of smoke.
steps.mistake: Taking it too far, so it turns black and acrid; or stopping at pale gold, which gives a weak, sweet caramel.
steps.fix: If it smells burnt and acrid, it is too far; let it cool, soak the pan, start again. Never taste hot caramel.

steps.do: Immediately pour about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of caramel into each ramekin and tilt each quickly to coat the base. Work fast: it sets within seconds. Leave to harden.
steps.look: A glossy amber layer covering each base.
steps.mistake: Hesitating, so the caramel hardens in the pan.
steps.fix: If it hardens, warm the pan briefly to loosen it. To clean the pan, fill it with water and boil.

steps.do: In the bowl, gently stir the yolks, condensed milk, evaporated milk, vanilla and zest with a spoon until just evenly combined. Stir, do not whisk.
steps.look: A smooth, pale yellow liquid with almost no bubbles.
steps.mistake: Whisking vigorously, which beats in air; the bubbles become holes in the set custard.
steps.fix: If foam forms, let it stand 5 minutes and skim it off.

steps.do: Pour the custard through the fine sieve into a jug. Strain it a second time.
steps.look: A completely smooth custard with no strands of egg.
steps.mistake: Skipping the straining; chalazae and bits of white leave specks and holes.
steps.fix: Two strains give a glass-smooth flan.

steps.do: Pour the custard over the set caramel, dividing it evenly. Skim any bubbles from the surface. Cover each ramekin tightly with foil.
steps.look: Smooth surfaces with no bubbles; foil sealed tight.
steps.mistake: Leaving the ramekins uncovered, so a skin and bubbles form on top.
steps.fix: Cover tightly so condensation cannot drip in.

steps.do: Pull out the oven rack, set the roasting tin on it and pour hot water from the kettle into the tin to come halfway up the ramekins. Slide the rack back in gently. Bake 35 to 40 minutes.
steps.look: The water bath steams but does not boil.
steps.mistake: Splashing water into the ramekins, or letting the bath boil, which makes the custard bubbly and porous.
steps.fix: Pour carefully. If the bath bubbles, lower the oven to 300°F (150°C).

steps.do: Test by lifting the foil on one ramekin and nudging it: the edges should be set and the centre should wobble like a jelly. A probe in the centre reads 170 to 175°F (77 to 80°C).
steps.look: A uniform, gentle tremble; a knife near the centre comes out clean.
steps.mistake: Overbaking until it is firm and full of holes.
steps.fix: Pull them as soon as they tremble; they firm as they cool.

steps.do: Lift the ramekins out of the bath with tongs, cool on a rack for 30 minutes, then refrigerate at least 6 hours, ideally overnight.
steps.look: A cold, firm custard; the caramel has partly dissolved into a sauce beneath.
steps.mistake: Unmoulding while warm, so it breaks.
steps.fix: Give it the full chill.

steps.do: To unmould, run a thin knife around the edge of each flan. Set a plate upside down on top, hold both firmly and turn over. Lift the ramekin; the caramel sauce pours over.
steps.look: A glossy, golden flan with amber caramel flowing around it.
steps.mistake: Not loosening the edges, so it sticks.
steps.fix: If it resists, dip the base in hot water for 10 seconds and try again.

science: A dry caramel is pure sucrose heated with no water. Around 320°F (160°C) it melts; from about 340 to 360°F (170 to 180°C) the molecules break down and recombine into hundreds of compounds that turn it amber and give it bitter, toasty depth. In the fridge, moisture from the custard slowly dissolves the hardened caramel into a sauce. The custard sets because egg yolk proteins unfold and bond as they heat, starting near 150°F (66°C). A water bath keeps the custard’s surroundings at or below 212°F (100°C), so it heats slowly and evenly; without it, the edges overcook and water inside turns to steam, leaving holes.
plating: Turn the flan out onto a small, chilled plate with a raised rim so the caramel pools around it. Leave the surface clean and glossy. A few fine strips of lime zest on top, or a single fresh berry beside it, is all it needs.

pairing.drink: A cup of strong coffee, the classic Filipino partner, or a small glass of tawny port. New Orleans chicory coffee is a fine match for the bitter caramel.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory: Brennan's chicory coffee, bitter enough for the dark caramel

variations: Steamed leche flan: steam over gently simmering water, covered, for 20 to 25 minutes.
Crème caramel: whole eggs and fresh milk with sugar in place of yolks and canned milks, for a lighter custard.
Ube leche flan: a layer of purple yam halaya beneath the custard.
safety: Caramel is much hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Never touch or taste it, and keep children away.
Pour the water bath with the tin already on the oven rack, and lift it out only once cooled.
Keep the flan refrigerated and eat within 4 days.

title: Basque Burnt Cheesecake
summary: The crustless cheesecake of San Sebastián: a simple batter of cream cheese, sugar, eggs and cream baked very hot until the top is caramelised almost black while the centre still sways, then cooled into a creamy, slumping custard. A custard baked hot rather than gently shows how far the wobble can be pushed for a molten centre.
skills: very high heat for a caramelised top
equipment: 6 inch (15 cm) springform tin, at least 3 inches (7.5 cm) deep
Stand mixer with paddle, or a hand mixer and large bowl
Sheet pan to set the tin on

ingredients.note: completely at room temperature, about 3 hours out of the fridge

mise: Take the cream cheese, eggs and cream out of the fridge about 3 hours ahead. Cold cream cheese leaves lumps that no amount of beating removes.
Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) for at least 30 minutes, with a rack just below the centre.
Crumple two sheets of parchment, smooth them out and press them crossways into the tin, letting them stand at least 2 inches (5 cm) above the rim. The pleats and folds are part of the look.
Set the lined tin on the sheet pan.

timeline.do: Bring cream cheese, eggs and cream to room temperature.
Heat the oven 30 minutes; line the tin.
Beat the batter; strain into the tin.
Bake 30 to 40 minutes until the top is very dark and the centre sways.
Out of the oven; cool in the tin at room temperature at least 2 hours.
Slice at room temperature, or chill and bring back to room temperature for 1 hour.

steps.do: Beat the cream cheese and sugar on medium-low speed for 2 to 3 minutes, scraping the bowl, until completely smooth with no lumps.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, thick mixture.
steps.mistake: Using cold cream cheese, which stays lumpy.
steps.fix: If lumpy, set the bowl over warm water for a minute and beat again.

steps.do: Add the eggs one at a time, beating on low after each until incorporated and scraping the bowl.
steps.look: A smooth, loose batter.
steps.mistake: Beating on high, which whips in air; the cheesecake puffs, then cracks and sinks unevenly.
steps.fix: Keep the mixer on low.

steps.do: Beat in the cream, vanilla and salt on low. Sift the flour over and beat just until combined.
steps.look: A thin, pourable batter, much looser than a classic cheesecake batter.
steps.mistake: Assuming the thin batter is a mistake; it is right.
steps.fix: Trust it: the batter should pour like heavy cream.

steps.do: Pour the batter through the sieve into the lined tin.
steps.look: A silky, lump-free batter filling the tin about three quarters.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve, so lumps show in the cut slice.
steps.fix: Press any lumps through the sieve with the spatula.

steps.do: Bake on the sheet pan for 30 to 40 minutes.
steps.look: The cheesecake puffs well above the rim, the top turns deep mahogany and nearly black at the edges, and when the pan is nudged the centre 3 inches (7.5 cm) sways like a water bed.
steps.mistake: Pulling it when the top is only golden; the burnt caramel top is the flavour and the point.
steps.fix: Leave it in until the top is very dark; if the centre is set firm, it has gone too far, and will be dense rather than creamy.

steps.do: Check the centre with the thermometer if you are serving anyone vulnerable to food poisoning: the centre should reach 160°F (71°C), which gives a softer-set, still creamy middle. A very loose centre stays below that.
steps.look: A reading in the centre of the cheesecake.
steps.mistake: Serving a liquid centre to someone pregnant, elderly, very young or with a weakened immune system.
steps.fix: For a very loose centre, use pasteurised eggs. Otherwise bake until 160°F (71°C) in the centre.

steps.do: Set the tin on a rack and cool at room temperature in the tin for at least 2 hours.
steps.look: The cheesecake sinks dramatically into a crater with a collapsed centre: this is how it should look.
steps.mistake: Chilling it hot, or cutting it warm, when the centre is still liquid.
steps.fix: Let it cool fully at room temperature; it sets as it cools.

steps.do: Open the springform, lift the cheesecake out by the parchment and peel the paper away from the sides. Serve at room temperature for the creamiest texture, cut with a hot, wiped knife.
steps.look: A dark, caramelised top and edges, and a pale, creamy, custardy interior that slumps slightly on the plate.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the fridge, when it is firm and dense.
steps.fix: If chilled, rest it 1 hour at room temperature before slicing.

science: Most cheesecakes bake slowly in a water bath so the egg proteins set evenly without cracking. This one does the opposite. At 450°F (230°C), the sugars and milk proteins on the surface caramelise and brown deeply through the Maillard reaction, forming a bitter, toasty crust in place of a biscuit base. The heat penetrates from the outside in, so the edges set firm while the centre is still barely cooked when it comes out. As it cools, carryover heat continues to set the egg proteins, and the cream cheese firms as its fat cools, giving a soft, custardy centre. The puff and collapse come from steam that escapes as it cools.
plating: Cut a tall wedge and stand it on a plain plate with the dark top and creamy cut face both visible, leaving a little of the crinkled parchment edge if you like. Serve it unadorned, or with a spoon of fresh berries or a drizzle of sweet sherry on the side.

pairing.drink: A rich, sweet white such as Sauternes or a Barsac, whose honeyed acidity cuts the cheese and echoes the caramel top; in San Sebastián, Pedro Ximénez sherry is a favourite.
pairing.brennans: Château Climens Barsac Premier Cru Classé 2010: the Barsac on the list, honeyed acidity for cheese and burnt caramel

variations: Larger cake: double everything for a 9 inch (23 cm) tin and bake 50 to 60 minutes.
Chocolate Basque cheesecake: beat in 4 oz (115 g) melted dark chocolate with the cream.
With a little lemon zest and served with lightly sugared strawberries.
safety: A very loose centre may not reach 160°F (71°C), the temperature at which eggs are fully safe; use pasteurised eggs, or bake until the centre reaches 160°F (71°C), for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or immunocompromised.
The oven is at 450°F (230°C): use heavy mitts and pull the rack out rather than reaching in.
Refrigerate within 2 hours of cooling and eat within 4 days.
